Chapter 4 Energy principles and virtual work

4.7 Virtual forces and complementary energy

In sections 4.4 and 4.5 we wrote equilibrium with work. We imagined small displacements that the supports allow, and we left the forces as they really are. The work of the true forces on the imagined displacements gave the principle of virtual displacements (4.51), which holds exactly when the body is in equilibrium. The imagined displacements were a tool with which we expressed equilibrium. In this section we swap the roles. We imagine forces that are in equilibrium among themselves, and we leave the displacements true. Imagined forces of this kind are called virtual forces (virtualne sile) (EP §3.4.2, p. 131). We will see that the work of virtual forces on the true displacements gives an equation that does not speak about equilibrium but about geometry: about the strains coming from a single displacement field that respects the supports, that is, about the strains being compatible (definition 1.123).

The goal of the section is twofold. First, we want to compute the displacement of a chosen point of a structure without knowing all its displacements. So far we got the displacement of the joint \(C\) of the bracket by solving two equations for both components at once, in section 4.4 from the changes of the lengths of the bars, in section 4.6 from the smallest value of the energy. Virtual forces give each part of the displacement separately, with a single sum over the bars. Second, we want a new principle of a smallest value. The principle of section 4.6 compares displacement fields that respect the supports and picks from them the one in which the body is in equilibrium. The new principle will compare stress fields that satisfy equilibrium and pick from them the one whose strains fit together. With it we will compute the forces in a truss for which equilibrium alone does not determine them.

The model is the same as in sections 4.5 and 4.6. Let us list the assumptions and for each say where we use it.

  1. Strains and displacements are small. We compute all quantities on the shape of the body before loading, and the strain with the small strain tensor (definition 1.115). For a truss it follows that the change of length of a bar is the projection of the displacement of the joint onto the direction of the bar. We use this in all proofs of the section.
  2. The truss is idealized as in definition 4.4: frictionless pins, forces only at the joints and negligible weight of the bars. Each bar therefore carries only an axial force, which is constant along the bar (lemma 4.5). As in section 4.1, we do not treat buckling of compressed bars.
  3. For the work of virtual forces we need no property of the material. So the first two subsections hold for every material, except where we compute the changes of length of the bars from the axial forces. From subsection 4.7.3 on, however, the material is ideal elastic (definition 3.43) and linear elastic, with a strain energy density that is positive for every small strain that is not zero, as in section 4.6. We also assume that the stresses determine the strains uniquely, as Hooke's law (3.12) determines them for an isotropic material. For a bar of such a material the length changes by \(\Delta L = N L/(EA)\).
  4. The displacement and stress fields are continuously differentiable (definition 1.90) on an open set that contains the body together with its surface. The body is a box or made of boxes, and the parts of the surface with supports and with prescribed forces are made of whole rectangles on the faces of these boxes, as in section 4.5. We have proved the divergence theorem for such bodies, for bodies cut into pieces between graphs (section 4.2.12), and for bodies cut into pieces between graphs and curved boxes, like a ball and a thick spherical shell (section 4.3.7). For all these bodies the proofs hold with the same changes as for the principle of virtual displacements (end of section 4.5.4), and all the bodies of our examples are of this kind.

The route is as follows. First, on the bracket of two bars, we show what virtual forces are and what their work on the true displacements gives. From this we get a simple formula for the displacement of a joint in a chosen direction and with it both parts of the displacement of the joint \(C\). Then we write the same for a body of any shape. Next comes an energy that we build from the complementary strain energy density, and the principle of its smallest value. From it we derive how a displacement is obtained as a derivative of energy with respect to a force. At the end we add a third bar to the bracket, so that the forces in the bars can no longer be computed from equilibrium, and we find them from the smallest value of the energy.

4.7.1 Virtual forces on a truss

Let us return to the bracket of section 4.1 and repeat its setting (figure 4.81, left). The bracket lies in a vertical plane. The axis \(x\) points horizontally to the right, the axis \(y\) vertically up, and the origin is at the joint \(C = (0, 0, 0)\). The horizontal bar \(AC\) of length \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m is pinned to the wall at \(A = (-4, 0, 0)\) m, and the inclined bar \(BC\) of length \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m at \(B = (-4, 3, 0)\) m. A load hangs at the joint \(C\) and acts on it with the force \(\vek F = (0, -F, 0)\), \(F = 10\) kN. Both bars are of steel, with Young's modulus \(E = 196\) GPa and cross-section area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\). The unit vectors along the bars from the wall toward the joint are \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0)\). From the equilibrium of the pin \(C\) we got the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F = 16{,}67\) kN (tension) and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 F = -13{,}33\) kN (compression), and from them the changes of length

\[\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,L_{\mathrm{BC}}}{E\,A_{\mathrm{BC}}} = 4{,}252\ \text{mm} , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,L_{\mathrm{AC}}}{E\,A_{\mathrm{AC}}} = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} .\]

When the forces in all bars of a truss are known from equilibrium, we compute the elongations of the bars with Hooke's law. The question is how to get the displacements of the joints from the elongations of the bars (TIMO, PDF p. 250).

From history

In 1864 (EP, PDF p. 701), before Castigliano, Maxwell calculated the displacement of a truss joint with an imagined force (EP, PDF p. 3, TIMO, PDF p. 250), but he wrote the method in such an abstract form that engineers overlooked it (TIMO, PDF p. 250). It came into use only when Mohr, who did not know of Maxwell's work, found it again in 1874 (TIMO, PDF p. 250). Mohr looked for the relation between the elongation of one bar and the displacement of the joint. He removed the bar and replaced its action by two equal and opposite forces. He treated the remaining bars as rigid, so that he described the position of the system with a single number. On this system act an imagined force of 1 N at the joint, the reactions of the supports and the forces of the removed bar. These forces are in equilibrium, so their work in every imagined displacement is zero. From this equation he obtained the relation between the elongation of the bar and the displacement of the joint, and by summing over all bars the displacement due to the true loads (TIMO, PDF p. 250 and 251). His result coincides with Maxwell's (TIMO, PDF p. 251). The literature calls it the Maxwell-Mohr method (Maxwell-Mohrova metoda), and in this section we derive it with virtual forces (theorem 4.95).

Back to the truss with the load at joint \(C\) and to the question of how to get the displacement of this joint from the elongations of the bars. We denote the displacement of the joint \(C\) by \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\), as in sections 4.4 and 4.6: \(u\) is the horizontal part, positive to the right, and \(v\) the vertical part, positive upward. How is the displacement related to the two changes of length? In section 4.4 we derived for a virtual displacement of the joint that the elongation of a bar is, to first approximation, the projection of the displacement of the joint onto the direction of the bar. The derivation used only that the displacement is small and that the attached end does not move, so there we used it for the true displacement as well:

\[\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} .\]

We have left out the term \(\big(|\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}|^2 - (\vek n\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})^2\big)/(2L)\), the square of the part of the displacement perpendicular to the bar divided by \(2L\), where \(\vek n\) is the unit vector and \(L\) the length of the bar. For our bracket, whose joint moves by a good centimetre, this term is \(0{,}014\) mm for the bar \(AC\) and \(0{,}010\) mm for the bar \(BC\), less than a hundredth of the change of length of the bar. These are two equations for the two unknown components of the displacement in the plane, and in section 4.4 we solved them. We look, however, for a route that we can repeat for a body of any shape and that picks out of all the displacements only the one we are interested in.

Let us imagine that instead of the load another force, \(\delta\vek F\), of any size and direction, acts on the same bracket at \(C\) (figure 4.81, right). This force does not really exist, so it is a virtual force. The sign \(\delta\) in front of a quantity means a virtual quantity, as in section 4.4. We denote the axial forces that would balance the pin \(C\) under this force by \(\delta N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\delta N_{\mathrm{BC}}\). We write the equilibrium of the pin as for the load. A bar with axial force \(\delta N\) acts on the pin with the force \(-\delta N\,\vek n\), where \(\vek n\) is its unit vector from the wall toward \(C\) (section 4.1), so (figure 4.82)

\[\delta\vek F - \delta N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} - \delta N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek 0 .\]

The virtual state is just a set of forces that are in equilibrium. It says nothing about displacements, and no material needs to actually produce it. Now we have two states of the same bracket: the true one, in which we know the changes of length of the bars, and the virtual one, in which we know the forces. What do we get if we multiply the forces of the virtual state by the displacements of the true one?

Let us write the answer for a joint at which any number of bars meet, since a bracket with three bars also awaits us. We number the bars \(k = 1, \dots, m\).

Lemma 4.94 Virtual forces on a truss (virtualne sile na paličju)

Let \(m\) bars of a truss meet at the joint \(C\), with their other ends pinned to fixed supports, and let \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the unit vector along the bar \(k\) from the support toward \(C\), for \(k = 1, \dots, m\). Let the joint move by a small displacement \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\), and let the bar \(k\) lengthen by \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). Let \(\delta N_1, \dots, \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\) be numbers and \(\delta\vek F\) a vector such that

\[\delta N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \delta\vek F .\]

Then

\[\Delta L_1\,\delta N_1 + \dots + \Delta L_{\mathrm{m}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{m}} = \delta\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} . \tag{4.63}\]
Proof

We have to show that the scalar product of the virtual force with the true displacement splits into the products of the virtual axial forces with the true changes of length. We use only the equilibrium of the virtual forces and the properties of the scalar product.

  1. The vectors on the two sides of the equality in the assumption are equal, so their scalar products with \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) are equal too: \((\delta N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}})\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \delta\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\).
  2. The scalar product of a sum with a vector is the sum of the scalar products, and a number can be taken out of a scalar product (lemma 2.12). The left side is therefore \(\delta N_1\,(\vek n_1\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}) + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{m}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})\).
  3. By assumption \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\) for every \(k\). Inserting this gives (4.63).

Source: EP §4.4.2, example 4.4.1 (pp. 198-199), where the equality is written for a truss of two bars. The lemma and the proof are not from the source.

The proof is short, but it says something important. We multiplied the forces of one state by the displacements of another. We used only two things: that the virtual forces are in equilibrium and that the changes of length of the bars come from a single displacement of the joint. We did not use the material. EP calls the left side of (4.63) the internal complementary virtual work (notranje komplementarno virtualno delo), and the right side with the opposite sign the external complementary virtual work, so that their sum is zero (EP (4.4.3)-(4.4.5), pp. 196-197). Let us compare with the principle of virtual displacements for the truss of section 4.4, where we multiplied the true axial forces by the virtual elongations. There we took the scalar product of the equilibrium of the true forces with a virtual displacement, here of the equilibrium of the virtual forces with the true displacement. The computation is the same, the roles are swapped.

How do we use the lemma for a displacement? We choose the virtual force so that the component of the displacement we are looking for remains on the right. If \(\delta\vek F\) points in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek d\), the right side is the size of the force times the component of the displacement in the direction \(\vek d\). The left side contains only the changes of length, which we know from the true axial forces, and the virtual axial forces, which we get from equilibrium.

Theorem 4.95 Unit dummy load method (metoda enotske sile)

Let the truss be as in lemma 4.94 on virtual forces on a truss, with bars of a linear elastic material. Let the bar \(k\) have length \(L_{\mathrm{k}}\), cross-section area \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and Young's modulus \(E_{\mathrm{k}}\), and under the true load of the joint the axial force \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\), which makes it lengthen by \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\). Let the joint move by \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) in this, so that \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) for every \(k\). Let \(\vek d\) be a unit vector and let \(\hat N_1, \dots, \hat N_{\mathrm{m}}\) be numbers such that

\[\hat N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \hat N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek d .\]

Then the component of the displacement of the joint \(C\) in the direction \(\vek d\) is

\[\vek d\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{E_{\mathrm{k}}\,A_{\mathrm{k}}} . \tag{4.64}\]
Proof

We have to show that the equality of lemma 4.94, for a suitably chosen virtual force, is (4.64).

  1. Let \(\delta F > 0\) be any number with the unit newton. We take the virtual force \(\delta\vek F = \delta F\,\vek d\) and the virtual axial forces \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} = \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta F\). Multiplying the equality in the assumption by \(\delta F\) gives \(\delta N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \delta\vek F\), the equilibrium the lemma requires.
  2. By lemma 4.94 therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\,\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta F = \delta F\,(\vek d\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})\).
  3. The number \(\delta F\) is not zero, so we divide both sides by it and get \(\vek d\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  4. We insert \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\) and get (4.64).

Source: EP (4.4.11), (4.4.12) (p. 198), where the method is written for a body, and example 4.4.1 (pp. 198-199) for a truss of two bars.

What are the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\)? Let us multiply their equation by \(1\) N. It then says that the axial forces \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}} \cdot 1\ \text{N}\) balance a force of \(1\) N in the direction \(\vek d\). When equilibrium alone determines the axial forces, as for the bracket of two bars, the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the axial forces that a force of size \(1\) N in the direction \(\vek d\) would cause in the bars, divided by \(1\) N, and they have no unit. The theorem, however, asks of them only that they balance the unit force, which we shall use in subsection 4.7.5. Hence the name of the method: the virtual force has size one. The hat over the letter \(N\) reminds us of this unit force. The formula (4.64) says that each bar contributes to the displacement its change of length, multiplied by how strongly a unit force in the direction of the displacement sought would load it. For the bracket of two bars we get the true axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) from equilibrium alone, so we need nothing else for the displacement. In the proof we used the linearity of the material only in step 4. The equality of step 3, \(\vek d\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\), holds for bars of any material, only the changes of length must then be computed by the law of that material, as EP does for bars with a nonlinear relation between stress and strain (EP example 4.4.1, pp. 199-200). For large displacements, however, the equation \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) no longer holds, and with it the method fails.

Let us apply the method to our bracket (figure 4.83).

  1. The horizontal part of the displacement. We take \(\vek d = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 0, 0)\). The equation for the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}}\) reads \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(1, 0, 0) + \hat N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) = (1, 0, 0)\). The component \(y\) gives \(-\tfrac35\,\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), so \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), and the component \(x\) gives \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1\). By (4.64)
    \[u = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 1 \cdot \Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} + 0 \cdot \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} .\]
    The joint moves \(2{,}721\) mm to the left.
  2. The vertical part of the displacement. We take \(\vek d = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, -1, 0)\), in the direction of the load. The component \(y\) of the equation gives \(-\tfrac35\,\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -1\), so \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53\), and the component \(x\) gives \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} + \tfrac45 \cdot \tfrac53 = 0\), so \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43\). By (4.64)
    \[\begin{aligned} -v &= -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -\tfrac43 \cdot (-2{,}721\ \text{mm}) + \tfrac53 \cdot 4{,}252\ \text{mm} \\ &= 3{,}628\ \text{mm} + 7{,}086\ \text{mm} = 10{,}71\ \text{mm} . \end{aligned}\]
    The joint drops by \(10{,}71\) mm.

The displacement of the joint is therefore \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (-2721, -10\,714, 0)\) µm. The component \(v\) equals \(-2U/F = -10{,}71\) mm of section 4.1. There we got it by assuming that all the work of the load is stored in the bars, here from equilibrium, geometry and the material law, with which we computed the two changes of length. The agreement is no accident. For \(\vek d\) in the direction of the load the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the true axial forces divided by \(F\), and the right side of (4.64) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}/F\), which by section 4.1 is twice the energy \(U = 53{,}57\) J divided by \(F\).

There are two patterns in the numbers, which we explain. Why does the horizontal part of the displacement depend only on the bar \(AC\)? A horizontal force at \(C\) loads only the bar \(AC\), because the bar \(BC\) cannot give a horizontal force without also giving a vertical one, and nothing balances that. Geometrically the same is even more direct: the bar \(AC\) is horizontal, so by the equation \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) its change of length is just the horizontal part of the displacement. And where do the contributions \(3{,}628\) mm and \(7{,}086\) mm to the vertical part come from, and why with the factors \(\tfrac43\) and \(\tfrac53\)? Let us split the displacement into two parts, as in figure 4.84.

  1. Let only the bar \(AC\) shorten, while the bar \(BC\) keeps its length. Then the joint moves perpendicular to the bar \(BC\), because \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\), and horizontally by \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = -2{,}721\) mm. Perpendicular to \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0)\) is the direction \((3, 4, 0)\), in which the vertical part is \(\tfrac43\) times the horizontal one. The joint therefore drops by \(\tfrac43 \cdot 2{,}721\) mm \(= 3{,}628\) mm. When the bar \(AC\) shortens, it pulls the joint toward the wall, and the bar \(BC\) turns it about \(B\) downward as it does.
  2. Let only the bar \(BC\) lengthen, while the bar \(AC\) keeps its length. Then the joint moves perpendicular to the bar \(AC\), that is, vertically. The elongation of the bar \(BC\) is the projection of this displacement onto \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\), whose vertical component is \(-\tfrac35\), so the vertical displacement is \(\tfrac53\) times the elongation, \(\tfrac53 \cdot 4{,}252\) mm \(= 7{,}086\) mm down.

To first approximation the two changes of length are linear functions of the displacement, so the displacements of the two parts add up to the true displacement, \((-2721, -3628, 0) + (0, -7086, 0) = (-2721, -10\,714, 0)\) in micrometres. The factors \(\tfrac43\) and \(\tfrac53\) are exactly the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}}\) in size. The unit dummy load method thus does by itself the geometric computation that we would otherwise have to draw.

The same displacement of the joint, \(u = -2{,}721\) mm and \(v = -10{,}71\) mm, we obtained in section 4.4 from the changes of the lengths of the bars, and in section 4.6 as the lowest point of the total potential energy, a function of the two components of the displacement. Both times we solved two equations for both components at once, here each component of the displacement is a sum of two terms. The advantage shows in large structures. We proved the lemma and the theorem only for a truss with one free joint. For a truss with several free joints we write the equilibrium of each joint separately, take its scalar product with the displacement of that joint and add the equalities. Each bar appears twice in the sum, once at each end and with opposite unit vectors, and together it gives the product of its virtual axial force and its change of length. We do not write this computation out here, and EP states the unit dummy load method for every elastic structure (EP §4.4.2, p. 198). If we want the displacement of one point of a truss with a hundred bars, the unit dummy load method needs only the axial forces due to the load and due to one unit force, while the search for the smallest value needs all displacements of all joints at once. When equilibrium does not determine the axial forces, the true axial forces must be found first, which we show in subsection 4.7.5.

4.7.2 Virtual forces on a body

Now let us write the same for a body of any shape. We repeat the setting of section 4.5. Before loading the body occupies the set of points \(V\) with the surface \(S\). On the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface there are supports that prescribe the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\). On the remaining part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) with which the surroundings act on the body is prescribed, and a body force with density \(\vek b\) acts on the matter. In the truss the virtual forces were axial forces in the bars that balanced the pin. In a body the role of the axial forces is taken by a virtual stress field, and the role of the equilibrium of the pin by the equilibrium equations. Which fields do we allow?

Definition 4.96 Statically admissible virtual stress field (statično dopustno virtualno polje napetosti)

Let the body occupy the set of points \(V\) before loading, and let its surface be divided into the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), where the displacement is prescribed, and the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), where the force per unit area is prescribed. A virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\), which assigns to every point of the body a matrix of nine numbers \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), is statically admissible (statično dopustno) if:

  1. the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuously differentiable (definition 1.90) on an open set that contains the body together with its surface,
  2. at every point of the body the field is symmetric, \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\),
  3. at every point of the body it satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force,
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} = 0 ,\]
    and the same with the second index \(y\) and \(z\) instead of \(x\),
  4. at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\), where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal.

Source: EP (4.4.1), (4.4.2) (p. 196), where a statically admissible field also allows a virtual body force, SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139).

The word statically says that the conditions speak only about forces, not about displacements, just as the word kinematically in an admissible virtual displacement spoke only about displacements. We explain each condition by what we will use it for. Symmetry and the equilibrium equations are the two conditions of equilibrium from chapter 2, written for the virtual field. In the proof they will remove the volume integral with the derivatives of the stress. There is no body force because we will multiply the virtual field by the true displacement and we do not want the true displacement at every point of the body to appear in the equation. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the virtual traction vector is zero, which means that there are no virtual loads there. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), however, the virtual traction vector \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) may be anything. These are the virtual forces of the supports, and their work on the prescribed displacements will remain in the equation. Continuous differentiability is needed for the divergence theorem.

A simple example is a steel bar welded with both ends between two walls, as in figure 4.85. The faces at the walls are \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the mantle is \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). Let the axis \(x\) point along the bar. The field in which \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the same number everywhere and all other components are zero is statically admissible. The components are constant, so they are continuously differentiable and all their derivatives are zero, which satisfies the equilibrium equations. The field is symmetric. On the mantle the normal has the component \(x\) equal to zero, so \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = (\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0) = \vek 0\). On the faces at the walls the virtual traction vectors are \(\pm\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), virtual forces of the walls that pull the bar apart.

In the truss the work of the virtual forces on the true displacements was the sum of the products of the virtual axial forces and the true changes of length. In a body the strain of a small piece of the body takes the place of the change of length of a bar, and an integral over the body the place of the sum over the bars. The proof will be short, because we did all the analysis in section 4.5. Lemma 4.81 on internal virtual work through the surface does not speak about the physical meaning of its fields. It holds for every symmetric continuously differentiable field of nine numbers and every continuously differentiable vector field. There we used it with the true stress and a virtual displacement, here we use it with a virtual stress and the true displacement.

Theorem 4.97 Principle of virtual forces (načelo virtualnih sil)

Let the body before loading occupy the set of points \(V\), which is a box or made of boxes, and let its surface be divided into the parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), which do not overlap and are made of whole rectangles on the faces of these boxes. Let \(\vek u\) be a displacement field that is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body together with its surface and equals the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), and let

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\]

be the components of its small strain tensor, where the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) and \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). Then for every statically admissible virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) (definition 4.96)

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.65}\]

where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal of the surface.

Proof

We have to show that the integral on the left turns into the work of the virtual forces of the supports on the prescribed displacements. We use lemma 4.81 with the roles of the fields swapped, then the conditions of the definition of a statically admissible field and the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\).

  1. The components of the field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) are by definition 4.96, items 1 and 2, continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body with its surface, and symmetric at every point. The components of the field \(\vek u\) are by assumption continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body with its surface. The intersection of the two sets is an open set containing the body with its surface. By lemma 4.81, in which we take \(\delta\ten\sigma\) in place of the stress and \(\vek u\) in place of the virtual displacement, therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)\,u_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
    The numbers that the lemma calls the virtual strain are here the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek u\), because we compute them with the same formula from the same partial derivatives. The traction vector of the lemma is here \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\).
  2. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\) for \(j = x\) equals \(\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial x + \partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial y + \partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}/\partial z\), which by definition 4.96, item 3, is zero at every point of the body. The same for \(j = y\) and \(j = z\). The function under the second volume integral is therefore zero at every point, and this integral is zero.
  3. The surface is made of the rectangles of the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and the rectangles of the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), which do not overlap, so the surface integral is the sum of the integrals over \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) (section 4.2).
  4. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\) by definition 4.96, item 4, so there \((\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek u = 0\), and the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero.
  5. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) we have \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) by assumption, so the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) equals \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  6. The order of the factors in the product \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) does not matter. Inserting steps 2 to 5 into step 1 gives (4.65).

Source: EP (4.4.5)-(4.4.8) (p. 197), SADD (6.6.1), (6.6.2) (PDF p. 139). The sources state the theorem for a general body, with a virtual body force and with virtual forces on the whole surface. The proof with lemma 4.81 is not from the sources.

The proof showed where the equation comes from. The lemma moved the derivative from the true displacement to the virtual stress. The equilibrium equations of the virtual field cancelled the volume integral with the derivatives of the stress, and on the surface the work of the virtual forces of the supports on the prescribed displacements remained. The lemma needed the symmetry of the virtual field to write the strain instead of the partial derivatives of the displacement.

What is not in the theorem? There is no relation between stress and strain. The virtual stress only has to be in equilibrium, and the strains have to come from one displacement field that equals the prescribed one on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). The theorem therefore holds for every material, also for one that deforms permanently, and for strains that are not caused by stress, such as the strains caused by temperature of section 3.3. It does not hold, however, for large strains, where we may not identify the shapes before and after loading and may not compute the strains with the small strain tensor. The principle is a statement about geometry. EP writes that the strains and displacements are compatible and consistent with the supports exactly when the equation holds for every statically admissible field (EP (4.4.5), p. 197). We proved the direction we will need: the equation follows from compatibility. EP derives the converse by obtaining from the equation the conditions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\) in the body and \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) (EP (4.4.9), (4.4.10), p. 198). We prove the converse for a body in subsections 4.7.10 and 4.7.11: if the equation holds for every statically admissible virtual stress field, the strains satisfy the compatibility equations of section 1.18, and in a connected and simply connected body, a box for instance, we also get from them a displacement field that fits a support in one piece, or the walls between which a bar is welded. How the equation demands compatibility, however, we will see on a truss in subsection 4.7.5.

How is the theorem related to the lemma on virtual forces on a truss? Take a bar of length \(L\) and cross-section area \(A\) in which the virtual stress \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \delta N/A\) is constant and the true strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \Delta L/L\) is constant too, while the other components are zero. The integral on the left side of (4.65) is then the product of the two numbers and the volume of the bar,

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \frac{\Delta L}{L} \cdot \frac{\delta N}{A} \cdot A L = \Delta L\,\delta N ,\]

which is the term of the bar in (4.63). In the truss the virtual force \(\delta\vek F\) acted at the joint where the true load acts too. For a body we get such a case if on a part of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), instead of \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\), we require the virtual traction vector to equal a chosen virtual force per unit area \(\delta\bar{\vek t}\). Then only step 4 of the proof changes. The integral over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is no longer zero but \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \delta\bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\), and the equation becomes

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \delta\bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]

as SADD (6.6.2) (PDF p. 139) writes it. If the virtual force is spread over a small patch of the surface and has the total size \(1\) N in a chosen direction, the first term on the right is approximately the component of the displacement of the patch in this direction, multiplied by \(1\) N, and we get the unit dummy load method for a body (EP (4.4.12), p. 198). We will use it for bars in bending in chapter 5.

4.7.3 Complementary energy

We obtained the principle of minimum total potential energy of section 4.6 by taking as the virtual displacement the difference of two admissible displacement fields. We do the same with virtual forces: as the virtual stress field we take the difference of two stress fields that satisfy equilibrium. For this we need an energy written with forces, not with displacements.

We met the complementary strain energy density \(w^*\) in section 3.6 (definition 3.49). In a uniaxial state it is the area between the curve of stress against strain and the stress axis, and for an ideal elastic material it depends only on the final state. For a linear elastic material it equals the strain energy density in value, \(w^* = w = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (section 3.6), but we write it as a function of the stresses. For an isotropic material we express it with Hooke's law.

  1. In the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) there are three terms with equal indices. We insert into them the strains of the left column of (3.12): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 - 2\nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}})\big)/E\). Each product of two different normal stresses appears twice, once from each of the two rows, hence the factor \(2\nu\).
  2. The six terms with different indices form three pairs, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\). By the symmetry of stress and strain and by the right column of (3.12) this pair is \(2\,(1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2/E\).
  3. We add and divide by \(2\):
    \[\begin{aligned} w^* &= \frac{1}{2E}\Big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 - 2\nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}) \\ &\qquad + 2\,(1 + \nu)\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}^2)\Big) . \end{aligned}\]

This is how EP (3.2.23) (p. 108) writes it. In a bar only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N/A\) is not zero, so \(w^* = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2/(2E) = N^2/(2EA^2)\), the same as the strain energy density.

Definition 4.98 Complementary energy (komplementarna energija)

Let the body be of an ideal elastic material whose complementary strain energy density \(w^*\) at every point is a function of the components of stress at that point, and let the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) be prescribed on the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface. For a stress field \(\ten\sigma\) in the body the complementary energy (komplementarna energija) of the body is the number

\[U^*(\ten\sigma) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} w^*\,\mathrm{d}V ,\]

where \(w^*\) at every point is computed from the components of the field \(\ten\sigma\) at that point, and the total complementary energy (celotna komplementarna energija) is the number

\[\Pi^*(\ten\sigma) = U^*(\ten\sigma) - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.66}\]

where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal of the surface.

Source: EP (3.2.10) (p. 106) for \(U^*\) and (4.5.3) (p. 204) for \(\Pi^*\), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 140).

What kind of object is \(\Pi^*\)? Like the total potential energy, it is a function whose input is a whole field and whose output is one number in joules, except that the input here is a stress field, not a displacement field. The first term is the complementary energy the body would have with the field \(\ten\sigma\). The second term is the work that the forces of the supports \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) would do on the prescribed displacements if they were constant all the time, with a minus sign. In the total potential energy the second term had known forces on unknown displacements, here it has the known displacements of the supports on the unknown forces of the supports. For fixed supports, \(\bar{\vek u} = \vek 0\), the second term is zero, and \(\Pi^* = U^*\).

In a truss the stress in each bar is constant, so the complementary energy of the bar \(k\) is the product of the density and the volume, \(A_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}} \cdot N_{\mathrm{k}}^2/(2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}^2) = N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 L_{\mathrm{k}}/(2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\). The complementary energy of the truss is the sum over the bars. For our bracket with the fixed pins \(A\) and \(B\)

\[\Pi^* = U^* = \frac{N_{\mathrm{AC}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2E\,A_{\mathrm{AC}}} + \frac{N_{\mathrm{BC}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{BC}}}{2E\,A_{\mathrm{BC}}} = 18{,}14\ \text{J} + 35{,}43\ \text{J} = 53{,}57\ \text{J} ,\]

equal to the strain energy \(U\) of section 4.1. They are equal because the material is linear. The difference lies in what the input is: \(U^*\) is written with the axial forces, while the energy for a displacement field we wrote with the displacements in section 4.6 (EP, p. 107).

Which stress fields will we compare? Those that could be the true one if we look only at equilibrium.

Definition 4.99 Statically admissible stress field (statično dopustno polje napetosti)

Let the body be as in definition 4.96, with the prescribed force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and the body force with density \(\vek b\). A stress field \(\ten\sigma\) is statically admissible (statično dopustno) if its components are continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body together with its surface, if at every point of the body it is symmetric and satisfies the equilibrium equations (2.31) with the body force \(\vek b\), and if at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) it gives \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\).

Source: EP (4.4.1), (4.4.2) (p. 196) and p. 205, SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139).

A statically admissible field fulfils all conditions of equilibrium, but not necessarily those of geometry. The strains that the material law would assign to it need not come from any displacement field. The difference of two statically admissible fields, however, is a statically admissible virtual stress field. When we subtract the equilibrium equations of the two fields, the body force cancels, and on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the difference of the traction vectors is \(\bar{\vek t} - \bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\). We will need this in the proof.

Theorem 4.100 Principle of minimum complementary energy (načelo najmanjše komplementarne energije)

Let the body be as in theorem 4.97 on the principle of virtual forces, of an ideal elastic and linear elastic material whose strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero, and in which the stresses determine the strains uniquely. Let \(\vek u\) be a displacement field that is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body with its surface and equals the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), and let the stress field \(\ten\sigma\) that the material law assigns to the strains of the field \(\vek u\) be statically admissible. Then for every statically admissible stress field \(\tilde{\ten\sigma}\) to which the material law assigns small strains:

  1. the difference of the total complementary energies is the complementary energy of the difference of the fields,
    \[\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) - \Pi^*(\ten\sigma) = U^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma} - \ten\sigma) \ge 0 , \tag{4.67}\]
  2. equality \(\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = \Pi^*(\ten\sigma)\) holds only if \(\tilde{\ten\sigma} = \ten\sigma\) at every point of the body.

The strain that the material law assigns to the difference \(\tilde{\ten\sigma} - \ten\sigma\) need not be small, so we compute \(U^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma} - \ten\sigma)\) with the density \(w^*\) that at every point is the value of the polynomial \(w\) from lemma 4.90 at this strain.

Proof

We have to show that the difference of the energies splits into an expression from the principle of virtual forces, which is zero, and the complementary energy of the difference of the fields, which is not negative. We follow the proof of theorem 4.91 on the principle of minimum total potential energy with the roles swapped.

1. The difference of the energies.

  1. Let \(\ten\tau = \tilde{\ten\sigma} - \ten\sigma\). The components of both fields are continuously differentiable on open sets containing the body with its surface, so the components of the field \(\ten\tau\) are continuously differentiable on their intersection. Both fields are symmetric, so \(\ten\tau\) is symmetric too. When we subtract the equilibrium equations of the field \(\ten\sigma\) from those of the field \(\tilde{\ten\sigma}\), \(\vek b\) cancels, and since the partial derivative of a difference is the difference of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.81), the field \(\ten\tau\) satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\ten\tau\,\vek n = \tilde{\ten\sigma}\,\vek n - \ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t} - \bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\) (lemma 1.97). The field \(\ten\tau\) is therefore a statically admissible virtual stress field.
  2. At every point of the body let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be the strains of the field \(\vek u\), which by assumption belong to the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the strains that the material law assigns to the stresses \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The material law is linear, so the stresses \(\tilde\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} + \tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\) have the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are small by assumption 1 at the start of the section, the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) by the assumption of the theorem. Their difference \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) need not be small, since two components below the bound in absolute value can differ by almost twice the bound. Lemma 4.90 does not need smallness, because it only expands the polynomial \(w\).
  3. For a linear elastic and ideal elastic material the complementary strain energy density equals in value the strain energy density in the same state (section 3.6), \(w^* = w\). Therefore at every point \(w^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\})\), \(w^*(\ten\sigma) = w(\{\varepsilon\})\) and \(w^*(\ten\tau) = w(\{\eta\})\), where the braces, as in section 4.6, denote the Voigt column of the six strain components. When \(\{\eta\}\) is not a small strain, the last equality is the definition of the density \(w^*(\ten\tau)\) from the theorem.
  4. By lemma 4.90 on the energy density of a sum of strains, \(w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\}) = w(\{\varepsilon\}) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} + w(\{\eta\})\).
  5. We use the same lemma with the two strains swapped, \(\{\eta\}\) in the first place and \(\{\varepsilon\}\) in the second. The stresses belonging to \(\{\eta\}\) are \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so \(w(\{\eta\} + \{\varepsilon\}) = w(\{\eta\}) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + w(\{\varepsilon\})\). The left sides of steps 4 and 5 are equal, because the sum of the strains is the same, so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  6. From steps 3, 4 and 5, at every point
    \[w^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = w^*(\ten\sigma) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{ij}} + w^*(\ten\tau) .\]
  7. We integrate over the body and use the linearity of the integral over a body (section 4.2):
    \[U^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = U^*(\ten\sigma) + \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V + U^*(\ten\tau) .\]
  8. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) we have \(\tilde{\ten\sigma}\,\vek n = \ten\sigma\,\vek n + \ten\tau\,\vek n\) (lemma 1.97), the scalar product is distributive (lemma 2.12), and by linearity the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) in (4.66) splits into an integral with \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) and an integral with \(\ten\tau\,\vek n\).
  9. We insert steps 7 and 8 into equation (4.66), which defines the total complementary energy, and arrange the terms:
    \[\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = \Pi^*(\ten\sigma) + \Big[ \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\ten\tau\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A \Big] + U^*(\ten\tau) .\]
  10. The field \(\vek u\) satisfies the assumptions of theorem 4.97, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the components of its small strain tensor, and \(\ten\tau\) is by step 1 a statically admissible virtual stress field. By the principle of virtual forces the expression in square brackets is therefore zero, and \(\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) - \Pi^*(\ten\sigma) = U^*(\ten\tau)\).
  11. By step 8 of item 1 of the proof of theorem 4.91 the polynomial \(w\) is zero at the zero column and positive at every other column, also when that column is not a small strain. There we used only that the energy density is positive at small strains, which this theorem assumes too. So \(w^*(\ten\tau) = w(\{\eta\}) \ge 0\) at every point. The integral of a non-negative function is not negative (section 4.2), so \(U^*(\ten\tau) \ge 0\).

2. Equality.

  1. Let \(\Pi^*(\tilde{\ten\sigma}) = \Pi^*(\ten\sigma)\). By item 1 then \(U^*(\ten\tau) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} g\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\), where \(g = w(\{\eta\})\) at every point of the body.
  2. The function \(g\) is continuous and non-negative. The components \(\tau_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuous, the strains \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are by the linear material law sums of their multiples, and \(g\) is a sum of products of the components \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) with constant numbers, so it is continuous by corollary 1.69 on the continuity of sums, products and polynomials in space. It is non-negative by step 11 of item 1.
  3. A continuous non-negative function whose integral over the body is zero is zero at every point of the body. We showed this in steps 3 to 7 of item 2 of the proof of theorem 4.91: if it were positive at some interior point, it would be positive on a small cube around it and the integral would be positive, and on the surface it is zero by continuity. Therefore \(g = 0\) at every point of the body.
  4. By step 11 of item 1 the polynomial \(w\) is positive at every column that is not zero, so \(\{\eta\}\) is the zero strain at every point. The stresses are linear functions of the strains, so the stress \(\ten\tau\) belonging to zero strain is zero, and \(\tilde{\ten\sigma} = \ten\sigma\) at every point.

Source: EP §4.5.1, (4.5.2)-(4.5.12) (pp. 204-205), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 140), which states the principle and leaves the proof to other books. EP proves the minimum with the compliance coefficients and their symmetry. The proof with lemma 4.90 and item 2 are not from the sources.

What does the theorem say? Among all stress fields that fulfil equilibrium and the prescribed forces, the true field has the smallest total complementary energy. Every other field has a larger one, larger by exactly the complementary energy of the difference. The proof showed where this comes from. The mixed term of the expanded energy, the work of the difference of stresses on the true strains, cancels against the work of the difference of the forces of the supports on the prescribed displacements, because the true strains are compatible and the difference is a statically admissible virtual field. Only the energy of the difference remains, and it is not negative because the material is stable.

Let us compare the two principles of a smallest value. The principle of minimum total potential energy searches among displacement fields that respect the supports, that is, among fields that fulfil the conditions of geometry, and picks from them the one that fulfils equilibrium as well. The principle of minimum complementary energy searches among stress fields that fulfil equilibrium and picks from them the one that fulfils the conditions of geometry as well, that is, whose strains come from a displacement field that equals the prescribed one on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). For the true state all three sets of equations must hold: equilibrium, geometry and the material law. Each principle requires two of them in advance and finds the third as the condition for the smallest value.

Where does the theorem stop holding? We used the linearity of the material in steps 2 to 5, where we added strains and used lemma 4.90. SADD states the principle also for nonlinear elastic materials (SADD, PDF p. 140), but the proof needs more about the shape of the function \(w^*\) than we have developed. For large strains the principle of virtual forces does not hold in this form, because we may not compute the strains with the small strain tensor. Item 2 says moreover that the true stress field is unique. For displacement fields we got less in section 4.6: the true displacement field is unique only up to a difference without strain, for example a rigid motion, which does not change the stresses.

For a truss with fixed supports we translate the theorem directly. The proof is shorter, because sums over the bars take the place of integrals.

Corollary 4.101 Minimum complementary energy of a truss (najmanjša komplementarna energija paličja)

Let the truss be as in lemma 4.94 on virtual forces on a truss, with the joint \(C\) on which the force \(\vek P\) acts, and with bars of a linear elastic material with lengths \(L_{\mathrm{k}}\), cross-section areas \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and Young's moduli \(E_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\). Let \(N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{m}}\) be the true axial forces, that is, forces that balance the joint, \(N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek P\), and whose changes of length \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\) come from one displacement of the joint, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). Let \(N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) be any axial forces that also balance the joint. Then

\[U^*(N_1 + \delta N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{m}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}) - U^*(N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{m}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} \ge 0 ,\]

where \(U^*(N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{m}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 L_{\mathrm{k}}/(2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\), and equality holds only if all \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are zero.

Proof

We have to show that the mixed terms of the expanded squares cancel. For this we use the lemma on virtual forces on a truss with zero virtual force.

  1. Subtracting the equilibrium of the true forces from the equilibrium of the other ones gives \(\delta N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \delta N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = \vek P - \vek P = \vek 0\). The numbers \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are therefore virtual axial forces in equilibrium with the virtual force \(\delta\vek F = \vek 0\).
  2. We expand the square of the sum as the product \((N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}})(N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}}) = N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 + 2N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). The difference of the energies is therefore
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{2N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} ,\]
    where in the first sum we used \(N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}) = \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. By lemma 4.94 with \(\delta\vek F = \vek 0\) we have \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\,\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek 0\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\).
  4. The second sum remains. Each of its terms is a square times the positive number \(L_{\mathrm{k}}/(2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}})\), so it is not negative and is zero only for \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\). The sum is therefore non-negative and is zero only if all \(\delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are zero.

Source: EP §4.5.1 (pp. 204-205) for a body and example 4.5.1 (p. 207) for a truss of two bars. The corollary and the proof are not from the source.

For the bracket of two bars the corollary says nothing new. The equilibrium of the joint is two equations for two axial forces, so \(\delta N_{\mathrm{AC}} = \delta N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\) is the only solution of the equation of step 1, and there are no other axial forces that would balance the joint. There is nothing to compare. The corollary becomes important for a truss with more bars than equilibrium can determine. Before we treat one, let us derive from the complementary energy a formula for a displacement.

4.7.4 Displacement as a derivative of the complementary energy

In section 4.6 we got a force from the strain energy written with displacements, as the derivative of the energy with respect to a displacement. The complementary energy is written with the axial forces, which depend on the load. What is its derivative with respect to a force? For a single bar with the force \(F\) at its end \(U^* = F^2 L/(2EA)\), and its derivative with respect to \(F\) is \(F L/(EA)\), the elongation of the bar, the displacement of the end in the direction of the force. For a truss the same holds.

Castigliano differentiated the energy written with forces with respect to a force. In doing so he always assumed that displacements are linear functions of the forces (TIMO, PDF p. 229). Such a derivative gives the displacement of the point where the force acts, in the direction of the force, as for the bar above. For a pair of equal and opposite forces acting along the same line it gives the change of the distance between their points of application, and for a pair of forces with a moment the angle of rotation (TIMO, PDF p. 230-231 and 250). For cases where displacements are not linear functions of the forces, Engesser, whom we met in section 3.6.7, showed that the derivatives of his complementary energy with respect to independent forces always give displacements (TIMO, PDF p. 231).

Theorem 4.102 Castigliano's second theorem (drugi Castiglianov izrek)

Let the truss be as in theorem 4.95 on the unit dummy load method. Let the force \(F_1\,\vek d_1 + F_2\,\vek d_2\) act on the joint \(C\), where \(\vek d_1\) and \(\vek d_2\) are unit vectors of two chosen directions and \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) are numbers with the unit newton. Let the axial forces be written as functions \(N_{\mathrm{k}}(F_1, F_2)\), each of which is the sum of a constant number and multiples of the numbers \(F_1\) and \(F_2\). For all values of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) let them balance the joint,

\[N_1(F_1, F_2)\,\vek n_1 + \dots + N_{\mathrm{m}}(F_1, F_2)\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}} = F_1\,\vek d_1 + F_2\,\vek d_2 ,\]

and for the actual values of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) let them equal the true axial forces. Let

\[U^*(F_1, F_2) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}(F_1, F_2)^2\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} .\]

Then for the actual values of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) the component of the displacement of the joint in the direction \(\vek d_1\) is

\[\vek d_1\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \frac{\partial U^*}{\partial F_1} , \tag{4.68}\]

and likewise \(\vek d_2\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \partial U^*/\partial F_2\).

Proof

We have to show that the derivative of the energy with respect to \(F_1\) is the right side of the formula (4.64) for suitably chosen numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\). For this we obtain the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) as the derivatives of the axial forces with respect to \(F_1\).

  1. Let \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}} = \partial N_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial F_1\). The function \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the sum of a constant number and multiples of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), so \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a number that does not depend on \(F_1\) and \(F_2\): a multiple of \(F_1\) has its factor as derivative, and the other terms are constant for constant \(F_2\) and have derivative zero (lemma 1.81).
  2. The equilibrium equation holds for all \(F_1\) and \(F_2\). Each of its components is therefore an equality of two functions of the variable \(F_1\) for constant \(F_2\), and the derivatives of the two sides are equal. By the rules for differentiating a sum and a multiple, the derivative of the left side is \(\hat N_1\,\vek n_1 + \dots + \hat N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{m}}\), that of the right side \(\vek d_1\). The numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) therefore satisfy the equation of theorem 4.95 with the direction \(\vek d = \vek d_1\).
  3. By the product rule (lemma 1.81) the derivative of the square \(N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) with respect to \(F_1\) is \(2\,N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\). Therefore
    \[\frac{\partial U^*}{\partial F_1} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \frac{2\,N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{2E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} .\]
  4. For the actual values of \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) the \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the true axial forces, so by theorem 4.95 the right side of step 3 equals \(\vek d_1\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). This proves (4.68). For \(F_2\) we repeat steps 1 to 4 with derivatives with respect to \(F_2\).

Source: EP §4.5.2, (4.5.13) (p. 206), where the theorem is derived from the principle of minimum complementary energy for every elastic structure, and example 4.5.1 (p. 207) for a truss of two bars. The proof with the unit dummy load method is not from the source.

Why does the derivative of energy with respect to a force give a displacement? Figure 4.86 shows the mechanism for a structure with a single force \(F\) whose point of application moves by \(\Delta\) in the direction of the force. The complementary energy is the area between the line of force against displacement and the force axis. When we raise the force by a small number \(h\), the area grows by a strip whose height is \(h\) and whose width is the displacement \(\Delta\), and by a small triangle at the end of the strip. The increase of energy is therefore almost \(h\,\Delta\), and when we send the quotient of the increase of energy and the increase of force \(h\) toward zero, we get \(\Delta\). The theorem holds also for nonlinear elastic structures, where the line becomes a curve (EP, p. 206), but we proved it only for linear bars.

Let us apply the theorem to the bracket of two bars. The load points down, so we take \(\vek d_1 = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(F_1 = F\). For the horizontal part of the displacement we also need a force in the horizontal direction, which does not really exist. We add it in our minds, with \(\vek d_2 = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and size \(F_2 = Q\). After differentiating we set \(Q = 0\). Books call such a force a fictitious load (navidezna sila) (EP, p. 206). Why do we need it? The energy written only with \(F\) does not tell how it would change if we added a horizontal force, and by the theorem that is exactly the horizontal displacement.

  1. The equilibrium of the joint under the force \((Q, -F, 0)\) reads \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(1, 0, 0) + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) = (Q, -F, 0)\). The component \(y\) gives \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F\), the component \(x\) gives \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = Q - \tfrac43 F\). Both are sums of multiples of \(F\) and \(Q\), as the theorem requires.
  2. The complementary energy is
    \[U^*(F, Q) = \frac{(Q - \tfrac43 F)^2 \cdot 4\ \text{m} + (\tfrac53 F)^2 \cdot 5\ \text{m}}{2EA} ,\]
    where \(EA = 196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\) N.
  3. The derivative with respect to \(F\) at \(Q = 0\) is
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial U^*}{\partial F} &= \frac{2\,(-\tfrac43 F)(-\tfrac43) \cdot 4\ \text{m} + 2\,(\tfrac53 F)\,\tfrac53 \cdot 5\ \text{m}}{2EA} = \frac{(\tfrac{64}{9} + \tfrac{125}{9})\,F \cdot 1\ \text{m}}{EA} \\ &= \frac{21\ \text{m} \cdot F}{EA} = 10{,}71\ \text{mm} . \end{aligned}\]
  4. The derivative with respect to \(Q\) at \(Q = 0\) is
    \[\frac{\partial U^*}{\partial Q} = \frac{2\,(-\tfrac43 F) \cdot 4\ \text{m}}{2EA} = -\frac{16\ \text{m} \cdot F}{3EA} = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} .\]

The joint drops by \(10{,}71\) mm and moves \(2{,}721\) mm to the left, as we got with the unit dummy load method. The numbers \(\tfrac{64}{9}\) and \(\tfrac{125}{9}\) in step 3 are the contributions of the bars \(AC\) and \(BC\), \(\tfrac43 \cdot \tfrac43 \cdot 4\) and \(\tfrac53 \cdot \tfrac53 \cdot 5\), which we saw in figure 4.84 as \(3{,}628\) mm and \(7{,}086\) mm. The unit dummy load method and Castigliano's second theorem are the same computation written in two ways. The derivative \(\partial N_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial F_1\) is exactly the axial force due to a unit force in the direction \(\vek d_1\), divided by \(1\) N.

Let us compare with Castigliano's first theorem of section 4.6. There a force was the derivative of the strain energy, written with displacements, with respect to a displacement. Here a displacement is the derivative of the complementary energy, written with forces, with respect to a force. For a linear material the two energies are equal in value, but since they are written with different variables, they have different derivatives (EP, p. 206).

4.7.5 A statically indeterminate truss

Let us add a third bar to the bracket (figure 4.87). Below the joint \(C\) we place a vertical bar \(CD\) standing on the floor, with the pin \(D = (0, -3, 0)\) m. It has length \(L_{\mathrm{CD}} = 3\) m, is of steel with the same cross section \(A_{\mathrm{CD}} = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\), and its unit vector from the floor toward the joint is \(\vek n_{\mathrm{CD}} = (0, 1, 0)\). Everything else stays: the bars \(AC\) and \(BC\), the pins on the wall and the load \(F = 10\) kN at \(C\). Here too we do not treat buckling.

The equilibrium of the pin \(C\) is now

\[N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(1, 0, 0) + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) + N_{\mathrm{CD}}\,(0, 1, 0) = (0, -F, 0) .\]

These are two equations, for the components \(x\) and \(y\), for three unknown axial forces. Equilibrium does not determine them. Such a truss is called a statically indeterminate truss (statično nedoločeno paličje). EP calls a structure indeterminate when there are more unknown forces than equations of equilibrium (EP, p. 116), and FELIPPA calls a truss whose forces follow from equilibrium statically determinate (FELIPPA, PDF p. 54). The word statically says that we do not get the forces from statics, from the conditions of equilibrium alone. The truss of two bars was statically determinate. Let us choose the axial force in the post as the unknown and denote it by \(X = N_{\mathrm{CD}}\). For a chosen \(X\) the two equations give the other two forces.

  1. Component \(y\): \(-\tfrac35\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} + X = -F\), so \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53\,(F + X)\).
  2. Component \(x\): \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} + \tfrac45\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), so \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43\,(F + X)\).

Every number \(X\) thus gives axial forces that balance the joint. For \(X = 0\) the post carries nothing, and the forces in the bars \(AC\) and \(BC\) are the same as for the bracket with two bars. For \(X = -F\) the post carries the whole load and the bars on the wall carry nothing. Which number \(X\) is the true one? Equilibrium cannot tell. Geometry must tell: the changes of length of all three bars must come from one displacement of the joint.

From history

Engineers looked for the answer in several ways. In 1858 the Italian military engineer L. F. Menabrea proposed that the forces in the redundant bars should be such that the strain energy is smallest, and this is the principle of least work (načelo najmanjšega dela). He gave no acceptable proof (TIMO, PDF p. 228). Clebsch showed that if we take the displacements of the joints as unknowns, we can always write as many equations as there are unknowns (TIMO, PDF p. 255). The next step was made by Maxwell, who in 1864 (EP, PDF p. 701) used the imagined force, which we will meet in section 4.7.1, also for trusses with redundant bars (EP, PDF p. 3, TIMO, PDF p. 255). We remove the redundant bar and replace its action by an unknown force, as we did above (TIMO, PDF p. 255). Castigliano offered his own way. He removed the redundant bars and replaced them by forces. The force that replaces a bar pulls the two joints together, so the derivative of the energy of the remaining truss with respect to it tells by how much the joints approach. The negative of this derivative is therefore the increase of the distance between the two joints that the bar connected (TIMO, PDF p. 231). This increase must equal the elongation of the bar in the original truss. The elongation of a bar, however, is the derivative of its energy with respect to the force in it, so the derivative of the total energy with respect to the force is zero (TIMO, PDF p. 231). EP states that Castigliano published this form of the method in 1875 but attributed the idea to Menabrea (EP, PDF p. 3). Maxwell's way, which Mohr found again, has been used by structural engineers ever since (section 4.7.1, TIMO, PDF p. 250, 255). Below we use the principle of least work and prove it with corollary 4.101.

Back to the question which number \(X\) is the true one. By corollary 4.101 the true force in the post has the smallest complementary energy of all, because every other choice of \(X\) gives axial forces that also balance the joint and are therefore of the form \(N_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta N_{\mathrm{k}}\) of the corollary. Let us write the energy as a function of \(X\) and find its smallest value.

  1. We insert the axial forces into the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 L_{\mathrm{k}}/(2EA)\) and factor out \((F + X)^2\):
    \[\begin{aligned} U^*(X) &= \frac{\tfrac{16}{9}\,(F + X)^2 \cdot 4\ \text{m} + \tfrac{25}{9}\,(F + X)^2 \cdot 5\ \text{m} + X^2 \cdot 3\ \text{m}}{2EA} \\ &= \frac{21\ \text{m} \cdot (F + X)^2 + 3\ \text{m} \cdot X^2}{2EA} , \end{aligned}\]
    where we added \(\tfrac{64}{9} + \tfrac{125}{9} = \tfrac{189}{9} = 21\).
  2. We expand the square \((F + X)^2\) as the product \((F + X)(F + X) = F^2 + 2FX + X^2\) and order the numerator by powers of \(X\): \(21\,(F + X)^2 + 3X^2 = 24X^2 + 42FX + 21F^2\), where each term is multiplied by 1 m.
  3. We complete the square, as for the bar with a load in section 4.6. The expanded square \(24\,(X + \tfrac78 F)^2\) is \(24X^2 + 42FX + \tfrac{147}{8}F^2\), because \(2 \cdot 24 \cdot \tfrac78 = 42\) and \(24 \cdot \tfrac{49}{64} = \tfrac{147}{8}\). Therefore \(24X^2 + 42FX + 21F^2 = 24\,(X + \tfrac78 F)^2 + \tfrac{21}{8}F^2\), and
    \[U^*(X) = \frac{24\ \text{m} \cdot \big(X + \tfrac78 F\big)^2 + \tfrac{21}{8}\ \text{m} \cdot F^2}{2EA} .\]
  4. The first term of the numerator is never negative and is zero only at \(X = -\tfrac78 F\). The second term does not depend on \(X\). The energy is therefore smallest at \(X = -\tfrac78 F = -8{,}75\) kN and only there (figure 4.88), and its smallest value is \(\tfrac{21}{16}\ \text{m} \cdot F^2/(EA) = 6{,}696\) J. At \(X = 0\) it would be \(53{,}57\) J.
  5. The true force in the post is therefore \(N_{\mathrm{CD}} = -8{,}75\) kN, the post is compressed. The other two axial forces are \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 \cdot \tfrac18\,F = 2{,}083\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 \cdot \tfrac18\,F = -1{,}667\) kN.

The post carries seven eighths of the load, the bars on the wall only one eighth. Why so unequally? Let us look at the two paths along which the load reaches the supports as two springs that the joint \(C\) connects (figure 4.89). The bracket of two bars drops under a vertical force \(P\) at \(C\) by \(21\ \text{m} \cdot P/(EA)\), as we computed above, and the post shortens under the force \(P\) by \(3\ \text{m} \cdot P/(EA)\). Under the same force the post therefore moves seven times less, or for the same displacement it needs a seven times larger force. The ratio of a force to the displacement it causes is called the stiffness (togost), and the stiffness of the post \(EA/(3\ \text{m})\) is seven times the stiffness of the bracket \(EA/(21\ \text{m})\). The two paths must have the same vertical displacement at \(C\), because they meet at the same joint. The post acts on the joint only vertically, because it carries only an axial force along its axis (lemma 4.5), and it does not resist a horizontal displacement of the joint, because the length of the vertical bar does not change, to first approximation, under a small horizontal displacement. Let the bracket carry the vertical force \(P_1\) and the post \(P_2\). The displacements of the two paths are \(21\ \text{m} \cdot P_1/(EA)\) and \(3\ \text{m} \cdot P_2/(EA)\). Then \(P_1 + P_2 = F\) and \(21\,P_1 = 3\,P_2\), so \(P_2 = 7\,P_1\), \(P_1 = F/8\) and \(P_2 = 7F/8\). The load divides in the ratio of the stiffnesses: the stiffer path carries more.

What does it mean that the energy is smallest? At the lowest point of the parabola the derivative of \(U^*\) with respect to \(X\) is zero. From the form in step 3 this derivative is \(48\ \text{m} \cdot (X + \tfrac78 F)/(2EA)\), which is indeed zero at \(X = -\tfrac78 F\). Let us write the same derivative with the changes of length. By the product rule (lemma 1.81) the derivative of the term of the bar \(k\) is \((N_{\mathrm{k}} L_{\mathrm{k}}/(EA))\,\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{k}}/\mathrm{d}X = \Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{k}}/\mathrm{d}X\), and the derivatives of the axial forces from the formulas above are \(\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{AC}}/\mathrm{d}X = -\tfrac43\), \(\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{BC}}/\mathrm{d}X = \tfrac53\) and \(\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{CD}}/\mathrm{d}X = 1\). The condition that the derivative is zero therefore reads

\[-\tfrac43\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} + \tfrac53\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} + \Delta L_{\mathrm{CD}} = 0 .\]

The numbers \(-\tfrac43\), \(\tfrac53\) and \(1\) are virtual axial forces that balance the joint without any force at it, since \(-\tfrac43\,(1, 0, 0) + \tfrac53 \cdot \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) + (0, 1, 0) = (0, 0, 0)\). Such axial forces are called self-equilibrating (samouravnotežene) (EP, p. 196). The condition is therefore the equation (4.63) with zero virtual force.

What does the condition say? By the unit dummy load method the first two terms are the downward vertical displacement of the joint that the bars on the wall allow, since \(-\tfrac43\) and \(\tfrac53\) are the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}}\) of subsection 4.7.1. The third term is the change of length of the post, which is negative when it shortens, and is therefore the downward vertical displacement of the joint that the post allows, with the opposite sign. The condition thus demands that the two paths give the joint the same vertical displacement. At \(X = 0\) we do not fulfil it: the bars on the wall would let the joint drop by \(10{,}71\) mm, while the unloaded post would leave it in place. If the changes of length come from one displacement of the joint, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\), the condition holds for every displacement: with \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\) the left side is \(-\tfrac43\,u + \tfrac53 \cdot \tfrac15\,(4u - 3v) + v = -\tfrac43\,u + \tfrac43\,u - v + v = 0\). With two bars the ends can always meet again when the bars turn about the pins (figure 4.11). A third bar, however, adds a third requirement for the same two components of the displacement. Three changes of length come from two components of the displacement, so they must satisfy one equation. This is the compatibility condition of the truss, just as the compatibility equations of section 1.18 are the condition that six strains come from three components of the displacement. The principle of minimum complementary energy picked from all distributions of forces in equilibrium the one whose changes of length fit together.

Let us check the result in another way too, by searching for the smallest total potential energy of section 4.6, where the unknowns are displacements. Let the displacement of the joint be \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\). The changes of length of the bars are \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = u\), \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4u - 3v)\) and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{CD}} = v\), the energy of a bar with the change of length \(\Delta L\) is \(EA\,\Delta L^2/(2L)\), and the work of the load is \(\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -F v\). The total potential energy is therefore

\[\Pi(u, v) = \frac{EA}{2}\Big(\frac{u^2}{4\ \text{m}} + \frac{(4u - 3v)^2}{25 \cdot 5\ \text{m}} + \frac{v^2}{3\ \text{m}}\Big) + F v .\]

By section 4.6 the true displacement is the lowest point of the function \(\Pi\), so its partial derivatives with respect to \(u\) and \(v\) are zero there (lemma 1.82, applied to each variable separately). The solution of these two equations, computed with SymPy, is \(u = -\tfrac23 \cdot 1\ \text{m} \cdot F/(EA) = -0{,}3401\) mm and \(v = -\tfrac{21}{8} \cdot 1\ \text{m} \cdot F/(EA) = -1{,}339\) mm. From it the changes of length are \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = -0{,}3401\) mm, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0{,}5315\) mm and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{CD}} = -1{,}339\) mm, and the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{k}} = EA\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{k}}/L_{\mathrm{k}}\) are \(-1{,}667\) kN, \(2{,}083\) kN and \(-8{,}75\) kN, the same as with the minimum complementary energy. The check also shows that axial forces that balance the joint and whose changes of length come from one displacement really exist, which corollary 4.101 assumed. The joint drops by only \(1{,}339\) mm, eight times less than without the post, because the bracket with the post is eight times stiffer than the bracket without it: the stiffnesses \(EA/(21\ \text{m})\) and \(EA/(3\ \text{m})\) add up to \(8\,EA/(21\ \text{m})\).

Finally, one more peculiarity of the unit dummy load method. Theorem 4.95 asks of the numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) only that they balance the unit force, not that they be the axial forces that the unit force would really cause. In a statically indeterminate truss there are many such sets of numbers, and each gives the same displacement.
