For the vertical displacement let us simply take the numbers of the bracket without the post, \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43\), \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{CD}} = 0\), which balance the downward unit force without the post carrying anything. With the true changes of length (4.64) gives

\[\begin{aligned} -v &= -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -\tfrac43 \cdot (-0{,}3401\ \text{mm}) + \tfrac53 \cdot 0{,}5315\ \text{mm} + 0 \cdot (-1{,}339\ \text{mm}) \\ &= 0{,}4535\ \text{mm} + 0{,}8858\ \text{mm} = 1{,}339\ \text{mm} , \end{aligned}\]

which is the true displacement. The numbers \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) only have to balance the unit force, but the changes of length have to be the true ones. In a statically indeterminate truss we get the true changes of length only once we know the true axial forces, which was the task of the minimum complementary energy.

4.7.6 Mathematics: a field from its partial derivatives

For the bracket with the post of subsection 4.7.5, the equation of virtual forces demanded that the changes of length of all three bars come from one single displacement of the joint. For a body the same demand takes the form of the six compatibility equations (1.68) of section 1.18. There we proved that the strains of every displacement field with continuous partial derivatives up to third order satisfy them (theorem 1.127). The converse, that in a simply connected body the equations imply that a displacement field exists, we only stated, as theorem 1.137. We postponed it because it needs the summation of small changes of the displacement along a path through the body, for which we had no integral then. Now we have it. In this subsection and the next we prove the theorem for bodies in which every point can be joined to one chosen point by a straight segment that does not leave the body. All the bodies we have computed with so far are of this kind: the box, the strip and the round bar. For all bodies whose interior points form a connected and simply connected set we prove it in subsections 4.7.8 and 4.7.9.

How we will find the displacement we described in words already in section 1.18.5. We choose a point \(P_0\) and the displacement zero there. The displacement at another point \(P\) we get by walking from \(P_0\) to \(P\) in short steps and adding up the changes of the displacement. By theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step, the change of the component \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) over a short step is almost exactly the sum of the products of the partial derivatives \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) with the components of the step. The strains, however, do not give us all partial derivatives of the displacement, only the symmetric part of the displacement gradient. The antisymmetric part, the rotation of the material (definition 1.116), we must first find ourselves, and in the same way, because by lemma 1.128 its partial derivatives are determined by the derivatives of the strains. Both times we solve the same problem. Three functions of three variables are given, \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\), and we look for a function \(\varphi\) whose partial derivatives are exactly these three functions:

\[\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x} = w_{\mathrm{x}} , \qquad \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y} = w_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z} = w_{\mathrm{z}} .\]

From history

When given functions are the derivatives of a single function is a question that arose in the 18th century in the study of differential equations. Alexis Claude Clairaut, Alexis Fontaine des Bertins and Euler noticed at the same time criteria of integrability, and Euler also showed how to use them to find integrating factors (CAJORI, PDF p. 255). In 1747, in the vibrating string that we met in section 1.3.1, d'Alembert had a function \(u\) of the place \(x\) and the time \(t\) with partial derivatives \(p\) with respect to \(x\) and \(q\) with respect to \(t\). From the equation of the string he concluded that the derivative of \(p\) with respect to \(x\) and the derivative of \(q\) with respect to \(t\) are equal, so there is also a function \(v\) whose derivatives with respect to \(t\) and \(x\) are \(p\) and \(q\) (BALL, PDF p. 404). The conclusion is a criterion for two functions: on a region without holes they are the derivatives with respect to \(t\) and \(x\) of one function if the derivative of the first with respect to \(x\) equals the derivative of the second with respect to \(t\). For three functions we prove it below, in theorem 4.104.

In 1773, in computing the attraction of celestial bodies, Lagrange took a sum in which the mass of each piece of a body is divided by the distance of the piece from a chosen point (CAJORI, PDF p. 488, BALL, PDF p. 434). He showed that from the value of this sum at a point outside the body the attraction in any direction follows at once (BALL, PDF p. 435). Why? By Newton's law of gravitation the attraction of a piece of mass \(m\) at distance \(r\) is proportional to \(m/r^2\), and we hide the constant of proportionality in the unit of mass. If the point approaches the piece by a small step \(s\), the quotient \(m/r\) grows by about \(m\,s/r^2\), that is by \(s\) times the attraction of the piece. The attraction in a given direction is therefore the rate at which the sum grows as the point moves in that direction, and the attraction of all pieces together is the sum of these rates. The three components of the attraction are thus three functions, and the sum is a function that has exactly these three functions for its derivatives, like the function \(\varphi\) in our problem.

In 1784 Laplace took over the idea from Lagrange and showed that the sum at a point outside the body satisfies an equation in which its second derivatives appear (BALL, PDF p. 441). Green, whom we met at the divergence theorem (section 4.2.5), was the first to use it outside celestial mechanics, for electric and magnetic phenomena, and gave it the name potential (potencial) (CAJORI, PDF p. 488, BALL, PDF p. 441). Hamilton called it the force function, and Gauss around 1840 achieved its general acceptance (CAJORI, PDF p. 488).

This subsection solves the problem we posed before the story: for given functions \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) to find a function \(\varphi\) with these three partial derivatives. First we name the sets in which we can add up along segments from one point, then we show how a function changes along a segment, and finally we write down the solution.

We will add up along straight segments that all start at the same point \(P_0\). Each such segment must lie in the body entirely, otherwise the summation would need strains at points where there is no material. We write the points of the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) with one single number. Let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). The point \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) is the point \(P_0\) at \(t = 0\), the point \(P\) at \(t = 1\), the midpoint of the segment at \(t = \tfrac12\), and as \(t\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\), the point runs through the whole segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\).

Definition 4.103 Star-shaped set (zvezdasta množica)

Let \(D\) be a set of points of space and \(P_0\) a point of \(D\). The set \(D\) is star-shaped with respect to the point \(P_0\) (zvezdasta glede na točko \(P_0\)) if for every point \(P\) of \(D\) the whole segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) lies in \(D\), that is, if the point \(P_0 + t\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) is in \(D\) for every number \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). A set is star-shaped (zvezdasta) if it is star-shaped with respect to at least one of its points. A set that is star-shaped with respect to every one of its points is convex (konveksna).

Source: LEBL2 Def. 9.3.5 (PDF p. 86), for open sets in \(\mathbb R^n\). Convex set: LEBL2 §8.1.4 (PDF p. 16).

The definition is written for the points of our space. In a space with \(n\) coordinates it reads the same (LEBL2, PDF p. 86). The name says what such a set looks like: from the point \(P_0\) we see every one of its points, as from the centre of a star we see all its arms. Figure 4.90 shows four bodies drawn as plane shapes, as if they were thin plates.

  1. The box \([a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) is convex. Let \(P_0\) and \(P\) be two of its points. The coordinate \(x\) of the point \(P_0 + t\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) is \(x_{\mathrm{P}_0} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{P}} - x_{\mathrm{P}_0}) = (1 - t)\,x_{\mathrm{P}_0} + t\,x_{\mathrm{P}}\). Let \(m\) be the smaller and \(M\) the larger of the numbers \(x_{\mathrm{P}_0}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\). For \(0 \le t \le 1\) the factors \(1 - t\) and \(t\) are not negative, so the number \((1 - t)\,x_{\mathrm{P}_0} + t\,x_{\mathrm{P}}\) lies between \((1 - t)\,m + t\,m = m\) and \((1 - t)\,M + t\,M = M\), hence in \([a_1, b_1]\). The same holds for the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The same computation with strict inequalities shows that the set of interior points of a box is convex too.
  2. The ball with centre \(C\) and radius \(R\), the set of points \(Q\) with \(|CQ| < R\), is convex by lemma 1.129 on the distance to the points of a segment, item 3: if \(P_0\) and \(P\) are at a distance less than \(R\) from \(C\), then for \(0 \le t \le 1\) the point \(P_0 + t\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) is also at a distance less than \(R\) from \(C\). A cylinder is convex too, for example a round bar with axis \(x\), radius \(r\) and length \(L\). The coordinate \(x\) stays between \(0\) and \(L\) as for the box, and the distance from the axis stays below \(r\) by the same lemma, used on the points \((0, y_{\mathrm{P}_0}, z_{\mathrm{P}_0})\), \((0, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(C = O\). We used both already in section 1.18.4, when we checked which bodies are connected.
  3. The L-shaped bracket (figure 4.90, top right) is made of two boxes, a horizontal and a vertical leg, which overlap in the corner square. Let \(P_0\) be a point of the corner square and \(P\) any point of the bracket. The point \(P\) lies in one of the legs, and \(P_0\) lies in the same leg too. The leg is a box, so by item 1 the whole segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) lies in that leg. The bracket is therefore star-shaped with respect to every point of the corner square. It is not convex, however: the segment from the point \(P_1\) at the end of the horizontal leg to the top of the vertical leg passes the corner and leaves the bracket.
  4. The ring with centre \(O\) is not star-shaped (figure 4.90, bottom left). Let \(P_0\) be any point of the ring and \(P\) the point with \(\overrightarrow{OP} = -\overrightarrow{OP_0}\), which is as far from \(O\) as \(P_0\) and therefore also in the ring. The midpoint of the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) has the vector from \(O\) equal to \(\overrightarrow{OP_0} + \tfrac12\,(\overrightarrow{OP} - \overrightarrow{OP_0}) = \tfrac12\,(\overrightarrow{OP_0} + \overrightarrow{OP}) = \vek 0\), so the midpoint is the point \(O\), which is in the hole. From no point of the ring do we see all its points. The same holds for the cut ring of section 1.18.5 (figure 4.90, bottom right). If the point \(P\) falls on the cut, we take a point right next to it, and the segment passes right next to \(O\), still through the hole.

The cut ring shows that a star-shaped set is a special case of a simply connected one (definition 1.136). Every star-shaped set is simply connected. We shrink a closed curve in it to the point \(P_0\) by moving every one of its points \(Q\) at the same time to the point \(P_0 + (1 - \lambda)\,\overrightarrow{P_0 Q}\), as the number \(\lambda\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\). These points lie on the segment from \(P_0\) to \(Q\), which is entirely in the set, the curve does not tear on the way, and at \(\lambda = 1\) it is gathered entirely at \(P_0\). We prove this precisely in subsection 4.7.8. The converse does not hold, because the cut ring is simply connected, which we prove in the same subsection, but not star-shaped. LEBL2 chooses star-shaped sets for the same reason as we do: the proof is simpler, and it writes the function sought with one single formula (LEBL2, PDF p. 86).

For the summation along a segment we will need two properties of continuously differentiable functions (definition 1.90). The first is that they are continuous, that is, without jumps (lemma 1.91 of section 1.15.6).

The second property tells how fast the function changes as we move along a segment. We proved it in lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment. If \(f\) is continuously differentiable on an open set \(D\) and the point \(P + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), then the function \(g(t) = f(P + t\,\vek d)\) is differentiable at \(t\) with the derivative \(g'(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}}\), and this derivative is continuous at \(t\). A step \(h\,\vek d\) along the segment therefore changes the function by almost \(h\) times the sum of the products of the partial derivatives with the components of the vector \(\vek d\).

Now let us write the solution of the problem from the start of the subsection. Suppose for a moment that a function \(\varphi\) with the partial derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) exists and that \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\). Then \(\varphi(P)\) is the change of the function from \(P_0\) to \(P\). We cut the segment into short pieces. On the piece from \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) to \(P_0 + (t + \Delta t)\,\vek d\) the step is \(\Delta t\,\vek d\) with the components \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta t\), and by the theorem on the change of a field \(\varphi\) changes on it by about \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta t\) (figure 4.91). The sum of these changes is a Riemann sum of the function \(t \mapsto \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\) on the interval \([0, 1]\), and as the pieces shrink, it approaches the integral. So we propose

\[\varphi(P) = \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}t , \qquad \vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P} .\]

The notation \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}}\) means the sum over \(k = x, y, z\), and the numbers \(d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the components of the vector \(\vek d\). This reasoning is only the idea, since it assumed that \(\varphi\) exists. The theorem will show that the function given by this formula really has the required derivatives when the three given functions agree with each other.

What must the agreement be? If \(\varphi\) has continuous second partial derivatives and \(\partial\varphi/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = w_{\mathrm{k}}\) for every \(k\), then by theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives

\[\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} = \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\]

for every two indices \(k\) and \(l\). Three functions that do not satisfy this are not the partial derivatives of any function with continuous second partial derivatives. Take for example \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}} = x\), \(w_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), where \(\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = 0\) and \(\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = 1\). The formula still gives some function. With \(P_0 = O\) we have \(\vek d = (x, y, z)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{y}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d) = t\,x\), so \(\varphi(P) = \int_0^1 t\,x\,y\,\mathrm{d}t = \tfrac12\,x\,y\). Its partial derivatives, however, are \(\tfrac12\,y\), \(\tfrac12\,x\) and \(0\), not \(0\), \(x\) and \(0\). The theorem says that the condition is also sufficient when the set is star-shaped.

Theorem 4.104 A field from its partial derivatives (polje iz parcialnih odvodov)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points that is star-shaped with respect to the point \(P_0\) (definition 4.103), and let \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) be functions that are continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90) and satisfy at every point of \(D\)

\[\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} = \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} \quad \text{for all } \ix{k}, \ix{l} \in \{x, y, z\} , \tag{4.69}\]

where \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). For a point \(P\) of \(D\) let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) with the components \(d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{z}}\) and

\[\varphi(P) = \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{4.70}\]

Then \(\varphi\) is defined at every point of \(D\), \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\), and at every point of \(D\)

\[\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} = w_{\mathrm{l}} \quad \text{for } \ix{l} = x, y, z .\]

The function \(\varphi\) is therefore continuously differentiable on \(D\).

Proof

We must show that the integral exists and that its partial derivative with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{l}}\) equals \(w_{\mathrm{l}}\). We will differentiate under the integral sign. The condition (4.69) will turn the integrand into the derivative of a function of the variable \(t\), and the fundamental theorem of calculus will give the value of the integral.

  1. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\) and \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). Since \(D\) is open, there are numbers \(r_0 > 0\) and \(r > 0\) such that all points at a distance less than \(r_0\) from \(P_0\) and all points at a distance less than \(r\) from \(P\) are in \(D\). Let \(\vek d \neq \vek 0\). The point \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\) for every \(t\) of the open interval \(I = (-r_0/|\vek d|,\ 1 + r/|\vek d|)\), which contains \([0, 1]\). For \(0 \le t \le 1\) this holds because \(D\) is star-shaped with respect to \(P_0\). For \(t < 0\) the point is at the distance \(|t|\,|\vek d| < r_0\) from \(P_0\). For \(t > 1\) we have \(P_0 + t\,\vek d = P + (t - 1)\,\vek d\), and the point is at the distance \((t - 1)\,|\vek d| < r\) from \(P\). If \(\vek d = \vek 0\), then \(P = P_0\), all points \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) are \(P_0\), and we take for \(I\) the set of all numbers.
  2. By lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment, item 1, every function \(t \mapsto w_{\mathrm{k}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\) is differentiable at every point of \(I\), so by lemma 1.79 it is continuous on \([0, 1]\). The integrand in (4.70) is a sum of such functions multiplied by the numbers \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\), so it is continuous on \([0, 1]\) (corollary 1.64) and by theorem 3.38 integrable. The number \(\varphi(P)\) therefore exists. At \(P = P_0\) we have \(\vek d = \vek 0\), the integrand is zero, and \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\).
  3. Let us choose an index \(l\). For a number \(s\) with \(|s| < r\) the point \(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\) is at the distance \(|s| < r\) from \(P\), so it is in \(D\). Its vector from \(P_0\) is \(\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\). Its component \(l\) is \(d_{\mathrm{l}} + s\), the other two equal the components of the vector \(\vek d\). We write the component \(k\) of this vector as \((\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})_{\mathrm{k}}\). By (4.70)
    \[\varphi(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}) = \int_0^1 f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t , \qquad f(t, s) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}\big(Q(t, s)\big)\,\big(\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\big)_{\mathrm{k}} ,\]
    where \(Q(t, s) = P_0 + t\,(\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})\) is a point of the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\). Since \(D\) is star-shaped with respect to \(P_0\), the point \(Q(t, s)\) is in \(D\) for all \(t \in [0, 1]\) and \(|s| < r\) (figure 4.91).
  4. For a fixed \(t\) we have \(Q(t, s) = (P_0 + t\,\vek d) + s\,(t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})\). By lemma 1.132, item 1, with the point \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) and the vector \(t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\), which we may use at every \(s\) with \(|s| < r\), because there the point \(Q(t, s)\) is in \(D\), the derivative of the function \(s \mapsto w_{\mathrm{k}}(Q(t, s))\) is the sum of the products of the partial derivatives with the components of the vector \(t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\). Only its component \(l\), equal to \(t\), can differ from zero, so this derivative is \(t\,\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,(Q(t, s))\). The factor \((\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})_{\mathrm{k}}\) has the derivative \(1\) with respect to \(s\) when \(\ix{k} = \ix{l}\) and \(0\) otherwise. By the product rule (lemma 1.81) therefore
    \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s) = t \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}}\big(Q(t, s)\big)\,\big(\vek d + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\big)_{\mathrm{k}} + w_{\mathrm{l}}\big(Q(t, s)\big) .\]
  5. The functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) are continuous on the rectangle \([0, 1] \times [-r/2, r/2]\), whose point \((t, s)\) we treat as the point \((t, s, 0)\) of the plane \(z = 0\), as the rectangles of section 4.2.2. Let a sequence of points \((t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) of the rectangle converge to \((t, s)\). By lemma 1.66 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, \(t_{\mathrm{n}}\) then converges to \(t\) and \(s_{\mathrm{n}}\) to \(s\). The coordinates of the points \(Q(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) are sums and products of the numbers \(t_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(s_{\mathrm{n}}\) and constants, so by lemma 1.60 on limit laws for sequences they converge to the coordinates of the point \(Q(t, s)\), and by the same lemma on convergence coordinate by coordinate the points \(Q(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to \(Q(t, s)\). The function \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuous at \(Q(t, s)\) by lemma 1.91, and its partial derivative \(\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\) by assumption. By lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points, the values of both at the points \(Q(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to the values at \(Q(t, s)\). By the lemma on limit laws for sequences, \(f(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) therefore tends to \(f(t, s)\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\,(t_{\mathrm{n}}, s_{\mathrm{n}})\) to \(\partial f/\partial s\,(t, s)\), and by lemma 1.68 the functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) are continuous.
  6. We use lemma 4.19 on differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter, item 1, on the rectangle \([0, 1] \times [-r/2, r/2]\). Its hypotheses hold: the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial s\) exists at every point of the rectangle by step 4, since there \(|s| \le r/2 < r\), and the functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) are continuous on the rectangle by step 5. The function \(G(s) = \int_0^1 f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\) of the lemma equals \(\varphi(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})\) by step 3, and the number \(0\) lies in \((-r/2, r/2)\). By the lemma, the function \(s \mapsto \varphi(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})\) is therefore differentiable at \(s = 0\), with the derivative \(\int_0^1 \partial f/\partial s\,(t, 0)\,\mathrm{d}t\). This derivative is the limit of the quotient \((\varphi(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}) - \varphi(P))/s\), so by the definition of the partial derivative 1.25 it is the partial derivative \(\partial\varphi/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,(P)\).
  7. At \(s = 0\) we have \(Q(t, 0) = P_0 + t\,\vek d\) and \((\vek d + 0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}})_{\mathrm{k}} = d_{\mathrm{k}}\). By step 4 and by the condition (4.69), which replaces \(\partial w_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\) by \(\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\),
    \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, 0) = t \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}} + w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d) .\]
  8. Let \(h(t) = t\,w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\) for \(t \in I\). By lemma 1.132, items 1 and 2, the function \(t \mapsto w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\) has the derivative \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \partial w_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\), which is continuous on \(I\). By the product rule, \(h'(t)\) is exactly the right side of step 7. The function \(h'\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\) as a sum of products of continuous functions (corollary 1.64), and \(h\) is continuous because it is differentiable.
  9. By step 6 and by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 1, with the function \(h\) on the interval \([0, 1]\),
    \[\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}}(P) = \int_0^1 h'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = h(1) - h(0) = 1 \cdot w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + \vek d) - 0 = w_{\mathrm{l}}(P) .\]
  10. The functions \(w_{\mathrm{l}}\) are continuous at every point of \(D\) by lemma 1.91. The partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) therefore exist and are continuous at every point of \(D\), and \(\varphi\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\).

Source: LEBL2 Thm. 9.3.6 (Poincaré lemma, PDF p. 87), for star-shaped domains in \(\mathbb R^n\), with the same formula and with differentiation under the integral sign. Steps 1, 3 to 5 and 8, which check the hypotheses of the differentiation under the integral and of the fundamental theorem of calculus, are not from the source.

The proof has shown why the formula works. The derivative with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{l}}\) under the integral gave two terms: the change of the values \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) when the segment moves together with its end \(P\), and the change of the component \(d_{\mathrm{l}}\). The condition (4.69) combined both terms into the derivative of the function \(t\,w_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\) with respect to \(t\), and the fundamental theorem of calculus turned the integral of this derivative into the difference of the values at the ends, \(w_{\mathrm{l}}(P) - 0\). Without the condition, step 7 would have left another integral, which for the example with \(w_{\mathrm{y}} = x\) above gave not \(0\) but \(\tfrac12\,y\). We will use the theorem twice in the next subsection.

Let us test the formula on the hanging bar, where we know the answer. The component \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\) of the field (1.18) has, by the first row of the table in section 1.7.2, the partial derivatives

\[w_{\mathrm{x}} = 2a\,(L - x) , \qquad w_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,y , \qquad w_{\mathrm{z}} = -0{,}6\,a\,z .\]

Let us forget \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) for a moment and ask which function has these three partial derivatives. The condition (4.69) holds, since all mixed derivatives are zero: \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) not on \(x\) and \(z\), \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) not on \(x\) and \(y\). The functions are polynomials, defined in all of space, and space is convex, since the point \(P_0 + t\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) is always in space. Let us take \(P_0 = O\). Then \(\vek d = (x, y, z)\) and \(P_0 + t\,\vek d = (t\,x, t\,y, t\,z)\), so the integrand of (4.70) is

\[2a\,(L - t\,x)\,x - 0{,}6\,a\,t\,y \cdot y - 0{,}6\,a\,t\,z \cdot z = 2aLx - \big(2a\,x^2 + 0{,}6\,a\,y^2 + 0{,}6\,a\,z^2\big)\,t .\]

The function \(G(t) = 2aLx\,t - \big(2a\,x^2 + 0{,}6\,a\,y^2 + 0{,}6\,a\,z^2\big)\,t^2/2\) has this integrand as its derivative by the rules of differentiation, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus

\[\varphi(P) = G(1) - G(0) = 2aLx - a\,x^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) = u_{\mathrm{x}} .\]

The formula returned exactly \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), because \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(O) = 0\), just as \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\). At the point \(P = (5\ \text{m}, 4\ \text{mm}, 0)\) this is \(1{,}464 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m, the displacement of section 1.7.1.

What does the formula mean? If we think of the functions \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) as the components of a force that depends on the position of the point, then \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta t\) is the work of this force over the short step \(\Delta t\,\vek d\) (definition 4.1, item 1), and \(\varphi(P)\) is the sum of such works along the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\). The condition (4.69) then tells when the work of a force does not depend on the path along which we move the point, but only on the initial and final positions. We will need this in chapter 8. Books call the theorem the Poincaré lemma (Poincaréjeva lema) (LEBL2, PDF p. 87). It also holds in connected and simply connected sets that are not star-shaped. The proof then needs integrals along paths and their continuous deformation (LEBL2, PDF p. 86), and in subsection 4.7.8 we carry it out with broken lines. KREYSZIG proves it for integrals along curves with Stokes's theorem (KREYSZIG §10.2, Theorem 3, PDF p. 449, Stokes's theorem with its proof in §10.9, PDF pp. 489-492, and the proof of part (b) of Theorem 3 at the end of §10.9, PDF p. 494).

4.7.7 Displacements from strains

Now let us prove the theorem on the sufficiency of the compatibility equations for star-shaped bodies. First we state the problem precisely. An open set of points \(D\) is given, for example the set of interior points of a body, which is star-shaped with respect to the point \(P_0\). In it six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are given, which we complete to nine with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). Their partial derivatives of first and second order shall exist and be continuous at every point of \(D\), and the compatibility equations (1.68) shall hold at every point of \(D\). Where the functions come from does not matter. They can be strains prescribed by uneven heating, or strains from the equation of virtual forces. We assume nothing about the material or the forces, the problem is purely geometric. We look for a continuously differentiable displacement field whose small strain tensor (definition 1.115) has the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

The route has two steps. First we find the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By lemma 1.128 on the derivatives of the rotation from the derivatives of the strains, item 1, its partial derivatives must be

\[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]

For chosen \(i\) and \(j\) the right sides for \(k = x, y, z\) are three given functions, and we get \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) with theorem 4.104 if the condition (4.69) holds for them. Then we find the displacement. The displacement gradient is the sum of the small strain tensor and the small rotation tensor, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (section 1.17.5), so for every \(i\) we know all three partial derivatives of \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\), and we get \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) with the same theorem.

What does the condition demand in the first step? For chosen \(i\) and \(j\) and indices \(k\) and \(l\) it reads

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}}\Big(\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\Big(\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) .\]

This is an equation with second derivatives of the strains and four indices, which can be arbitrary. The equations (1.68) are only six special cases. We must show that all of them follow from these six.

Lemma 4.105 Compatibility equations for all indices (enačbe kompatibilnosti za vse indekse)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}}\), where the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), be functions whose partial derivatives of first and second order exist and are continuous at every point of \(D\). For indices \(i\), \(j\), \(k\), \(l\) let

\[Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} . \tag{4.71}\]

If the compatibility equations (1.68) hold at a point \(P\) of \(D\), then at \(P\) the number \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) is zero for all \(3^4 = 81\) choices of the indices.

Proof

Each of the six equations (1.68) has the form left side equals right side. We must show that each of the 81 numbers \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) is zero, or equals the difference of the left and right sides of one of the six equations, or the opposite of this difference. We use three symmetries of the expression (4.71).

  1. Swapping \(i\) and \(j\). When we swap the indices \(i\) and \(j\) in (4.71), we get
    \[Z_{\mathrm{jikl}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} .\]
    These are the same four terms as in \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\), each with the opposite sign, so \(Z_{\mathrm{jikl}} = -Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\).
  2. Swapping \(k\) and \(l\). In the same way we get \(Z_{\mathrm{ijlk}} = \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} + \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} - \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} - \partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = -Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\).
  3. Swapping the pairs. When we swap the pair \(i\), \(j\) with the pair \(k\), \(l\), we get
    \[Z_{\mathrm{klij}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ki}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lj}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kj}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{li}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} .\]
    The functions are symmetric, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ki}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}\), and by theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives the order of differentiation does not matter. So the first term equals the first term of \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\), the second the second, the third the fourth and the fourth the third, and \(Z_{\mathrm{klij}} = Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\).
  4. If \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\), step 1 gives \(Z_{\mathrm{iikl}} = -Z_{\mathrm{iikl}}\), so \(Z_{\mathrm{iikl}} = 0\). In the same way step 2 gives \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkk}} = 0\). There are \(3 \cdot 9 = 27\) choices with \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\), likewise \(27\) choices with \(\ix{k} = \ix{l}\), and \(9\) choices with both, so there are \(27 + 27 - 9 = 45\) choices for which \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) is zero by the very structure of the expression.
  5. There remain \(81 - 45 = 36\) choices with \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k} \neq \ix{l}\). Without regard to order, the pair of different indices \(i\), \(j\) is one of three, \(x\) and \(y\), \(y\) and \(z\), or \(z\) and \(x\), and likewise the pair \(k\), \(l\). By steps 1 and 2, \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) only changes into the opposite number when we swap the order within a pair. Each of the 36 numbers therefore equals one of nine numbers, one for each choice of two pairs, or the opposite of this number.
  6. By step 3 the two numbers in which the pairs are swapped are equal. Of the nine, six remain: \(Z_{\mathrm{xyxy}}\), \(Z_{\mathrm{yzyz}}\) and \(Z_{\mathrm{zxzx}}\), where the same pair appears twice, and \(Z_{\mathrm{xyxz}}\), \(Z_{\mathrm{yzyx}}\) and \(Z_{\mathrm{zxzy}}\), where the pairs differ.
  7. Let us compute the first and the fourth. By (4.71), the symmetry \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the theorem on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives,
    \[\begin{aligned} Z_{\mathrm{xyxy}} &= \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y\,\partial x} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} - 2\,\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} , \\ Z_{\mathrm{xyxz}} &= \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} . \end{aligned}\]
    These are the differences of the left and right sides of the first and the fourth equation (1.68).
  8. When we rename the axes as in the proof of theorem 1.127, \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\), \(Z_{\mathrm{xyxy}}\) turns into \(Z_{\mathrm{yzyz}}\) and then into \(Z_{\mathrm{zxzx}}\), and \(Z_{\mathrm{xyxz}}\) into \(Z_{\mathrm{yzyx}}\) and then into \(Z_{\mathrm{zxzy}}\). In the same way the first equation turns into the second and the third, and the fourth into the fifth and the sixth. The six numbers of step 6 are therefore the differences of the left and right sides of the six equations (1.68).
  9. If the equations hold at \(P\), all six numbers of step 6 are zero. By steps 4 to 6 all 81 numbers \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) are therefore zero.

Source: SADD (2.6.1) (PDF p. 51), CM (3.7.10) (PDF p. 151). SADD says that the general form would give 81 equations, which are mostly identities or repetitions, and only six are meaningful, and CM that of the 81 equations only six are different. Neither derives the count. The proof is not from the sources.

Figure 4.92 shows all 81 numbers as the lemma gives them. The row gives the pair \(i\), \(j\), the column the pair \(k\), \(l\), and the number in the cell which of the six equations the expression \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) repeats and with which sign. The equations 1 to 3 appear four times each, once for each choice of the order within both pairs, and the equations 4 to 6 eight times each, because the swap of the pairs comes on top: \(3 \cdot 4 + 3 \cdot 8 = 36\). We checked all 81 cells with SymPy. SADD writes the same expression with differently named indices as the general form of the compatibility equations and obtains the six equations from it by choosing the indices (SADD (2.6.1), (2.6.2), PDF p. 51).

Theorem 4.106 Sufficiency of the compatibility equations in a star-shaped body (zadostnost enačb kompatibilnosti v zvezdastem telesu)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points that is star-shaped with respect to the point \(P_0\) (definition 4.103), and let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}}\), where the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), be functions whose partial derivatives of first and second order exist and are continuous at every point of \(D\) and which satisfy the compatibility equations (1.68) at every point of \(D\). For a point \(P\) of \(D\) let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) with the components \(d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{z}}\) and

\[\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P) = \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Big(\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big)(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{4.72}\]
\[u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\big)(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{4.73}\]

Then the displacement field \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), its components also have continuous second partial derivatives at every point of \(D\), and at every point of \(D\)

\[\frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} \quad \text{for all } \ix{i}, \ix{j} .\]

If \(D\) is the set of interior points of a body, the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are therefore compatible strains (definition 1.123).

Proof

We must show that the integrals exist, that the displacements have continuous first and second partial derivatives, and that the symmetric part of their gradient is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). We use theorem 4.104 twice, once for the rotation and once for the displacement.

1. The rotation.

  1. Let us choose indices \(i\) and \(j\) and write \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\) for \(k = x, y, z\). The partial derivatives of the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are differences of second partial derivatives of the functions \(\varepsilon\), which exist and are continuous by assumption, so the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(D\).
  2. The condition (4.69) for the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) demands that \(\partial\psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} - \partial\psi_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) for every \(k\) and \(l\). Written out,
    \[\frac{\partial\psi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} - \frac{\partial\psi_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
    By theorem 1.125 the order of differentiation does not matter, so the right side is exactly \(Z_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) of (4.71), which is zero by lemma 4.105.
  3. By theorem 4.104 with the functions \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}\), the function \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of (4.72) is defined and continuously differentiable on \(D\), with the derivatives
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} \quad \text{for } \ix{k} = x, y, z .\]
  4. When we swap \(i\) and \(j\), the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) change sign. By the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.39, item 1) therefore \(\omega_{\mathrm{ji}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every point of \(D\). For \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) the integrand is zero, so \(\omega_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\).

2. The displacement.

  1. Let us choose an index \(i\) and write \(w_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for \(j = x, y, z\). The partial derivatives \(\partial w_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} + \partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\) exist and are continuous: the first term by assumption, the second because by step 3 it is the difference of two first partial derivatives of the functions \(\varepsilon\). The functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\) are therefore continuously differentiable on \(D\).
  2. The condition (4.69) holds for the functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\). By step 3
    \[\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} - \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} + \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{il}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}} + \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lj}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lj}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = 0 ,\]
    because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lj}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{jl}}\).
  3. By theorem 4.104 with the functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\), the function \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) of (4.73) is defined and continuously differentiable on \(D\), with the derivatives
    \[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} \quad \text{for } \ix{j} = x, y, z .\]
  4. The second partial derivatives of the function \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) are the partial derivatives of the functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\), which exist and are continuous by step 5.

3. The strain.

  1. By step 7, step 4 and the symmetry \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), at every point of \(D\)
    \[\frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \frac12\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ji}}\big) = \frac12\,\big(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} - \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\big) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]

Source: SADD §2.6, (2.6.3)-(2.6.7) (PDF pp. 52-53). SADD writes the displacement as an integral along an arbitrary curve from \(P_0\) to \(P\), the rotation by the derivatives of the strains as in lemma 1.128, and shows with Stokes's theorem that in a simply connected body the result does not depend on the curve. BARBER (PDF p. 46) calls such integrals Cesàro integrals (Cesàrovi integrali). The proof along straight segments with the Poincaré lemma (LEBL2 Thm. 9.3.6, PDF p. 87) is not from the sources.

The proof has shown where the compatibility equations do their work. They are needed in the first step: with them the partial derivatives of the rotation that the derivatives of the strains prescribe agree with each other, and the rotation exists. In the second step the condition held by itself, because the rotation is exactly as lemma 1.128 demands. The functions \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) really are the small rotation tensor of the field obtained (definition 1.116), since by steps 7 and 4

\[\frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \frac12\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} - \omega_{\mathrm{ji}}\big) = \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]

Since the vector \(\vek d\) is zero at \(P = P_0\), we have \(\vek u(P_0) = \vek 0\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P_0) = 0\): the field obtained leaves the point \(P_0\) in place and does not turn the material next to it. The set \(D\) is connected (definition 1.130), since any two of its points \(P\) and \(Q\) are joined by the broken line with the points \(P\), \(P_0\) and \(Q\), whose two segments lie in \(D\) because \(D\) is star-shaped with respect to \(P_0\). By corollary 1.135, every other continuously differentiable field with the same strains therefore differs from the one obtained by a small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) with a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\). With such a displacement we fit the field to the supports of the body.

Let us test the theorem on the corrected strip of section 1.18.3 (figure 4.93). A thin steel strip of length 200 mm and height 20 mm lies in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\). The axis \(x\) points along the strip, and the origin is at the middle of the left end. The thickness of the strip in the direction of the axis \(z\) does not matter for the computation, because no function depends on \(z\). The prescribed strains are

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 , \qquad k = -10\ \text{m}^{-2} ,\]

and the other three components are zero. In section 1.18.3 we checked that they satisfy the compatibility equations, and said that the number \(k\) is strongly exaggerated. At the right end \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}4\), far beyond the bound of small strains. All computations are linear in \(k\), so with a realistic \(k\) they hold in the same way, only the numbers are smaller. The interior points of the strip make up the interior of a box, which is convex, so it is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. For \(P_0\) we take the centre of the strip, \(P_0 = (x_0, 0, 0)\) with \(x_0 = 100\) mm.

  1. The rotation. For the pair \(x\), \(y\) the functions of the proof are \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial y - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial x = 2k\,y\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}/\partial x = 2k\,x\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The condition holds, \(\partial\psi_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = 2k = \partial\psi_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\). For the pairs with the index \(z\) all functions are zero, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are zero and no strain depends on \(z\), so \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero. For the point \(P = (x, y, z)\) we have \(\vek d = (x - x_0, y, z)\) and \(P_0 + t\,\vek d = (x_0 + t\,(x - x_0),\ t\,y,\ t\,z)\), so by (4.72)
    \[\begin{aligned} \omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(P) &= \int_0^1 \Big(2k\,t\,y\,(x - x_0) + 2k\,\big(x_0 + t\,(x - x_0)\big)\,y\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &= k\,y\,(x - x_0) + 2k\,x_0\,y + k\,y\,(x - x_0) = 2k\,x\,y . \end{aligned}\]
    We computed the integral with the fundamental theorem of calculus: a term with the factor \(t\) has an antiderivative with the factor \(t^2/2\), which equals \(\tfrac12\) at \(t = 1\).
  2. The displacement. For \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xj}} + \omega_{\mathrm{xj}}\) are \(k\,y^2\), \(2k\,x\,y\) and \(0\), and for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) they are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} + \omega_{\mathrm{yx}} = -2k\,x\,y\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \omega_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\) and \(0\), because \(\omega_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\). For \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) all three are zero. The two integrals (4.73), computed with SymPy, are
    \[u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2 , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 .\]

This is exactly the field we guessed in section 1.18.3. Exactly, not only up to a rigid displacement, because that field has zero displacement at \(P_0\), where \(y = 0\), and the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2k\,x_0 \cdot 0 = 0\). At the point \(P = (10\ \text{mm}, 5\ \text{mm}, 0)\) near the left end the rotation is \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2 \cdot (-10\ \text{m}^{-2}) \cdot 0{,}01\ \text{m} \cdot 0{,}005\ \text{m} = -0{,}001\), and the displacement has the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -2{,}5\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = 5\ \mu\text{m}\). In figure 4.93 the bands of the strip, deformed by the field obtained, fit together without gaps, since one single field moves all points. Had we chosen the point \((100\ \text{mm}, 5\ \text{mm}, 0)\) for \(P_0\), the formulas would have given a field with zero displacement and zero rotation at that point. By SymPy it differs from ours by \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\), where \(a_{\mathrm{x}} = -25\ \mu\text{m}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}} = 500\ \mu\text{m}\), \(a_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -W_{\mathrm{yx}} = 0{,}01\), and the other entries of the matrix \(\mat W\) are zero. This is a small rigid displacement of corollary 1.135.

And the strip with the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), which does not satisfy the first equation? The proof stops already in the first step. For the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the functions are \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}} = 2k\,y\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and the condition fails, since \(\partial\psi_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = 2k = -20\ \text{m}^{-2}\) and \(\partial\psi_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = 0\). The rotation would have to change along the strip at the rate \(2k\,y\), which differs at different heights, while it would not be allowed to change with height. In section 1.18.3 we saw this as bands that curve differently (figure 1.143, right). The formula (4.72) still gives some function, for \(P_0 = (x_0, 0, 0)\) the function \(k\,y\,(x - x_0)\), but its derivative with respect to \(x\) is \(k\,y\), not \(2k\,y\).

Why does the theorem not help with the ring of section 1.18.5? The ring is not star-shaped (figure 4.90): the segment from a point \(P_0\) to the opposite point passes through the hole, where there is no material and the strains are not defined. The formulas (4.72) and (4.73) need the strains and their derivatives at every point of the segment, so for such points we cannot write them down. That this is not merely a shortcoming of the proof we saw in section 1.18.5: the strains of the ring satisfy the compatibility equations, but there is no displacement field. The cut ring has a displacement field although it is not star-shaped. Our theorem does not show this. In the next two subsections we therefore extend it to all connected and simply connected bodies, among them the cut ring. We will add up along broken lines that avoid the holes, and show that the result does not depend on the choice of the line. The books show this with Stokes's theorem (SADD, PDF p. 53, KREYSZIG §10.2, Theorem 3, PDF p. 449), but theorem 4.104 in small balls will be enough for us. For the box, the strip, the round bar and the ball, which are convex, the theorem of this subsection is already enough.

4.7.8 Mathematics: simply connected bodies

Theorem 4.106 of the previous subsection gives a displacement field from the strains in every star-shaped body. We added the displacement up along a straight segment from a chosen point \(P_0\) to the point \(P\), so the whole segment had to lie in the body. The cut ring of section 1.18.5 is not star-shaped (figure 4.90, bottom right), and yet it takes the prescribed shortening of the fibres around the hole, since it closes like a fan (figure 1.154). So it does have a displacement field, but our theorem does not show this. The U-shaped bracket, which we meet in the next subsection, is not star-shaped either. Both bodies are simply connected (definition 1.136): every closed curve in them can be shrunk continuously to a point without leaving the body. The goal of this and the next subsection is the sufficiency of the compatibility equations for every body whose interior points form a connected and simply connected set. This is theorem 1.137, which section 1.18.5 stated with a source.

Where the compatibility equations come from and what happens for a body with a hole, we said in sections 1.18 and 1.18.5. A region with a hole becomes simply connected by a cut, and the displacement may jump across the cut (LOVE, PDF p. 241). This is the idea of this subsection.

We described the idea in words already in section 1.18.5. We walk from \(P_0\) to \(P\) along a path in the body and add up the small changes. Instead of one segment we take a broken line made of several segments that avoids the hole. The new question is whether the sum depends on the path. If we go from \(P_0\) to \(P\) along one path and back along another, we get a closed path, and the sum along it is the difference of the sums along the two paths. So we must show that the sum is zero along every broken line in the body that ends where it starts. This is where simple connectedness helps. We shrink the closed line continuously to a point and look at it in finitely many intermediate positions. Between consecutive positions the line moves so little that each of its pieces stays in a small ball that lies in the body. A ball is star-shaped, so by theorem 4.104 there is a function with the prescribed partial derivatives in it, and with this function we show that the sum does not change between consecutive positions. In the last position the line is a single point, and the sum is zero.

The route is this. First we show that star-shaped sets and the cut ring are simply connected. Then we write the sum along a broken line as an integral and prove that it is zero along every broken line in a simply connected set that ends where it starts. From this it will follow that the ring is not simply connected, and that in a connected and simply connected set there is a function with the prescribed partial derivatives. At the end we show that a thick spherical shell and a cylinder with a spherical cavity are simply connected too, although they are not star-shaped. In the next subsection we use the function with the prescribed partial derivatives for the rotation and for the displacement, as in the proof of theorem 4.106.

Definition 1.136 writes the shrinking with a rule \(H\) whose input is a point \((s, t)\) of the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) and whose output is a point \(H(s, t)\) of the set. The number \(s\) says where on the curve we are, the number \(t\) how far the shrinking has gone (figure 1.153). We treat the point \((s, t)\) as the point \((s, t, 0)\) of the plane \(z = 0\), as we did with rectangles in section 4.2.2. For functions of the point \((s, t)\) we therefore use the definition of continuity 1.67 and the lemmas on continuous functions of a point. First let us prove precisely what subsection 4.7.6 showed in words: a curve in a star-shaped set is shrunk by moving each of its points at the same time along the segment towards the point \(P_0\).

Lemma 4.107 A star-shaped set is simply connected (zvezdasta množica je enostavno povezana)

Let \(D\) be a set of points that is star-shaped with respect to a point \(P_0\) (definition 4.103). Then \(D\) is simply connected (definition 1.136).

Proof

We must show that every closed curve in \(D\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\). For the rule \(H\) we take the motion of each point of the curve along the segment towards \(P_0\).

  1. Let \(\gamma\) be a closed curve in \(D\). Its coordinates \(\gamma_{\mathrm{x}}(s)\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{y}}(s)\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{z}}(s)\) are continuous functions on \([0, 1]\), and \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\).
  2. The function that assigns \(\gamma_{\mathrm{x}}(s)\) to the point \((s, t)\) of the square is continuous on the square. Let a sequence of points \((s_{\mathrm{n}}, t_{\mathrm{n}})\) of the square converge to the point \((s, t)\). By lemma 1.66 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, \(s_{\mathrm{n}}\) tends to \(s\), and by lemma 1.61 on continuity through sequences, \(\gamma_{\mathrm{x}}(s_{\mathrm{n}})\) tends to \(\gamma_{\mathrm{x}}(s)\). By lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points the function is therefore continuous at \((s, t)\). In the same way the functions that assign \(\gamma_{\mathrm{y}}(s)\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{z}}(s)\) and \(t\) to the point \((s, t)\) are continuous.
  3. For a point \((s, t)\) of the square let
    \[H(s, t) = P_0 + (1 - t)\,\overrightarrow{P_0\,\gamma(s)} ,\]
    that is \(H_{\mathrm{x}}(s, t) = x_{\mathrm{P}_0} + (1 - t)\,\big(\gamma_{\mathrm{x}}(s) - x_{\mathrm{P}_0}\big)\), and likewise for the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). By step 2 and corollary 1.69 on continuity of sums, products and polynomials in space, item 1, \(H_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\) of the square.
  4. The number \(1 - t\) lies between \(0\) and \(1\), so \(H(s, t)\) is a point of the segment from \(P_0\) to \(\gamma(s)\). The point \(\gamma(s)\) is in \(D\), and \(D\) is star-shaped with respect to \(P_0\), so \(H(s, t)\) is in \(D\).
  5. At \(t = 0\) we have \(H(s, 0) = P_0 + \overrightarrow{P_0\,\gamma(s)} = \gamma(s)\), and at \(t = 1\) we have \(H(s, 1) = P_0\) for every \(s\). Since \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\), \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\) for every \(t\). The rule \(H\) meets all requirements of definition 1.136, and we have shrunk \(\gamma\) continuously in \(D\) to the point \(P_0\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.2 (PDF p. 449) gives the interior of a sphere and of a cube as examples of simply connected sets. The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

The box, the ball and the round bar are convex (subsection 4.7.6), hence star-shaped, and therefore simply connected by the lemma. We will need step 2 several more times: a continuous function of the number \(s\) is also continuous as a function of the point \((s, t)\) that ignores \(t\).

For the cut ring, segments towards one point are not enough, since the ring is not star-shaped. We write the shrinking differently. To every point of the cut ring we assign three numbers that say how far it is from the axis, where it lies around the axis and how high it is. These numbers fill an unbounded slab without holes, in which we shrink the curve along segments. For this we need the continuity of a square root and of a quotient, and later also the derivative of a quotient. For sums, multiples and products we have proved all of this already (corollary 1.69, lemma 1.81).

Lemma 4.108 Square root and quotient (koren in količnik)

Let \(M\) be a set of numbers or a set of points, \(P\) an element of it, and let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions that are defined on \(M\) and continuous at \(P\), with continuity as in definitions 1.58 and 1.67.

  1. If \(f(Q) \ge 0\) for every \(Q\) in \(M\) and \(f(P) > 0\), the function \(Q \mapsto \sqrt{f(Q)}\) is continuous at \(P\).
  2. If \(g(Q) \ne 0\) for every \(Q\) in \(M\), the function \(Q \mapsto f(Q)/g(Q)\) is continuous at \(P\).
  3. Let the functions \(f\) and \(g\) be defined on an open interval \(I\) and have a derivative (definition 1.9) at a point \(x \in I\), and let \(g(y) \ne 0\) for every \(y \in I\). Then the function \(f/g\) is differentiable at \(x\) and
    \[\Big(\frac fg\Big)'(x) = \frac{f'(x)\,g(x) - f(x)\,g'(x)}{g(x)^2} . \tag{4.74}\]
Proof

We must show three items. For the first two we use the lemma on continuity through sequences (lemma 1.61 for numbers, lemma 1.68 for points), for the third the recipe with completed quotients from the proof of lemma 1.81.

1. Square root.

  1. Let a sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) from \(M\) converge to \(P\). By the lemma on continuity through sequences, \(a_{\mathrm{n}} = f(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) tends to \(b = f(P) > 0\).
  2. We multiply out the brackets: \(\big(\sqrt{a_{\mathrm{n}}} - \sqrt b\big)\big(\sqrt{a_{\mathrm{n}}} + \sqrt b\big) = a_{\mathrm{n}} - b\), because the square of a square root is the number under the root (section 1.8.6).
  3. A square root is not negative, so \(\sqrt{a_{\mathrm{n}}} + \sqrt b \ge \sqrt b > 0\). Dividing the equation of step 2 by this number we get
    \[\big|\sqrt{a_{\mathrm{n}}} - \sqrt b\big| = \frac{|a_{\mathrm{n}} - b|}{\sqrt{a_{\mathrm{n}}} + \sqrt b} \le \frac{|a_{\mathrm{n}} - b|}{\sqrt b} .\]
  4. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.38 there is an index \(N\) with \(|a_{\mathrm{n}} - b| < \eta\,\sqrt b\) for every \(n \ge N\). For these \(n\), step 3 gives \(|\sqrt{a_{\mathrm{n}}} - \sqrt b| < \eta\), so \(\sqrt{a_{\mathrm{n}}}\) converges to \(\sqrt b\).
  5. The sequence was arbitrary, so by the lemma on continuity through sequences the square root is continuous at \(P\).

2. Quotient.

  1. Let a sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) from \(M\) converge to \(P\). By the lemma on continuity through sequences, \(f(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) tends to \(f(P)\) and \(b_{\mathrm{n}} = g(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) tends to \(b = g(P) \ne 0\). Let \(c = |b|/2 > 0\).
  2. There is an index \(N_1\) with \(|b_{\mathrm{n}} - b| < c\) for every \(n \ge N_1\). By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1), \(|b| \le |b_{\mathrm{n}}| + |b - b_{\mathrm{n}}|\), so for these \(n\) we have \(|b_{\mathrm{n}}| > |b| - c = c\).
  3. For \(n \ge N_1\) therefore
    \[\Big|\frac{1}{b_{\mathrm{n}}} - \frac1b\Big| = \frac{|b - b_{\mathrm{n}}|}{|b_{\mathrm{n}}|\,|b|} \le \frac{|b_{\mathrm{n}} - b|}{c\,|b|} .\]
  4. We choose \(\eta > 0\). There is an index \(N_2\) with \(|b_{\mathrm{n}} - b| < \eta\,c\,|b|\) for every \(n \ge N_2\). For \(n\) not smaller than \(N_1\) and \(N_2\), step 3 gives \(|1/b_{\mathrm{n}} - 1/b| < \eta\). So \(1/b_{\mathrm{n}}\) converges to \(1/b\).
  5. By lemma 1.60 on limit laws for sequences, item 3, \(f(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \cdot (1/b_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(f(P) \cdot (1/b)\). The sequence was arbitrary, so by the lemma on continuity through sequences the quotient is continuous at \(P\).

3. Derivative of a quotient.

  1. Let \(J\), \(q_{\mathrm{g}}\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{g}}\) be as in steps 1 to 3 of the preparation in the proof of lemma 1.81: for \(\Delta x \in J\) the number \(x + \Delta x\) is in \(I\), \(q_{\mathrm{g}}(\Delta x)\) is the difference quotient of the function \(g\), and the function \(Q_{\mathrm{g}}\) equals \(q_{\mathrm{g}}(\Delta x)\) at \(\Delta x \ne 0\), has the value \(g'(x)\) at \(0\) and is continuous at \(0\).
  2. Let \(G(\Delta x) = g(x + \Delta x)\) for \(\Delta x \in J\). As in step 3 of the third part of the same proof, \(G\) is continuous at \(0\), and \(G(\Delta x) \ne 0\), because \(x + \Delta x\) is in \(I\).
  3. For \(\Delta x \ne 0\)
    \[\frac{1}{\Delta x}\Big(\frac{1}{g(x + \Delta x)} - \frac{1}{g(x)}\Big) = \frac{g(x) - g(x + \Delta x)}{\Delta x\,g(x + \Delta x)\,g(x)} = -\frac{q_{\mathrm{g}}(\Delta x)}{G(\Delta x)\,g(x)} .\]
  4. The function \(-Q_{\mathrm{g}}/(G\,g(x))\) on \(J\) equals this quotient at \(\Delta x \ne 0\) and has the value \(-g'(x)/g(x)^2\) at \(0\). By item 2 of this lemma and by corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions, it is continuous at \(0\).
  5. The interval \(I\) is open, so \(x\) is not an end point of it, and by step 1 of the preparation \(J = (-r, r)\). By lemma 1.80 on limit and continuity, item 1, the function \(1/g\) is therefore differentiable at \(x\) with derivative \(-g'(x)/g(x)^2\).
  6. The function \(f/g\) is the product of the functions \(f\) and \(1/g\). By the product rule (lemma 1.81, item 3)
    \[\Big(\frac fg\Big)'(x) = \frac{f'(x)}{g(x)} - \frac{f(x)\,g'(x)}{g(x)^2} = \frac{f'(x)\,g(x) - f(x)\,g'(x)}{g(x)^2} .\]

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 2.2.5 (iv) and Prop. 2.2.6 (PDF pp. 63 and 65) for sequences, Prop. 3.2.5 (iv) (PDF p. 124) for the continuity of a quotient, Prop. 4.1.9 (PDF p. 159) for the derivative of a quotient, whose proof the source leaves to the reader. The proof of item 1 follows the source, which writes the estimate of step 3, and the proof of item 3 is not from the source.

A partial derivative is an ordinary derivative of a function of one variable in which the other two coordinates are fixed (definition 1.25). Item 3 therefore also gives partial derivatives of quotients. For example the function \(-y/(x^2 + y^2)\) with \(y\) and \(z\) fixed has the derivative with respect to \(x\) equal to \(-\big(0 \cdot (x^2 + y^2) - y \cdot 2x\big)/(x^2 + y^2)^2 = 2x\,y/(x^2 + y^2)^2\) wherever the denominator is not zero.

Now we can write how to shrink a curve in the cut ring. We restate the setting of lemma 1.131. Lengths are in millimetres, \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2}\) is the distance of the point \(P\) from the axis \(z\), the ring is the set of points with \(40 < \rho_{\mathrm{P}} < 60\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\), and the cut ring is the ring without the cut, that is without the points with \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}} > 0\). We describe the position of a point around the axis with one number and without angles (figure 4.94, left). The point \(P\) lies on the circle of radius \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\) about the axis \(z\), and this circle meets the cut at the point \(R = (\rho_{\mathrm{P}}, 0, z_{\mathrm{P}})\). The line through \(R\) and \(P\) meets the axis \(y\) at a height that we get from similar triangles: on the way from \(R\) to \(P\), \(x\) decreases by \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(y\) increases by \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\), so up to the axis \(y\), where \(x\) has decreased by \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(y\) increases by \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\,y_{\mathrm{P}}/(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} - x_{\mathrm{P}})\). The number

\[\tau_{\mathrm{P}} = \frac{y_{\mathrm{P}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{P}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}}\]

is this height divided by \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\). Just above the cut, \(\tau_{\mathrm{P}}\) is a very large positive number, on the negative axis \(x\) it is zero, and just below the cut it is a very large negative number. On the cut the denominator would be zero.

Lemma 4.109 The cut ring is simply connected (razrezani obroč je enostavno povezan)

Lengths are in millimetres, \(c > 0\) is a number, and \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2}\). The cut ring of lemma 1.131, that is the set of points \(P\) with \(40 < \rho_{\mathrm{P}} < 60\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\) without the points with \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}} > 0\), is simply connected (definition 1.136).

Proof

We must show that every closed curve in the cut ring can be shrunk continuously to a point in it. We write a point with the three numbers \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(\tau_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\), shrink the curve along segments in these numbers and return to points (figure 4.94).

  1. For a point \(P\) of the cut ring, \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} - x_{\mathrm{P}} > 0\). Indeed \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}^2 = x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 \ge x_{\mathrm{P}}^2\), so by lemma 1.28 \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} \ge |x_{\mathrm{P}}| \ge x_{\mathrm{P}}\). The equality \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = x_{\mathrm{P}}\) would require \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = \rho_{\mathrm{P}} > 0\), and such points are on the cut.
  2. For a point \(P\) of the cut ring let \(\tau_{\mathrm{P}} = y_{\mathrm{P}}/(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} - x_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(\Psi(P) = (\rho_{\mathrm{P}}, \tau_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), which is a map (definition 4.42). For a triple of numbers \((\rho, \tau, z)\) with \(40 < \rho < 60\) and \(|z| < c\) let
    \[\Phi(\rho, \tau, z) = \Big(\rho\,\frac{\tau^2 - 1}{\tau^2 + 1},\ \rho\,\frac{2\tau}{\tau^2 + 1},\ z\Big) .\]
  3. The point \(\Phi(\rho, \tau, z)\) lies in the cut ring. Squaring out the bracket, \((\tau^2 - 1)^2 + 4\tau^2 = (\tau^2 + 1)^2\), so the sum of the squares of the first two coordinates is \(\rho^2\). The distance of the point from the axis \(z\) is therefore \(\rho\), which lies between \(40\) and \(60\). The coordinate \(y\) is zero only at \(\tau = 0\), and then the coordinate \(x\) is \(-\rho < 0\), so the point is not on the cut.
  4. For a point \(P\) of the cut ring, \(\Phi(\Psi(P)) = P\). We write \(\rho = \rho_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(\tau = \tau_{\mathrm{P}}\). Since \(y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 = \rho^2 - x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 = (\rho - x_{\mathrm{P}})(\rho + x_{\mathrm{P}})\),
    \[\tau^2 + 1 = \frac{y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + (\rho - x_{\mathrm{P}})^2}{(\rho - x_{\mathrm{P}})^2} = \frac{(\rho - x_{\mathrm{P}})\,(\rho + x_{\mathrm{P}} + \rho - x_{\mathrm{P}})}{(\rho - x_{\mathrm{P}})^2} = \frac{2\rho}{\rho - x_{\mathrm{P}}} .\]
    So the first coordinate is \(\rho\,(\tau^2 - 1)/(\tau^2 + 1) = \rho - 2\rho/(\tau^2 + 1) = \rho - (\rho - x_{\mathrm{P}}) = x_{\mathrm{P}}\), and the second is \(2\rho\,\tau/(\tau^2 + 1) = 2\rho \cdot y_{\mathrm{P}}/(\rho - x_{\mathrm{P}}) \cdot (\rho - x_{\mathrm{P}})/(2\rho) = y_{\mathrm{P}}\).
  5. The function \(x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2\) is a polynomial and is larger than \(1600\) on the cut ring, so by lemma 4.108, item 1, and corollary 1.69 the function \(P \mapsto \rho_{\mathrm{P}}\) is continuous on the cut ring. By item 2 of the same lemma and step 1, \(P \mapsto \tau_{\mathrm{P}}\) is continuous too. The first two coordinates of the point \(\Phi(\rho, \tau, z)\) are quotients of polynomials in \(\rho\) and \(\tau\) with the denominator \(\tau^2 + 1 \ge 1\), and the third is \(z\), so by the same item and the same corollary all three are continuous functions of the point \((\rho, \tau, z)\).
  6. Let \(\gamma\) be a closed curve in the cut ring and \((\rho(s), \tau(s), z(s)) = \Psi(\gamma(s))\) for \(s \in [0, 1]\). By step 5 and lemma 4.35 on continuity of a composite function, \(\rho(s)\), \(\tau(s)\) and \(z(s)\) are continuous functions on \([0, 1]\). For a point \((s, t)\) of the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) let
    \[H(s, t) = \Phi\big((1 - t)\,\rho(s) + 50\,t,\ (1 - t)\,\tau(s),\ (1 - t)\,z(s)\big) .\]
  7. The triple in the bracket is admissible: the number \((1 - t)\,\rho(s) + 50\,t\) lies between \(\rho(s)\) and \(50\), hence between \(40\) and \(60\), and \(|(1 - t)\,z(s)| \le |z(s)| < c\). By step 3, \(H(s, t)\) is in the cut ring.
  8. By step 2 of the proof of lemma 4.107 and corollary 1.69, item 1, the three numbers in the bracket are continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\) of the square. By step 5 and lemma 4.35 the coordinates of the point \(H(s, t)\) are therefore continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\).
  9. At \(t = 0\), step 4 gives \(H(s, 0) = \Phi(\Psi(\gamma(s))) = \gamma(s)\). At \(t = 1\), \(H(s, 1) = \Phi(50, 0, 0) = (-50, 0, 0)\) for every \(s\). Since \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\), \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\) for every \(t\). We have shrunk the curve \(\gamma\) continuously in the cut ring to the point \((-50, 0, 0)\).

Source: SADD §2.6 (PDF p. 53) says that a multiply connected region becomes simply connected when cuts are introduced. The proof is not from the sources.

The number \(\tau_{\mathrm{P}}\) plays the role of an angle, which the book has not defined, but we do not need it. It does not change when the point moves along a ray from the axis \(z\), since \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\) are then multiplied by the same positive number, which cancels in the quotient. At the point \(K_3 = (0, 50, 0)\) we have \(\tau = 50/50 = 1\), at \(K_7 = (0, -50, 0)\) we have \(\tau = -1\), and at \(K_5 = (-50, 0, 0)\) we have \(\tau = 0\). The set of triples \((\rho, \tau, z)\) with \(40 < \rho < 60\), \(|z| < c\) and any number \(\tau\) is an unbounded slab, which is convex, so in it we shrink the curve along segments as in lemma 4.107. The map \(\Phi\) then carries the shrinking back into the cut ring. For the whole ring this does not work, because \(\tau_{\mathrm{P}}\) above and below the cut does not match. That no other shrinking succeeds for the ring either, we show at the end of the subsection.

Now let us write the sum of small changes along a broken line. On the segment from a point \(A\) to a point \(B\) with vector \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{AB}\) we wrote it in subsection 4.7.6 as the integral

\[\int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}(A + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}t ,\]

which is the limit of the sums of changes \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta t\) over short pieces of the segment (figure 4.91). The integral exists when \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuous on a set that contains the segment. The coordinates of the point \(A + t\,\vek d\) are polynomials in \(t\), so by lemma 4.35 on continuity of a composite function the integrand is continuous on \([0, 1]\), and by theorem 3.38 it is integrable. Along a broken line we add up the integrals of its segments.

Definition 4.110 Integral of a field along a broken line (integral polja vzdolž lomljene črte)

Let \(D\) be a set of points, let \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) be functions continuous on \(D\) (definition 1.67), and let \(\Gamma\) be a broken line \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}}\) with \(m \ge 1\) whose segments lie in \(D\) (definition 1.130). For \(k = 1, \dots, m\) let \(\vek d_{\mathrm{k}} = \overrightarrow{A_{\mathrm{k}-1} A_{\mathrm{k}}}\) with components \(d_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{x}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{y}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{z}}\). The integral of the field \(\vek w = (w_{\mathrm{x}}, w_{\mathrm{y}}, w_{\mathrm{z}})\) along the broken line \(\Gamma\) is the number

\[\int_\Gamma \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + t\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}})\,d_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{4.75}\]

The broken line is closed (sklenjena) if \(A_{\mathrm{m}} = A_0\).

Source: LEBL2 Def. 9.2.9 (PDF p. 74) and Def. 9.3.8 (PDF p. 88), for piecewise smooth paths: the integral over each smooth piece, added over the pieces. A broken line is such a path made of segments only.

The notation \(\mathrm{d}\vek r\) recalls the short step \(\Delta t\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}}\) along the segment, and the dot product recalls the sum of products of components. The integral is the sum of small changes of a function with the partial derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\), when such a function exists, or else the work of a force with the components \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) along the path, as in subsection 4.7.6. We will need this in chapter 8.

Let us try the definition on the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) points down from the centre \(O\) of the top end, and \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). For \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 2a\,(L - x)\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,y\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}} = -0{,}6\,a\,z\), the partial derivatives of the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) from subsection 4.7.6, we take the broken line \(O\), \(A_1 = (5\ \text{m}, 0, 0)\), \(P = (5\ \text{m}, 4\ \text{mm}, 0)\), which goes first down the axis and then horizontally to the point \(P\). On the first segment \(\vek d_1 = (5\ \text{m}, 0, 0)\), and the integral is \(\int_0^1 2a\,(L - 5\ \text{m} \cdot t) \cdot 5\ \text{m}\,\mathrm{d}t = 2a\,(50 - 12{,}5)\ \text{m}^2 = 75\ \text{m}^2 \cdot a\). On the second \(\vek d_2 = (0, 4\ \text{mm}, 0)\), and the integral is \(\int_0^1 (-0{,}6\,a \cdot 0{,}004\ \text{m} \cdot t) \cdot 0{,}004\ \text{m}\,\mathrm{d}t = -4{,}8 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 \cdot a\). The sum is \(1{,}464 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m, which is \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(P)\), the same as along the straight segment from \(O\) to \(P\) in subsection 4.7.6. We computed both numbers with SymPy.

Along a broken line too we will compute the integral with a function that has the prescribed partial derivatives, where we know one. In a ball we always know one when condition (4.69) holds, since a ball is star-shaped.

Lemma 4.111 Integral inside a ball (integral v krogli)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, let \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) be functions continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90) that satisfy condition (4.69) at every point of \(D\), and let the ball \(B\) with centre \(C\) and radius \(r > 0\), that is the set of all points at distance less than \(r\) from \(C\), lie in \(D\). Let \(\varphi\) be the function (4.70) of theorem 4.104 with the set \(B\) instead of \(D\) and the point \(C\) instead of \(P_0\). Then:

  1. if \(A\) is a point, \(\vek d\) a vector and \(\alpha < \beta\) numbers such that the point \(A + t\,\vek d\) is in \(B\) for every \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\),
