    \[\int_\alpha^\beta \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}(A + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}t = \varphi(A + \beta\,\vek d) - \varphi(A + \alpha\,\vek d) ,\]
  2. for every broken line \(\Gamma\) in \(B\) from a point \(X\) to a point \(Y\), \(\int_\Gamma \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = \varphi(Y) - \varphi(X)\), so the integral along every closed broken line in \(B\) is zero.
Proof

We must show that theorem 4.104 holds in the ball, and then compute the integral with the fundamental theorem of calculus.

  1. The ball \(B\) is open. Let \(Y\) be a point of \(B\) and \(r' = r - |CY| > 0\). For a point \(Z\) with \(|YZ| < r'\), the triangle inequality for distances (corollary 2.16) gives \(|CZ| \le |CY| + |YZ| < r\), so \(Z\) is in \(B\).
  2. The ball \(B\) is star-shaped with respect to \(C\). For a point \(P\) of \(B\), both \(C\) and \(P\) are at distance less than \(r\) from \(C\), so by lemma 1.129 on the distance to the points of a segment, item 3, the whole segment from \(C\) to \(P\) lies in \(B\).
  3. The functions \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(B\) and satisfy condition (4.69) there, because \(B\) lies in \(D\). By theorem 4.104, \(\varphi\) is continuously differentiable on \(B\) and \(\partial\varphi/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} = w_{\mathrm{l}}\) for \(\ix{l} = x, y, z\).
  4. Let \(g(t) = \varphi(A + t\,\vek d)\). By lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment, items 1 and 2, applied to \(\varphi\) on \(B\), for every \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\) the function \(g\) is defined at all numbers near \(t\) and differentiable at \(t\) with derivative
    \[g'(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}(A + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}(A + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{i}} ,\]
    and \(g'\) is continuous at \(t\).
  5. By lemma 1.79, that a differentiable function is continuous, \(g\) is continuous on \([\alpha, \beta]\), and by step 4 so is \(g'\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 1, \(\int_\alpha^\beta g'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = g(\beta) - g(\alpha)\), which is item 1.
  6. Let \(\Gamma\) be a broken line \(X = A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = Y\) in \(B\). The points \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + t\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(t \in [0, 1]\) are points of the segment \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} A_{\mathrm{k}}\), which lies in \(B\). By item 1 with \(\alpha = 0\) and \(\beta = 1\), the term \(k\) of the sum (4.75) equals \(\varphi(A_{\mathrm{k}}) - \varphi(A_{\mathrm{k}-1})\).
  7. The sum of these differences telescopes: \(\int_\Gamma \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = \varphi(A_{\mathrm{m}}) - \varphi(A_0) = \varphi(Y) - \varphi(X)\). For a closed line \(Y = X\), and the integral is zero.

Source: LEBL2 (PDF pp. 86-87) says that the Poincaré lemma holds in every ball, because a ball is star-shaped. The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

Now we have everything for the main theorem of the subsection.

Theorem 4.112 Integral along a closed broken line (integral vzdolž sklenjene lomljene črte)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points that is simply connected (definition 1.136), and let \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) be functions continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90) that satisfy condition (4.69) at every point of \(D\). Then the integral of the field \(\vek w = (w_{\mathrm{x}}, w_{\mathrm{y}}, w_{\mathrm{z}})\) along every closed broken line in \(D\) (definition 4.110) is zero.

Proof

We must show that \(\int_\Gamma \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = 0\) for every closed broken line \(\Gamma\): \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = A_0\) with segments in \(D\). We write the broken line as a closed curve, shrink it continuously to a point and map a grid on the square into \(D\). The rows of the grid are closed broken lines that change little by little from the original line to a point, and we show that they all have the same integral (figure 4.95).

1. The broken line as a closed curve.

  1. For \(k = 1, \dots, m\) and \(s \in [(k - 1)/m,\ k/m]\) let \(\gamma(s) = A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + (m\,s - k + 1)\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}}\). As \(s\) runs from \((k - 1)/m\) to \(k/m\), the number \(m\,s - k + 1\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\), so \(\gamma(s)\) is a point of the segment \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and lies in \(D\). At the common end point \(s = k/m\) of two intervals both formulas give the same point, \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + \vek d_{\mathrm{k}} = A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{k}} + 0 \cdot \vek d_{\mathrm{k}+1} = A_{\mathrm{k}}\). At \(s = 0\), \(\gamma(0) = A_0\), and at \(s = 1\), \(\gamma(1) = A_{\mathrm{m}} = A_0\).
  2. Let \(c\) be the largest of the numbers \(m\,|d_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{i}}|\), \(k = 1, \dots, m\), \(\ix{i} = x, y, z\). For \(s\) and \(s'\) in the same interval, \(|\gamma_{\mathrm{i}}(s) - \gamma_{\mathrm{i}}(s')| = m\,|s - s'|\,|d_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{i}}| \le c\,|s - s'|\). If \(s < s'\) are in different intervals, we cut \([s, s']\) into pieces at the end points of the intervals between them. By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1, applied repeatedly), \(|\gamma_{\mathrm{i}}(s) - \gamma_{\mathrm{i}}(s')|\) is at most the sum of the differences over the pieces, and this is at most \(c\) times the sum of the lengths of the pieces, \(c\,(s' - s)\).
  3. By step 2, \(|\gamma_{\mathrm{i}}(s) - \gamma_{\mathrm{i}}(s')| \le c\,|s - s'|\) for all \(s, s' \in [0, 1]\). For an error \(\eta > 0\) the band \(\delta = \eta/c\) therefore satisfies the definition of continuity 1.58 (for \(c = 0\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant). By steps 1 and 3, \(\gamma\) is a closed curve in \(D\).

2. The grid.

  1. By definition 1.136 there is a rule \(H\) that assigns to every point \((s, t)\) of the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) a point \(H(s, t)\) of \(D\), with coordinates that are continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\), and with \(H(s, 0) = \gamma(s)\), \(H(s, 1) = Z\) for some point \(Z\) and every \(s\), and \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\) for every \(t\). We treat the square as a rectangle in the plane \(z = 0\), which is closed and bounded (subsection 4.2.2).
  2. By lemma 4.48 on the image of a closed bounded set, applied to the map \(H\) on the square (definition 4.42), the set \(K\) of all points \(H(s, t)\) is closed and bounded, and by step 4 it lies in \(D\). By lemma 4.38 on the neighbourhood of a closed bounded set there is \(\rho > 0\) such that every point at distance less than \(\rho\) from some point of \(K\) lies in \(D\). For a point \(X\) of \(K\) let \(B_{\mathrm{X}}\) be the ball of all points at distance less than \(\rho\) from \(X\). This ball lies in \(D\).
  3. By theorem 4.6, applied on the square to each of the functions \(H_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{z}}\) with the error \(\rho/3\), there are three bands. Let \(\delta > 0\) be the smallest of them. Then for points \((s, t)\) and \((s', t')\) of the square at distance less than \(\delta\), each coordinate of the points \(H(s, t)\) and \(H(s', t')\) differs by less than \(\rho/3\). The distance between two points is not larger than the sum of the absolute values of the differences of the coordinates (step 3 of the proof of lemma 1.66), so \(|H(s, t)\,H(s', t')| < \rho\).
  4. By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is a natural number \(M_0\) with \(M_0\,m\,\delta > 2\). Let \(N = M_0\,m\). For points of the square with \(|s - s'| \le 1/N\) and \(|t - t'| \le 1/N\), the same step of the proof of lemma 1.66 gives a distance of at most \(2/N < \delta\), so by step 6 \(|H(s, t)\,H(s', t')| < \rho\).
  5. For \(p, q = 0, 1, \dots, N\) let \(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}} = H(p/N, q/N)\). For every \(q\) let \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{q}}\) be the broken line \(P_{0,\mathrm{q}}, P_{1,\mathrm{q}}, \dots, P_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{q}}\), row \(q\) of the grid. Since \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\), \(P_{0,\mathrm{q}} = P_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{q}}\), and \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{q}}\) is closed. By step 7, \(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}}\) is in the ball \(B_{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}}}\), so by lemma 1.129, item 3, the whole segment from \(P_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}}\) to \(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}}\) lies in this ball and therefore in \(D\).

3. The first row has the same integral as \(\Gamma\).

  1. Let \(1 \le k \le m\), \(1 \le j \le M_0\) and \(p = (k - 1)\,M_0 + j\). Then \(p/N = (k - 1)/m + j/N\), so by step 1 \(P_{\mathrm{p},0} = \gamma(p/N) = A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + (j/M_0)\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}}\), and likewise \(P_{\mathrm{p}-1,0} = A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + ((j - 1)/M_0)\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  2. For \(t \in [(j - 1)/M_0,\ j/M_0]\), \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + t\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}} = \gamma(s)\) with \(s = (k - 1)/m + t/m\), which lies between \((p - 1)/N\) and \(p/N\). By step 7 with the points \((s, 0)\) and \(((p - 1)/N, 0)\), the point \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + t\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}}\) is therefore in the ball \(B = B_{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{p}-1,0}}\).
  3. Let \(\varphi\) be the function of lemma 4.111 for the ball \(B\). By item 1 of this lemma with \(A = A_{\mathrm{k}-1}\), \(\vek d = \vek d_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\alpha = (j - 1)/M_0\) and \(\beta = j/M_0\), and by item 2 for the segment from \(P_{\mathrm{p}-1,0}\) to \(P_{\mathrm{p},0}\), which lies in \(B\),
    \[\int_{(\mathrm{j}-1)/\mathrm{M}_0}^{j/M_0} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + t\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}})\,d_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}t = \varphi(P_{\mathrm{p},0}) - \varphi(P_{\mathrm{p}-1,0}) = \int_{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{p}-1,0} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{p},0}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r ,\]
    where the last integral means the integral along the broken line made of this one segment.
  4. By additivity of the integral (lemma 3.39, item 2), applied \(M_0 - 1\) times, the integral over \([0, 1]\) that (4.75) assigns to the segment \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} A_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the sum of the integrals over the intervals \([(j - 1)/M_0,\ j/M_0]\), so by step 11 it is the sum of the integrals along the segments from \(P_{\mathrm{p}-1,0}\) to \(P_{\mathrm{p},0}\) with \(p = (k - 1)\,M_0 + 1, \dots, k\,M_0\). Adding over \(k\) we get \(\int_\Gamma \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = \int_{\Gamma_0} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r\).

4. Neighbouring rows have the same integral.

  1. Let \(0 \le q < N\) and \(1 \le p \le N\). The points \(P_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}}\), \(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}}\), \(P_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}+1}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}+1}\) are the images of the corners of a small square of side \(1/N\), so by step 7 they are in the ball \(B = B_{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}}}\), and by lemma 1.129, item 3, so are the segments between them. Let \(\varphi\) be the function of lemma 4.111 for this ball. We denote the segment from \(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}}\) to \(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}+1}\) by \(V_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}}\), and likewise \(V_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}}\).
  2. By item 2 of lemma 4.111 the integral along each of the four segments is the difference of the values of the function \(\varphi\) at its end points. Therefore
    \[\begin{aligned} \int_{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r - \int_{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}+1} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}+1}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r &= \varphi(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}}) - \varphi(P_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}}) - \varphi(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}+1}) + \varphi(P_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}+1}) \\ &= \int_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{p}-1,\mathrm{q}}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r - \int_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{q}}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r . \end{aligned}\]
  3. We add over \(p\) from \(1\) to \(N\). On the left we get \(\int_{\Gamma_\mathrm{q}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r - \int_{\Gamma_{\mathrm{q}+1}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r\), on the right the telescoping sum \(\int_{\mathrm{V}_{0,\mathrm{q}}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r - \int_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{q}}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r\). Since \(P_{0,\mathrm{q}} = P_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{q}}\) and \(P_{0,\mathrm{q}+1} = P_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{q}+1}\), the segments \(V_{0,\mathrm{q}}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{q}}\) have the same end points, and by (4.75) the same integral. Therefore \(\int_{\Gamma_\mathrm{q}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = \int_{\Gamma_{\mathrm{q}+1}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r\).

5. The last row.

  1. All points \(P_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{N}} = H(p/N, 1)\) are the point \(Z\). Every segment of the line \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{N}}\) therefore has the vector \(\vek 0\), the integrand in (4.75) is zero, and by lemma 3.39, item 3, every integral is zero. So \(\int_{\Gamma_\mathrm{N}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = 0\).
  2. By steps 12, 15 and 16, \(\int_\Gamma \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = \int_{\Gamma_0} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = \int_{\Gamma_1} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = \dots = \int_{\Gamma_\mathrm{N}} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r = 0\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.2, Theorem 3 (PDF p. 449), for integrals along curves, with a proof by Stokes's theorem in §10.9. SADD (PDF p. 53) makes the same step with Stokes's theorem. LEBL2 Prop. 9.3.4 (PDF p. 85) says that the integral along every closed path is zero exactly when there is a function with the prescribed partial derivatives, and Theorem 9.3.6 (PDF p. 87) proves this only for star-shaped sets. The proof with a grid on the square and with balls is not from the sources.

The proof has shown where simple connectedness works. Without it we would have no rule \(H\) that changes the original line into a point little by little. The uniform continuity of \(H\) gave one single grid step \(1/N\) at which the images of all small squares are small enough to lie in balls in \(D\). In each ball the function of theorem 4.104 turned the integral around the edge of a quadrilateral into zero. There are finitely many of these quadrilaterals, \(N^2\), so we could add them up. The inner sides of the quadrilaterals cancelled in the sum, and the left and right edges of the grid match, because every intermediate position of the line is again closed.

What happens if the set is not simply connected? Take the ring of lemma 1.131 and the functions

\[w_{\mathrm{x}} = -\frac{y}{x^2 + y^2} , \qquad w_{\mathrm{y}} = \frac{x}{x^2 + y^2} , \qquad w_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 .\]

In the next subsection we will see that these are (up to a constant factor) the partial derivatives of the rotation of the material for the prescribed shortening of the fibres around the hole. Let us show that they satisfy the hypotheses of the theorem, but the integral around the hole is not zero.

Corollary 4.113 The ring is not simply connected (obroč ni enostavno povezan)

The ring of lemma 1.131, that is the set of points \(P\) with \(40 < \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2} < 60\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\), where lengths are in millimetres, is not simply connected (definition 1.136).

Proof

We must show that there are functions that satisfy the hypotheses of theorem 4.112 and a closed broken line in the ring along which the integral is not zero. Then the ring cannot be simply connected, since otherwise the theorem would make the integral zero.

  1. Let \(f = x^2 + y^2\), which is larger than \(1600\) on the ring, and \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = -y/f\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}} = x/f\), \(w_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). By lemma 4.108, item 3, applied with the other two coordinates fixed, and by lemma 1.81 the partial derivatives are
    \[\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} = \frac{2x\,y}{f^2} , \quad \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} = \frac{y^2 - x^2}{f^2} , \quad \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = \frac{y^2 - x^2}{f^2} , \quad \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} = -\frac{2x\,y}{f^2} ,\]
    and the derivatives with respect to \(z\) and all derivatives of the function \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) are zero. For \(\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y\), for example, the numerator is \(-\big(1 \cdot f - y \cdot 2y\big) = y^2 - x^2\).
  2. The partial derivatives are quotients of polynomials with the denominator \(f^2 > 0\), so by lemma 4.108, item 2, and corollary 1.69 they are continuous on the ring. The functions \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) are therefore continuously differentiable on the ring, which is open (lemma 1.131).
  3. Condition (4.69) holds: \(\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = \partial w_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\) by step 1, and for the other pairs of indices both sides are zero.
  4. Let \(\Gamma\) be the closed broken line \(K_1, K_2, \dots, K_8, K_1\) through the points on the circle of radius \(50\) from the proof of lemma 1.131. By step 3 of the second part of that proof it lies in the ring, and by step 2, \(1600 < |OT|^2 \le 2500\) for each of its points \(T\).
  5. On the segment from \(A = K_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) to \(K_{\mathrm{k}}\) with vector \(\vek d\), the numerator of the integrand at the point \(A + t\,\vek d\) is
    \[-(y_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,d_{\mathrm{y}})\,d_{\mathrm{x}} + (x_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,d_{\mathrm{x}})\,d_{\mathrm{y}} = x_{\mathrm{A}}\,d_{\mathrm{y}} - y_{\mathrm{A}}\,d_{\mathrm{x}} ,\]
    because the terms with \(t\) cancel. For \(K_1 = (50, 0, 0)\) and \(K_2 = (30, 40, 0)\) this is \(50 \cdot 40 - 0 \cdot (-20) = 2000\), for the other segments \(2000\) or \(1500\) (with SymPy). The numerator is positive, and the denominator \(f\) is at most \(2500\) by step 4.
  6. The integrand is therefore at least \(1500/2500 = 0{,}6\) on every segment. By lemma 3.39, item 3, the integral of every segment is at least \(0{,}6\), and the integral along \(\Gamma\) is at least \(8 \cdot 0{,}6 = 4{,}8\), so it is not zero.
  7. If the ring were simply connected, theorem 4.112 and steps 2 and 3 would make the integral along \(\Gamma\) zero. This contradicts step 6.

Source: SADD (PDF p. 53) and KREYSZIG (PDF p. 449) state that a body with a hole through which a curve passes is not simply connected. KREYSZIG (PDF p. 450, Example 4) shows with the same functions \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) that the hypothesis of simple connectedness cannot be omitted. The proof is not from the sources.

The exact value of the integral along the octagon, computed with SymPy, is \(2\pi = 6{,}283\). Where \(2\pi\) comes from we will see in the next subsection: it is the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its radius. For the cut ring, which is simply connected, the theorem does hold. The octagon crosses the cut at the point \(K_1\), so it does not lie in the cut ring.

The theorem gives the existence of a function with the prescribed partial derivatives. For two broken lines from \(P_0\) to \(P\) we go out along the first and back along the second, and the integral along this closed line is zero. We only need in addition that the integral of a segment changes into the opposite number when we traverse it in the opposite direction, and that the set is connected, so that we can reach every point at all.

Theorem 4.114 A field from its partial derivatives in a simply connected set (polje iz parcialnih odvodov v enostavno povezani množici)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points that is connected (definition 1.130) and simply connected (definition 1.136), let \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}}\) be functions continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90) that satisfy condition (4.69) at every point of \(D\), and let \(P_0\) be a point of \(D\). Then:

  1. for every point \(P\) of \(D\) the integrals of the field \(\vek w\) along all broken lines in \(D\) from \(P_0\) to \(P\) (definition 4.110) have the same value, which we denote by \(\varphi(P)\),
  2. \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\), and at every point of \(D\), \(\partial\varphi/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} = w_{\mathrm{l}}\) for \(\ix{l} = x, y, z\), so \(\varphi\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\).
Proof

We must show that the value does not depend on the broken line, and compute the partial derivatives. The first we get from theorem 4.112, the second from lemma 4.111 in a small ball around the point.

1. Independence of the broken line.

  1. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\). Since \(D\) is connected, there is at least one broken line in \(D\) from \(P_0\) to \(P\). For \(P = P_0\) this is also the line \(P_0, P_0\) with one single segment with vector \(\vek 0\).
  2. Opposite direction. Let the segment from \(A\) to \(B\) lie in \(D\). The broken line \(A, B, A\) is closed and lies in \(D\), so by theorem 4.112 its integral is zero. By (4.75) this integral is the sum of the integrals of the segments from \(A\) to \(B\) and from \(B\) to \(A\), so the integral of the segment from \(B\) to \(A\) is the opposite of the integral of the segment from \(A\) to \(B\).
  3. Let \(\Gamma_1\): \(P_0 = A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = P\) and \(\Gamma_2\): \(P_0 = B_0, B_1, \dots, B_{\mathrm{n}} = P\) be broken lines in \(D\). The broken line \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}}, B_{\mathrm{n}-1}, \dots, B_1, B_0\) goes along \(\Gamma_1\) to \(P\) and along \(\Gamma_2\) back to \(P_0\). It is closed, because \(B_0 = A_0\), and it lies in \(D\), because its segments are segments of the lines \(\Gamma_1\) and \(\Gamma_2\).
  4. By (4.75) its integral is the sum of the integrals of the segments of the line \(\Gamma_1\) and of the integrals of the segments from \(B_{\mathrm{k}}\) to \(B_{\mathrm{k}-1}\), which by step 2 are the opposites of the integrals of the segments of the line \(\Gamma_2\). The integral is therefore \(\int_{\Gamma_1} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r - \int_{\Gamma_2} \vek w\cdot\mathrm{d}\vek r\), and by theorem 4.112 it is zero. Both lines give the same value.

2. Partial derivatives.

  1. For \(P = P_0\) we use the line \(P_0, P_0\), whose segment has the vector \(\vek 0\) and the integral zero, so \(\varphi(P_0) = 0\).
  2. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\) and \(\ix{l}\) an index. Since \(D\) is open, there is \(r > 0\) such that the ball \(B\) of all points at distance less than \(r\) from \(P\) lies in \(D\). Let \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\) be the function of lemma 4.111 for this ball, with centre \(P\). By theorem 4.104, as in step 3 of the proof of that lemma, \(\partial\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}} = w_{\mathrm{l}}\) at every point of \(B\).
  3. Let \(|s| < r\). The point \(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\) is at distance \(|s|\) from \(P\), so it is in \(B\), and the segment from \(P\) to it lies in \(B\) (lemma 1.129, item 3). Let \(\Gamma\) be a broken line in \(D\) from \(P_0\) to \(P\). Adding the point \(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\) to it we get a broken line in \(D\) from \(P_0\) to \(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\). By item 1 of this theorem, by (4.75) and by lemma 4.111, item 2,
    \[\varphi(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}) = \varphi(P) + \varphi_{\mathrm{B}}(P + s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}) - \varphi_{\mathrm{B}}(P) .\]
  4. For \(0 < |s| < r\) the difference quotients of the functions \(\varphi\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\) at \(P\) in the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{l}}\) are therefore equal. The quotient of the function \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\) has the limit \(\partial\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,(P) = w_{\mathrm{l}}(P)\), so by definition 1.25 \(\varphi\) also has the partial derivative \(\partial\varphi/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\,(P) = w_{\mathrm{l}}(P)\) at \(P\).
  5. The functions \(w_{\mathrm{l}}\) are continuous by lemma 1.91, so \(\varphi\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\).

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 9.3.3 and 9.3.4 (PDF pp. 84-86), for piecewise smooth paths in connected open sets: the integral does not depend on the path exactly when the integral along every closed path is zero, and exactly when there is a function with the prescribed partial derivatives. KREYSZIG §10.2, Theorems 2 and 3 (PDF p. 449). The proof with broken lines and theorem 4.112 is not from the sources.

The theorem generalizes theorem 4.104 from star-shaped sets to connected and simply connected ones. In a star-shaped set one of the broken lines is the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) itself, and formula (4.70) is the special case \(m = 1\) of the integral (4.75). For the hanging bar above we indeed got the same number along the broken line and along the segment. We need connectedness to reach every point, and simple connectedness so that all paths give the same.

On the cut ring, which is connected (lemma 1.131) and simply connected (lemma 4.109), the theorem gives a function \(\varphi\) for the functions of corollary 4.113. With \(P_0 = K_5 = (-50, 0, 0)\) and broken lines through the points \(K_{\mathrm{i}}\), SymPy gives \(\varphi(K_3) = -1{,}571\) and \(\varphi(K_7) = 1{,}571\), which is a quarter of the number \(2\pi\), just above the cut \(\varphi\) is close to \(-\pi = -3{,}142\), and just below it close to \(\pi\). At the cut \(\varphi\) jumps by \(2\pi\), so it cannot be completed continuously on the whole ring. In the next subsection such a jump will be the jump of the rotation of the material at the cut of the ring.

The ring is not simply connected, because the hole goes through the whole body and a rubber band around it cannot get past it. What about a body with a cavity that the material surrounds on all sides? Such is a thick spherical shell, the body between two spheres with a common centre, which we cut into curved boxes in section 4.3.7 and which we will need in chapter 11. Such is also a cylinder with a spherical cavity, which SADD (PDF p. 53) gives as an example of a simply connected body. Neither is star-shaped, since the segment from a point of the shell to the opposite point passes through the cavity, as it passes through the hole in the ring. But a rubber band around the cavity can be slid over the cavity and shrunk on the other side, like a rubber band taken off a ball (figure 4.96, left). Let us show this precisely.

For the cut ring we described a point by its distance from the axis and by the number \(\tau_{\mathrm{P}}\), which we got with a line from the point \(R\) on the cut. For the shell we do the same, with a line from a point on a sphere. This point must lie in a direction from the centre in which there is no point of the curve, as there is no point of the curve of the cut ring on the cut. A continuous curve can be very complicated, and we cannot show directly that it misses some direction. A broken line, however, has only finitely many segments, and for each we can check which directions it hits. The route therefore has four steps. First we show that we may carry out two continuous deformations of a curve one after the other. Then we deform every closed curve into a broken line, show that the broken line misses some line through the centre, and shrink it without this line as we shrank a curve in the cut ring.

Lemma 4.115 Two deformations in a row (dve preoblikovanji zapored)

Let \(D\) be a set of points, let \(\gamma\) and \(\tilde\gamma\) be closed curves in \(D\) (definition 1.136), and let \(H_1\) be a rule whose input is a point \((s, t)\) of the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) and whose output is a point \(H_1(s, t)\) of \(D\), such that the coordinates of the point \(H_1(s, t)\) are continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\) and \(H_1(s, 0) = \gamma(s)\), \(H_1(s, 1) = \tilde\gamma(s)\) and \(H_1(0, t) = H_1(1, t)\) for all \(s\) and \(t\) in \([0, 1]\). If \(\tilde\gamma\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\), then \(\gamma\) can also be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\).

Proof

We must show that there is a rule \(H\) of definition 1.136 for \(\gamma\). We carry out the rule \(H_1\) and the rule that shrinks \(\tilde\gamma\) one after the other, each in half the time.

  1. By hypothesis there is a rule \(H_2\) with continuous coordinates that shrinks \(\tilde\gamma\) continuously to a point in \(D\): \(H_2(s, 0) = \tilde\gamma(s)\), \(H_2(s, 1) = Z\) for some point \(Z\) and every \(s\), and \(H_2(0, t) = H_2(1, t)\) for every \(t\).
  2. For \(t \in [0, 1]\) let \(a(t) = 2t\) and \(b(t) = 0\) for \(t \le \tfrac12\), and \(a(t) = 1\) and \(b(t) = 2t - 1\) for \(t \ge \tfrac12\). At \(t = \tfrac12\) both formulas give \(a = 1\) and \(b = 0\). The numbers \(a(t)\) and \(b(t)\) lie in \([0, 1]\). For numbers \(t\) and \(t'\), \(|a(t) - a(t')| \le 2\,|t - t'|\) and \(|b(t) - b(t')| \le 2\,|t - t'|\), which we check separately when both numbers are below \(\tfrac12\), both above it, or one on each side. For \(t \le \tfrac12 \le t'\), for example, \(|a(t) - a(t')| = 1 - 2t \le 2t' - 2t\). For an error \(\eta > 0\) the band \(\delta = \eta/2\) therefore satisfies the definition of continuity 1.58, and the functions \(a\) and \(b\) are continuous.
  3. For a point \((s, t)\) of the square let \(H(s, t)\) be the point \(H_1\big(s, a(t)\big)\) moved by the vector from \(\tilde\gamma(s)\) to \(H_2\big(s, b(t)\big)\):
    \[H(s, t) = H_1\big(s, a(t)\big) + \overrightarrow{\tilde\gamma(s)\,H_2\big(s, b(t)\big)} .\]
    For \(t \le \tfrac12\), \(b(t) = 0\) and \(H_2(s, 0) = \tilde\gamma(s)\), so the vector is zero and \(H(s, t) = H_1(s, 2t)\). For \(t \ge \tfrac12\), \(a(t) = 1\) and \(H_1(s, 1) = \tilde\gamma(s)\), so \(H(s, t) = H_2(s, 2t - 1)\). In both cases \(H(s, t)\) is a point of \(D\).
  4. As in step 2 of the proof of lemma 4.107, \(s\) and \(a(t)\) are continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\), and the point \((s, a(t))\) lies in the square. By lemma 4.35 on continuity of a composite function the coordinates of the point \(H_1(s, a(t))\) are therefore continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\), and so are the coordinates of the points \(H_2(s, b(t))\) and \(\tilde\gamma(s)\). The coordinates of the point \(H(s, t)\) are sums and differences of these coordinates, so they are continuous by corollary 1.69, item 1.
  5. At \(t = 0\), \(H(s, 0) = H_1(s, 0) = \gamma(s)\), and at \(t = 1\), \(H(s, 1) = H_2(s, 1) = Z\) for every \(s\). Since \(H_1(0, t) = H_1(1, t)\), \(H_2(0, t) = H_2(1, t)\) and \(\tilde\gamma(0) = \tilde\gamma(1)\), we have \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\). The rule \(H\) meets all requirements of definition 1.136, and we have shrunk \(\gamma\) continuously in \(D\) to the point \(Z\).

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

The rule \(H_1\) is like the rule \(H\) of the definition, except that at time \(1\) the curve is not gathered at a point but has become the curve \(\tilde\gamma\). The lemma says that we may first deform a curve into a simpler one and then shrink that one. The simpler one will be a broken line. We move the curve to it along short segments that lie in small balls in the set, as in the proof of theorem 4.112.

Lemma 4.116 It is enough to shrink broken lines (dovolj je skrčiti lomljene črte)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points. For a closed broken line \(\Gamma\): \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = A_0\) with segments in \(D\) (definition 4.110) let \(\gamma_\Gamma\) be the closed curve that runs along it as in step 1 of the proof of theorem 4.112: \(\gamma_\Gamma(s) = A_{\mathrm{k}-1} + (m\,s - k + 1)\,\overrightarrow{A_{\mathrm{k}-1} A_{\mathrm{k}}}\) for \(k = 1, \dots, m\) and \(s \in [(k - 1)/m,\ k/m]\). If for every such broken line the curve \(\gamma_\Gamma\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\), then \(D\) is simply connected (definition 1.136).

Proof

We must show that every closed curve \(\gamma\) in \(D\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\). We replace the curve by a broken line through its points \(\gamma(p/N)\), move every point of the curve to the broken line along a segment, and use lemma 4.115.

  1. Let \(\gamma\) be a closed curve in \(D\). By lemma 4.48 on the image of a closed bounded set, applied to the closed interval \([0, 1]\), the set \(K\) of all points \(\gamma(s)\) is closed and bounded, and it lies in \(D\). By lemma 4.38 on the neighbourhood of a closed bounded set there is \(\rho > 0\) such that every point at distance less than \(\rho\) from some point of the set \(K\) lies in \(D\).
  2. The coordinates \(\gamma_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuous on \([0, 1]\), so by theorem 3.37 they are uniformly continuous. The definition of uniform continuity 3.36 with the error \(\rho/3\) gives a band for each coordinate, and let \(\delta\) be the smallest of the three bands. By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is a natural number \(N\) with \(N\,\delta > 1\). For \(|s - s'| \le 1/N\) each coordinate of the points \(\gamma(s)\) and \(\gamma(s')\) therefore differs by less than \(\rho/3\), and by step 3 of the proof of lemma 1.66, \(|\gamma(s)\,\gamma(s')| < \rho\).
  3. For \(p = 0, 1, \dots, N\) let \(A_{\mathrm{p}} = \gamma(p/N)\) and let \(\Gamma\) be the broken line \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{N}}\). Since \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\), \(A_{\mathrm{N}} = A_0\), and \(\Gamma\) is closed. For \(p = 1, \dots, N\) let \(B_{\mathrm{p}}\) be the ball of all points at distance less than \(\rho\) from \(A_{\mathrm{p}-1}\). By step 1 it lies in \(D\), and by step 2, \(A_{\mathrm{p}}\) is in it. By lemma 1.129 on the distance to the points of a segment, item 3, the whole segment \(A_{\mathrm{p}-1} A_{\mathrm{p}}\) lies in \(B_{\mathrm{p}}\) and therefore in \(D\).
  4. Let \(\tilde\gamma = \gamma_\Gamma\), that is \(\tilde\gamma(s) = A_{\mathrm{p}-1} + (N\,s - p + 1)\,\overrightarrow{A_{\mathrm{p}-1} A_{\mathrm{p}}}\) for \(s \in [(p - 1)/N,\ p/N]\). The point \(\tilde\gamma(s)\) lies on the segment \(A_{\mathrm{p}-1} A_{\mathrm{p}}\) and therefore in \(B_{\mathrm{p}}\). By steps 1 to 3 of the proof of theorem 4.112, \(\tilde\gamma\) is a closed curve in \(D\).
  5. For a point \((s, t)\) of the square let \(H_1(s, t) = \gamma(s) + t\,\overrightarrow{\gamma(s)\,\tilde\gamma(s)}\), a point of the segment from \(\gamma(s)\) to \(\tilde\gamma(s)\). Let \(s \in [(p - 1)/N,\ p/N]\). By step 2 the point \(\gamma(s)\) is at distance less than \(\rho\) from \(A_{\mathrm{p}-1} = \gamma((p - 1)/N)\), and by step 4 the point \(\tilde\gamma(s)\) lies in \(B_{\mathrm{p}}\). By lemma 1.129, item 3, the point \(H_1(s, t)\) therefore also lies in \(B_{\mathrm{p}}\), and so in \(D\), for every \(t \in [0, 1]\).
  6. The coordinates of the point \(H_1(s, t)\) are \(\gamma_{\mathrm{x}}(s) + t\,\big(\tilde\gamma_{\mathrm{x}}(s) - \gamma_{\mathrm{x}}(s)\big)\) and likewise for \(y\) and \(z\). By step 2 of the proof of lemma 4.107 and corollary 1.69, item 1, they are continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\). At \(t = 0\), \(H_1(s, 0) = \gamma(s)\), at \(t = 1\), \(H_1(s, 1) = \tilde\gamma(s)\), and \(H_1(0, t) = H_1(1, t)\), because \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\) and \(\tilde\gamma(0) = A_0 = \tilde\gamma(1)\).
  7. By hypothesis \(\tilde\gamma\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\). By lemma 4.115 with the rule \(H_1\), \(\gamma\) can therefore also be shrunk to a point in \(D\). The curve \(\gamma\) was arbitrary, so \(D\) is simply connected.

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

Now let us find a line that the broken line avoids. We write the direction of the line with the vector \(\vek e = (1, c, c^2)\) and show that of \(2m + 1\) choices of the number \(c\) at least one is good. Each segment lies in a plane through the centre, and this plane contains only two of these directions.

Lemma 4.117 A broken line misses a line through the centre (lomljena črta zgreši premico skozi središče)

Let \(O\) be the origin and \(\Gamma\) a broken line \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}}\) (definition 1.130) whose segments do not contain the point \(O\). Then among the numbers \(c = 0, 1, \dots, 2m\) there is at least one for which no point \(P\) of the line \(\Gamma\) has a vector \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \overrightarrow{OP}\) of the form \(\mu\,\vek e\), where \(\mu\) is a number and \(\vek e = (1, c, c^2)\). So \(\Gamma\) does not meet the line through \(O\) with direction \(\vek e\).

Proof

We must show that each segment excludes at most two numbers \(c\). To each segment we assign a nonzero vector \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(\vek e\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) whenever the segment meets the line with direction \(\vek e\). Then we show that \(\vek e\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) is zero for at most two numbers \(c\).

  1. Choose \(k\) between \(1\) and \(m\) and write \(\vek a = \overrightarrow{OA_{\mathrm{k}-1}}\) and \(\vek b = \overrightarrow{OA_{\mathrm{k}}}\). The points of the segment \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} A_{\mathrm{k}}\) have the vectors \(\vek r = (1 - t)\,\vek a + t\,\vek b\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). Since the segment does not contain \(O\), \(\vek a \ne \vek 0\), and every point of it that lies on the line has a vector \(\mu\,\vek e\) with \(\mu \ne 0\).
  2. Let \(\vek a\times\vek b \ne \vek 0\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek a\times\vek b\). By lemma 2.12, items 2 and 3, and lemma 2.31, item 4, \(\vek r\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}} = (1 - t)\,\vek a\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) + t\,\vek b\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = 0\). If \(\vek r = \mu\,\vek e\), then \(\mu\,\vek e\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) and so \(\vek e\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\).
  3. Let \(\vek a\times\vek b = \vek 0\). By lemma 2.31, items 1 to 3, \(\vek r\times\vek a = (1 - t)\,\vek a\times\vek a + t\,\vek b\times\vek a = \vek 0\). By (2.32), \(\vek a\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (0, a_{\mathrm{z}}, -a_{\mathrm{y}})\) and \(\vek a\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (-a_{\mathrm{z}}, 0, a_{\mathrm{x}})\). They cannot both be zero, since otherwise \(a_{\mathrm{x}} = a_{\mathrm{y}} = a_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). For \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) we take the one that is not zero, \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek a\times\vek v\) with \(\vek v = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) or \(\vek v = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). If \(\vek r = \mu\,\vek e\), then \(\mu\,\vek e\times\vek a = \vek 0\), so \(\vek e\times\vek a = \vek 0\). The determinant is the scalar triple product of its columns (definition 2.50), which does not change under a cyclic permutation (lemma 2.51, item 1), so \(\vek e\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek e\cdot(\vek a\times\vek v) = \vek v\cdot(\vek e\times\vek a) = 0\).
  4. In both cases \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}} \ne \vek 0\), and if the segment meets the line with direction \(\vek e\), then by (2.6)
    \[\vek e\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}} = n_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{x}} + n_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{y}}\,c + n_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{z}}\,c^2 = 0 .\]
  5. The expression \(p(c) = n_{\mathrm{x}} + n_{\mathrm{y}}\,c + n_{\mathrm{z}}\,c^2\) with a nonzero vector \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) is zero for at most two different numbers \(c\). Suppose it is zero for three different numbers \(c_1\), \(c_2\) and \(c_3\). The difference \(p(c_1) - p(c_2) = (c_1 - c_2)\,\big(n_{\mathrm{y}} + n_{\mathrm{z}}\,(c_1 + c_2)\big)\) is zero, and \(c_1 \ne c_2\), so \(n_{\mathrm{y}} + n_{\mathrm{z}}\,(c_1 + c_2) = 0\). Likewise \(n_{\mathrm{y}} + n_{\mathrm{z}}\,(c_1 + c_3) = 0\). The difference of these two equations is \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\,(c_2 - c_3) = 0\), so \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), then \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), and from \(p(c_1) = 0\) also \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). This contradicts \(\vek n \ne \vek 0\).
  6. The line has \(m\) segments, and by steps 4 and 5 each excludes at most two numbers \(c\). Among the \(2m + 1\) numbers \(0, 1, \dots, 2m\) at least one remains for which no segment meets the line with direction \(\vek e = (1, c, c^2)\).

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

Let us try the lemma on the octagon \(K_1, K_2, \dots, K_8, K_1\) of corollary 4.113. Its points are between \(\sqrt{2000} = 44{,}7\) mm and \(50\) mm from \(O\) (with SymPy), so it also lies in the thick spherical shell with radii 40 mm and 60 mm. All segments lie in the plane \(z = 0\). For the first, \(\overrightarrow{OK_1}\times\overrightarrow{OK_2} = (50, 0, 0)\times(30, 40, 0) = (0, 0, 2000)\), for the others the vector product is \((0, 0, 2000)\) or \((0, 0, 1500)\), so \(\vek e\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) equals \(2000\,c^2\) or \(1500\,c^2\). For \(c = 0\) this is zero. The direction \(\vek e = (1, 0, 0)\) is the direction of the axis \(x\), and the octagon does meet this axis, at the point \(K_1\). For \(c = 1\), however, \(\vek e\cdot\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) is not zero for any segment, so the octagon does not meet the line through \(O\) with direction \((1, 1, 1)\). The lemma allowed a choice among the numbers \(0, 1, \dots, 16\), but already the second one was enough.

Now the shrinking of a broken line that misses the line through \(O\) with the direction of the unit vector \(\hat{\vek e}\). We describe a point \(P\) by its distance \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = |\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}|\) from the centre and by its direction, the unit vector \(\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} = \vek r_{\mathrm{P}}/\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\). We write the direction as a point of a plane, as for the cut ring we wrote the position around the axis with the number \(\tau_{\mathrm{P}}\) (figure 4.96, right). Through the point with vector \(\hat{\vek e}\) on the unit sphere and the point with vector \(\vek n_{\mathrm{P}}\) we lay a line. It meets the plane through \(O\) perpendicular to \(\hat{\vek e}\) at the point with vector

\[\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}} = \frac{\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} - c_{\mathrm{P}}\,\hat{\vek e}}{1 - c_{\mathrm{P}}} , \qquad c_{\mathrm{P}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{P}}\cdot\hat{\vek e} ,\]

when \(\vek n_{\mathrm{P}}\) is not \(\hat{\vek e}\) and so \(c_{\mathrm{P}} < 1\) (step 3 of the proof below). The point with vector \(\hat{\vek e} + (\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} - \hat{\vek e})/(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})\) lies on the line, and its vector is

\[\hat{\vek e} + \frac{\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} - \hat{\vek e}}{1 - c_{\mathrm{P}}} = \frac{(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})\,\hat{\vek e} + \vek n_{\mathrm{P}} - \hat{\vek e}}{1 - c_{\mathrm{P}}} = \frac{\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} - c_{\mathrm{P}}\,\hat{\vek e}}{1 - c_{\mathrm{P}}} = \vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}} .\]

It lies in the plane, because \(\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}\cdot\hat{\vek e} = (c_{\mathrm{P}} - c_{\mathrm{P}})/(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}}) = 0\). For the cut ring this was the line from the point \(R\) on the cut, which met the axis \(y\) at the height \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\,\tau_{\mathrm{P}}\). Books call this map the stereographic projection (stereografska projekcija). BOWER §3.12.1.3 (PDF p. 191) writes the same two formulas that we use below, only with the point on the opposite side of the sphere instead of \(\hat{\vek e}\). The vectors \(\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}\) lie in a plane without holes. There we shrink them along segments towards \(\vek 0\), which means that the points slide towards the point on the side opposite to \(\hat{\vek e}\), and at the same time we change the distance from \(O\) to a number \(R_{\mathrm{m}}\) that lies between the radii of the shell.

Theorem 4.118 A body with a spherical cavity is simply connected (telo z votlino v obliki krogle je enostavno povezano)

Let \(O\) be the origin, \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \overrightarrow{OP}\), and let \(0 < R_1 < R_2\) be numbers.

  1. The thick spherical shell, the set of points \(P\) with \(R_1 < |\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}| < R_2\), is simply connected (definition 1.136).
  2. Let \(C\) be a convex set of points (definition 4.103) that contains all points \(P\) with \(|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}| < R_2\). Then the set of points \(P\) of \(C\) with \(|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}| > R_1\), that is \(C\) without the ball of radius \(R_1\) and its sphere, is simply connected too.
Proof

We must show two items. For the first, by lemma 4.116 we shrink only broken lines. By lemma 4.117 such a line misses a line through \(O\), and without this line we describe points by their distance from \(O\) and by the vector \(\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}\). For the second we first push the curve along rays from \(O\) into the shell.

1. The thick spherical shell.

  1. The shell \(D\) is open. Let \(P\) be a point of it and \(r\) the smaller of the positive numbers \(|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}| - R_1\) and \(R_2 - |\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}|\). For a point \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < r\) the triangle inequality (corollary 2.16, item 2) gives \(|OQ| \le |OP| + |PQ| < R_2\), and from \(|OP| \le |OQ| + |QP|\) it follows that \(|OQ| > |OP| - r \ge R_1\). The point \(Q\) is therefore in \(D\).
  2. By lemma 4.116 it is enough to show that the curve \(\tilde\gamma = \gamma_\Gamma\) that runs along a closed broken line \(\Gamma\): \(A_0, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = A_0\) with segments in \(D\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\). The points of the line are at distance more than \(R_1 > 0\) from \(O\), so the segments do not contain \(O\). By lemma 4.117 there is a vector \(\vek e = (1, c, c^2)\) such that no point of the line has a vector \(\mu\,\vek e\). Let \(\hat{\vek e} = \vek e/|\vek e|\) (lemma 1.19).
  3. Let \(P\) be a point whose vector is not zero and not a positive multiple of the vector \(\hat{\vek e}\). Let \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = |\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}|\), \(\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} = \vek r_{\mathrm{P}}/\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(c_{\mathrm{P}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{P}}\cdot\hat{\vek e}\). By lemma 2.12, \(|\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} - \hat{\vek e}|^2 = 1 - 2c_{\mathrm{P}} + 1 = 2\,(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})\). The vector \(\vek n_{\mathrm{P}}\) is not \(\hat{\vek e}\), since otherwise \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \rho_{\mathrm{P}}\,\hat{\vek e}\), so \(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}} > 0\). Let \(\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}} = (\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} - c_{\mathrm{P}}\,\hat{\vek e})/(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})\). By the same lemma \(\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}\cdot\hat{\vek e} = 0\) and
    \[|\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}|^2 = \frac{1 - 2c_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + c_{\mathrm{P}}^2}{(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})^2} = \frac{(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})(1 + c_{\mathrm{P}})}{(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})^2} = \frac{1 + c_{\mathrm{P}}}{1 - c_{\mathrm{P}}} .\]
  4. For a number \(r\) and a vector \(\vek w\) with \(\vek w\cdot\hat{\vek e} = 0\) let \(\Phi(r, \vek w)\) be the point with vector
    \[\overrightarrow{O\,\Phi(r, \vek w)} = r\,\frac{2\,\vek w + (|\vek w|^2 - 1)\,\hat{\vek e}}{|\vek w|^2 + 1} .\]
    Since \(\vek w\cdot\hat{\vek e} = 0\), lemma 2.12 gives \(|2\,\vek w + (|\vek w|^2 - 1)\,\hat{\vek e}|^2 = 4\,|\vek w|^2 + (|\vek w|^2 - 1)^2 = (|\vek w|^2 + 1)^2\), so the point \(\Phi(r, \vek w)\) is at distance \(|r|\) from \(O\).
  5. For a point \(P\) as in step 3, \(\Phi(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}, \vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}) = P\). By step 3, \(|\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}|^2 + 1 = 2/(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(|\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}|^2 - 1 = 2c_{\mathrm{P}}/(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})\), so
    \[2\,\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}} + (|\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}|^2 - 1)\,\hat{\vek e} = \frac{2\,\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} - 2c_{\mathrm{P}}\,\hat{\vek e} + 2c_{\mathrm{P}}\,\hat{\vek e}}{1 - c_{\mathrm{P}}} = \frac{2\,\vek n_{\mathrm{P}}}{1 - c_{\mathrm{P}}} .\]
    Dividing this by \(|\vek\sigma_{\mathrm{P}}|^2 + 1 = 2/(1 - c_{\mathrm{P}})\) and multiplying by \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\) we get \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{P}} = \vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\).
  6. For \(s \in [0, 1]\), \(\tilde\gamma(s)\) is a point of the line \(\Gamma\), so by step 2 it meets the conditions of step 3. Let \(\rho(s) = \rho_{\tilde\gamma(\mathrm{s})}\), \(\vek w(s) = \vek\sigma_{\tilde\gamma(\mathrm{s})}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{m}} = (R_1 + R_2)/2\). For a point \((s, t)\) of the square let
    \[H(s, t) = \Phi\big((1 - t)\,\rho(s) + t\,R_{\mathrm{m}},\ (1 - t)\,\vek w(s)\big) .\]
    The vector \((1 - t)\,\vek w(s)\) is perpendicular to \(\hat{\vek e}\), so \(H(s, t)\) is defined.
  7. The point \(H(s, t)\) is in \(D\), since by step 4 it is at distance \((1 - t)\,\rho(s) + t\,R_{\mathrm{m}}\) from \(O\), which lies between \(\rho(s)\) and \(R_{\mathrm{m}}\), hence between \(R_1\) and \(R_2\).
  8. The coordinates of the point \(\tilde\gamma(s)\) are continuous functions of the number \(s\) (step 3 of the proof of theorem 4.112). The function \(\rho(s)\) is the square root of the positive sum of the squares of these coordinates, so it is continuous by lemma 4.108, item 1, and corollary 1.64. The coordinates of the vector \(\vek n_{\tilde\gamma(\mathrm{s})}\) are quotients with the denominator \(\rho(s) > 0\), the number \(c_{\tilde\gamma(\mathrm{s})}\) is a sum of products, and the coordinates of the vector \(\vek w(s)\) are quotients with the denominator \(1 - c_{\tilde\gamma(\mathrm{s})} > 0\). By the same lemma, item 2, and the same corollary they are all continuous, and by step 2 of the proof of lemma 4.107 they are continuous as functions of the point \((s, t)\) too. The coordinates of the point \(H(s, t)\) are sums, products and quotients of these functions and the number \(t\), with the denominator \((1 - t)^2\,|\vek w(s)|^2 + 1 \ge 1\), so they are continuous by corollary 1.69, item 1, and lemma 4.108, item 2.
  9. At \(t = 0\), step 5 gives \(H(s, 0) = \Phi(\rho(s), \vek w(s)) = \tilde\gamma(s)\). At \(t = 1\), \(H(s, 1) = \Phi(R_{\mathrm{m}}, \vek 0)\), the point with vector \(-R_{\mathrm{m}}\,\hat{\vek e}\), for every \(s\). Since \(\tilde\gamma(0) = \tilde\gamma(1)\), \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\). We have shrunk the curve \(\tilde\gamma\) continuously to a point in \(D\), and by lemma 4.116, \(D\) is simply connected.

2. A set with a cavity.

  1. Let \(D'\) be the set of points \(P\) of \(C\) with \(|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}| > R_1\) and \(\gamma\) a closed curve in \(D'\). The points \(\gamma(s)\) are not \(O\). Let \(M(s)\) be the point with vector \(R_{\mathrm{m}}\,\vek r_{\gamma(\mathrm{s})}/|\vek r_{\gamma(\mathrm{s})}|\), the point of the ray from \(O\) through \(\gamma(s)\) at distance \(R_{\mathrm{m}}\) from \(O\). As in step 8 its coordinates are continuous functions of the number \(s\), and \(M(0) = M(1)\). The curve \(M\) is therefore a closed curve in the shell \(R_1 < |\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}| < R_2\).
  2. For a point \((s, t)\) of the square let \(H_1(s, t) = \gamma(s) + t\,\overrightarrow{\gamma(s)\,M(s)}\). Its vector is \(\big(1 - t + t\,R_{\mathrm{m}}/|\vek r_{\gamma(\mathrm{s})}|\big)\,\vek r_{\gamma(\mathrm{s})}\), a positive multiple of the vector \(\vek r_{\gamma(\mathrm{s})}\), so it is at distance \((1 - t)\,|\vek r_{\gamma(\mathrm{s})}| + t\,R_{\mathrm{m}} > R_1\) from \(O\). The point \(M(s)\) is at distance \(R_{\mathrm{m}} < R_2\) from \(O\), so it is in \(C\), and \(\gamma(s)\) is in \(C\) too. The set \(C\) is convex, so the whole segment between these two points lies in it, and with it \(H_1(s, t)\). The point \(H_1(s, t)\) is therefore in \(D'\).
  3. The coordinates of the point \(H_1(s, t)\) are continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\) by step 2 of the proof of lemma 4.107 and corollary 1.69, item 1. At \(t = 0\), \(H_1(s, 0) = \gamma(s)\), at \(t = 1\), \(H_1(s, 1) = M(s)\), and \(H_1(0, t) = H_1(1, t)\), because \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\) and \(M(0) = M(1)\).
  4. By the first part the curve \(M\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in the shell. The shell lies in \(D'\), since by hypothesis each of its points is in \(C\) and at distance more than \(R_1\) from \(O\). By lemma 4.115 with the rule \(H_1\), \(\gamma\) can therefore be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D'\), and \(D'\) is simply connected.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.2 (PDF p. 449) gives the domain between two concentric spheres, and SADD §2.6 (PDF p. 53) a cylinder with a spherical cavity, as simply connected sets, both without proof. The formulas of the stereographic projection are written in BOWER §3.12.1.3 (PDF p. 191) with the pole on the opposite side. The proof is not from the sources.

Let us try the theorem on the bodies of the introduction. The thick spherical shell with inner radius 40 mm and outer radius 60 mm of section 4.3.7 is simply connected by item 1. The octagon of the test of the lemma above, which cannot be shrunk in the ring, slides in the shell over the cavity to the point on the line with direction \((1, 1, 1)\) at distance 50 mm from \(O\) (figure 4.96, left). For the ring we cannot use the shrinking of the proof, because the ring has no points in all directions from \(O\), for example none on the axis \(z\), and by corollary 4.113 no rule shrinks the octagon in the ring. Let a cylinder with radius 30 mm and length 100 mm have the axis \(z\) and its centre at \(O\), and let it contain a spherical cavity with radius 10 mm and centre \(O\). The set \(C\) of interior points of the solid cylinder, the points with \(x^2 + y^2 < 900\) and \(|z| < 50\) in millimetres, is convex, as we showed for the round bar in subsection 4.7.6. It contains all points with \(|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}| < 30\), since for them \(x^2 + y^2 \le |\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}|^2 < 900\) and \(|z| \le |\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}| < 30 < 50\) (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.66). By item 2 of the theorem with \(R_1 = 10\) and \(R_2 = 30\), the set of interior points of the cylinder with the cavity, the points of \(C\) with \(|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}| > 10\), is simply connected. The cavity may also have its centre elsewhere. We then put the origin at its centre, and the theorem holds if the cylinder contains a ball about this centre that is larger than the cavity. The same holds for a box with a spherical cavity, since a box is convex too.

4.7.9 Displacements in a simply connected body

Now let us prove the sufficiency of the compatibility equations for connected and simply connected bodies. The task is the same as in subsection 4.7.7. In an open set of points \(D\), for example the set of interior points of a body, six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are given, which we complete to nine with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). Their partial derivatives of first and second order exist and are continuous, and the compatibility equations (1.68) hold at every point of \(D\). We look for a continuously differentiable displacement field whose small strain tensor has the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Only the hypothesis on the set is new: instead of star-shaped, \(D\) is connected and simply connected. The route is the same as in the proof of theorem 4.106. First we find the rotation, then the displacement, both times as a function with prescribed partial derivatives, which is now given by theorem 4.114 instead of theorem 4.104.

Theorem 4.119 Sufficiency of the compatibility equations in a simply connected body (zadostnost enačb kompatibilnosti v enostavno povezanem telesu)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points that is connected (definition 1.130) and simply connected (definition 1.136), and let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}}\), where the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), be functions whose partial derivatives of first and second order exist and are continuous at every point of \(D\) and which satisfy the compatibility equations (1.68) at every point of \(D\). Let \(P_0\) be a point of \(D\). Then there is a displacement field \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\), continuously differentiable on \(D\), whose components also have continuous second partial derivatives at every point of \(D\), with \(\vek u(P_0) = \vek 0\), and at every point of \(D\)

\[\frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} \quad \text{for all } \ix{i}, \ix{j} .\]

We get it with the formulas (4.72) and (4.73) in which the integral along the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) is replaced by the integral along any broken line in \(D\) from \(P_0\) to \(P\) (definition 4.110). If \(D\) is the set of interior points of a body, the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are therefore compatible strains (definition 1.123).

Proof

We must show the same as in the proof of theorem 4.106. That proof used the star-shaped set only through theorem 4.104, so we repeat its steps with theorem 4.114.

1. Rotation.

  1. We choose indices \(i\) and \(j\) and for \(k = x, y, z\) write \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\). As in steps 1 and 2 of the proof of theorem 4.106, which do not use the star-shaped set, the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(D\) and by lemma 4.105 satisfy condition (4.69).
  2. By theorem 4.114 with the functions \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \psi_{\mathrm{k}}\), the integral of the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) along all broken lines in \(D\) from \(P_0\) to \(P\) has the same value \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P)\). The function \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P_0) = 0\), and
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} \quad \text{for } \ix{k} = x, y, z .\]
  3. When we swap \(i\) and \(j\), the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) change sign. The integral along the same broken line is a sum of integrals over \([0, 1]\), which change sign because the integral is linear (lemma 3.39, item 1), so \(\omega_{\mathrm{ji}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every point of \(D\). For \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are zero, so \(\omega_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\).

2. Displacement.

  1. We choose an index \(i\) and for \(j = x, y, z\) write \(w_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\). As in steps 5 and 6 of the proof of theorem 4.106, which use only the derivatives of step 2, the functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(D\) and satisfy condition (4.69).
  2. By theorem 4.114 the integral of the functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\) along all broken lines in \(D\) from \(P_0\) to \(P\) has the same value \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\). The function \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P_0) = 0\), and
    \[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} \quad \text{for } \ix{j} = x, y, z .\]
  3. The second partial derivatives of the function \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) are partial derivatives of the functions \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\), which exist and are continuous by step 4.

3. Strain.

  1. By step 5, step 3 and the symmetry \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), at every point of \(D\)
    \[\frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\Big) = \frac12\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ji}}\big) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]

Source: SADD §2.6, (2.6.3)-(2.6.7) (PDF pp. 52-53), where the displacement is an integral along an arbitrary curve from \(P_0\) to \(P\) and the independence of the curve follows from Stokes's theorem. SADD (PDF p. 53): the compatibility equations are necessary and sufficient conditions for continuous single-valued displacements in simply connected regions. The proof with broken lines and theorem 4.114 is not from the sources.

The proof has shown that for sufficiency only simple connectedness matters, not the shape of the body. The formulas for the rotation and the displacement are the same as for a star-shaped body, only the path from \(P_0\) to \(P\) may be a broken line that avoids notches and recesses. Simple connectedness makes sure that it does not matter which such line we choose. This also proves theorem 1.137 of section 1.18.5, which is this theorem for the set of interior points of a body. This set is open, since by lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point every point close to an interior point is again interior. By corollary 1.135 on two fields with equal strains, the field is determined up to a small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\), and with such a displacement we fit it to the supports of the body.

Let us try the theorem on a body that is simply connected but not star-shaped (figure 4.97). A steel U-shaped bracket is a thin plate of thickness 2 mm. Lengths are in millimetres. The axis \(x\) points horizontally along the bottom of the bracket, the axis \(y\) vertically up along the arms, the axis \(z\) perpendicular to the plate, and the origin is at the lower left corner in the middle plane of the plate. The set \(U\) of interior points of the bracket consists of the points \((x, y, z)\) with \(|z| < 1\) that lie in the bottom, where \(0 < x < 30\) and \(0 < y < 10\), in the left arm, where \(0 < x < 10\) and \(0 < y < 40\), or in the right arm, where \(20 < x < 30\) and \(0 < y < 40\). Nothing holds or loads the bracket. We heat it so that the temperature increases with height, by 1 K per millimetre, measured from the temperature at the height \(y = 0\), at which the bracket is free of stress. This is an idealization that gives a simple strain field. How heat would really spread in the bracket does not matter here, because the task is purely geometric. A small piece that nothing constrains stretches in all directions by \(\alpha\,\Delta T\) (definition 3.13), with \(\alpha = 15 \cdot 10^{-6}\) 1/K for the structural steel of chapter 3. The prescribed strains are therefore

\[\begin{aligned} &\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \kappa\,y , \\ &\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 , \\ &\kappa = 15 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \tfrac{1}{\text{K}} \cdot 1\ \tfrac{\text{K}}{\text{mm}} = 1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{mm}^{-1} . \end{aligned}\]

At the top of the arms, at \(y = 40\), the strain is \(6{,}0 \cdot 10^{-4}\), below the limit \(0{,}001\) for small strains. The functions are polynomials, so they have continuous derivatives of all orders. Their second derivatives are zero, because the strains are linear in \(y\), so all six compatibility equations hold in the form \(0 = 0\). Let us check the hypotheses on the set as well.

  1. The set \(U\) is open. Let \(P\) be a point of the left arm and \(\eta\) the smallest of the positive numbers \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(10 - x_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(40 - y_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(1 - |z_{\mathrm{P}}|\). For a point \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \eta\) every coordinate differs from the coordinate of the point \(P\) by less than \(\eta\) (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.66), so \(Q\) also lies in the left arm. For \(z\) we used the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|z_{\mathrm{Q}}| \le |z_{\mathrm{P}}| + |z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}| < 1\). The same holds for points of the bottom and of the right arm.
  2. The set \(U\) is connected. From the point \(P\) we go vertically to the point \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, 5, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), then straight to the point \((x_{\mathrm{Q}}, 5, z_{\mathrm{Q}})\) and vertically to \(Q\). On the first segment only \(y\) changes, and it stays between \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(5\), so the segment stays in the arm of the point \(P\) or in the bottom. On the second, \(y = 5\), \(x\) is between \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) and \(z\) between \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{Q}}\), so the segment lies in the bottom. The third is like the first.
  3. The set \(U\) is not star-shaped. Let \(P_0\) be a point of \(U\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}_0} \le 15\) and \(T = (25, 39, 0)\) a point at the top of the right arm. The point \(P_0 + \lambda\,\overrightarrow{P_0 T}\) with \(\lambda = (19 - x_{\mathrm{P}_0})/(25 - x_{\mathrm{P}_0}) = 1 - 6/(25 - x_{\mathrm{P}_0})\) has the coordinate \(x = 19\). Since \(25 - x_{\mathrm{P}_0} \ge 10\), \(\lambda \ge 0{,}4\), and its coordinate \(y\) is \((1 - \lambda)\,y_{\mathrm{P}_0} + 39\,\lambda \ge 15{,}6\). A point with \(x = 19\) and \(y > 10\) is not in \(U\), since it lies in the gap between the arms. The segment from \(P_0\) to \(T\) therefore leaves \(U\). For \(x_{\mathrm{P}_0} \ge 15\) we take \(T = (5, 39, 0)\) and the point with \(x = 11\). So from no point of \(U\) do we see all points of \(U\).
  4. The set \(U\) is simply connected. Let \(\gamma\) be a closed curve in \(U\) with coordinates \(x(s)\), \(y(s)\), \(z(s)\). The shrinking has two parts: first we lower the curve vertically towards the bottom, only then do we move it horizontally. Let \(m(t) = 0\) for \(t \le 6/7\) and \(m(t) = 7t - 6\) for \(t \ge 6/7\), and
    \[H(s, t) = \Big(x(s) + m(t)\,\big(15 - x(s)\big),\ (1 - t)\,y(s) + 5\,t,\ (1 - t)\,z(s)\Big) .\]
    For numbers \(t\) and \(t'\), \(|m(t) - m(t')| \le 7\,|t - t'|\), which we check separately when both numbers are below \(6/7\), both above it, or one on each side, so \(m\) is continuous. The coordinates of \(H\) are therefore continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\) by step 2 of the proof of lemma 4.107 and corollary 1.69. At \(t = 0\), \(H(s, 0) = \gamma(s)\), at \(t = 1\), \(H(s, 1) = (15, 5, 0)\), and \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\), because \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\).
  5. The points \(H(s, t)\) lie in \(U\). The coordinate \(z\) has absolute value at most \(|z(s)| < 1\). The coordinate \(y\) lies between \(y(s)\) and \(5\), hence between \(0\) and \(40\), and the coordinate \(x\) between \(x(s)\) and \(15\), hence between \(0\) and \(30\). For \(t \le 6/7\), \(x\) equals \(x(s)\). If \(\gamma(s)\) is in an arm, \(H(s, t)\) is in the same arm. If \(\gamma(s)\) is in the bottom, \(y(s)\) and \(5\) are smaller than \(10\), so \(H(s, t)\) is in the bottom. For \(t > 6/7\), \(y\) is smaller than \((1 - t) \cdot 40 + 5\,t = 40 - 35\,t < 10\), so \(H(s, t)\) is in the bottom.

For the computation we choose the point \(P_0 = A = (5, 35, 0)\) at the top of the left arm and the point \(B = (25, 35, 0)\) at the top of the right one. The segment from \(A\) to \(B\) passes through the point \((15, 35, 0)\) in the gap, where there is no material, so we cannot use the formulas of theorem 4.106 along it. We take the broken lines

\[\Gamma_1:\ A,\ (5, 5, 0),\ (25, 5, 0),\ B , \qquad \Gamma_2:\ A,\ (8, 9, 0),\ (15, 1, 0),\ (22, 9, 0),\ B .\]

Both lie in \(U\). The line \(\Gamma_1\) goes vertically down to the bottom, horizontally across the bottom and vertically up, and the line \(\Gamma_2\) goes obliquely down through the left arm, zigzags along the bottom and goes obliquely up through the right arm, so that the two lines touch only at \(A\) and \(B\). Of the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) of the proof of the theorem, the only ones different from zero are \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/\partial y - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}/\partial x = \kappa\) for the pair \(x\), \(y\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}/\partial z - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}/\partial y = -\kappa\) for the pair \(y\), \(z\). SymPy gives the same values at the point \(B\) along both lines,

\[\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(B) = 3{,}0 \cdot 10^{-4} , \qquad \vek u(B) = (0{,}0105,\ -0{,}0030,\ 0)\ \text{mm} ,\]

as the theorem demands. Along \(\Gamma_1\), on the way, for example \(\vek u(5, 5, 0) = (0, -0{,}0090, 0)\) mm: the left arm between \(y = 5\) and \(y = 35\) lengthens by \(\int_5^{35} \kappa\,y\,\mathrm{d}y = \kappa\,(35^2 - 5^2)/2 = 0{,}0090\) mm, and since \(A\) is at rest, the point at the bottom moves down.

What do the numbers mean? The component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(B) = 0{,}0105\) mm says by how much the distance between the tops of the arms increases in the first approximation, since \(A\) is at rest and the vector from \(A\) to \(B\) points along the axis \(x\). Why exactly \(0{,}0105\) mm? The field \(\kappa\,(x\,y,\ (y^2 - x^2 - z^2)/2,\ y\,z)\), defined in all of space, has the same strains, which we check by differentiating. This field also moves the points in the gap, where there is no material, and it lengthens a horizontal fibre at the height \(35\) as a steel fibre at that height would lengthen: by \(\kappa \cdot 35 \cdot 20\ \text{mm} = 0{,}0105\) mm. By corollary 1.135 our field on \(U\) differs from it only by a small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), which does not change the distance \(|AB|\) in the first approximation, since \((\mat W\,\overrightarrow{AB})\cdot\overrightarrow{AB} = 0\) (corollary 1.104, item 1). So the arms move apart as if they were connected at the top. The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(B) = -0{,}0030\) mm says that \(B\) moves down relative to the line that is horizontal at \(A\). The bracket bends like the strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\) of section 1.18.3, with \(1/R = \kappa\): the upper fibres stretch more than the lower ones, and over a distance of \(20\) mm the bracket drops by \(\kappa \cdot 20^2/2 = 0{,}0030\) mm. The rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(B) = \kappa \cdot 20 = 3{,}0 \cdot 10^{-4}\) says by how much the material near \(B\) turns relative to the material near \(A\).

Now let us return to the ring of section 1.18.5. By corollary 4.113 the ring is not simply connected, so the theorem does not apply to it. The cut ring, however, is connected (lemma 1.131) and simply connected (lemma 4.109), so it has a displacement field for any strains that satisfy the compatibility equations in the ring. The question is whether the field matches on the two sides of the cut. The difference between the sides, the jump of the displacement, says exactly what the whole ring lacks. Let the cut be the set \(S\) of points of the ring with \(y = 0\) and \(x > 0\). We look at the displacement at points of the ring that approach a point \(C\) of the cut from above, with \(y > 0\), and from below, with \(y < 0\) (figure 4.98). Around the cut we need a star-shaped set in which theorem 4.106 gives a displacement field also across the cut. Such is the set \(G\) of points with \(x > 40\), \(x^2 + y^2 < 3600\) and \(|z| < c\), the segment of the ring cut off by the plane \(x = 40\).

Lemma 4.120 The jump of the displacement across a cut (skok pomika na rezu)

Lengths are in millimetres. Let the ring and the cut ring be as in lemma 1.131 and \(S\) the cut, the set of points of the ring with \(y = 0\) and \(x > 0\). Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}}\) be functions whose partial derivatives of first and second order exist and are continuous at every point of the ring and which satisfy the compatibility equations (1.68) at every point of the ring. Let \(\vek u\) be a displacement field, continuously differentiable on the cut ring, whose small strain tensor has the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every point of the cut ring. Such a field exists by theorem 4.119. Then:

  1. for every point \(C\) of the cut there are vectors \(\vek u^+(C)\) and \(\vek u^-(C)\) such that for every sequence of points \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of the ring with \(y_{\mathrm{Q}_\mathrm{n}} > 0\) converging to \(C\) the sequence \(\vek u(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(\vek u^+(C)\), and for every sequence of points of the ring with \(y < 0\) converging to \(C\) the values of \(\vek u\) converge to \(\vek u^-(C)\),
  2. there are a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) such that the jump of the displacement is
    \[\vek u^+(C) - \vek u^-(C) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{C}} \tag{4.76}\]
    at every point \(C\) of the cut,
  3. on the whole ring there is a continuously differentiable displacement field whose small strain tensor has the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) exactly when \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(\mat W = \mat 0\).
Proof

We must show that on each side of the cut \(\vek u\) agrees, up to a rigid displacement, with a field that is continuous also across the cut, and that the rigid displacements on the two sides differ by \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\). We do this in the set \(G\) of points \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} > 40\), \(x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 < 3600\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\), which is divided into the upper part \(G^+\) with \(y_{\mathrm{P}} > 0\) and the lower part \(G^-\) with \(y_{\mathrm{P}} < 0\) (figure 4.98).

1. The set around the cut.

  1. The set \(G\) lies in the ring. For a point of it \(x_{\mathrm{P}} > 40 > 0\), so \(x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 \ge x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 > 1600\), and the distance from the axis \(z\) lies between \(40\) and \(60\) (lemma 1.28). Every point of the cut lies in \(G\), since it has \(y = 0\) and \(40 < x < 60\).
  2. The sets \(G\), \(G^+\) and \(G^-\) are open. The functions \(x\), \(y\), \(x^2 + y^2\) and \(z\) are continuous (corollary 1.69), so for a point \(P\) of \(G\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that at points \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) their values differ from the values at \(P\) by less than the smallest of the positive numbers \(x_{\mathrm{P}} - 40\), \(3600 - x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 - y_{\mathrm{P}}^2\) and \(c - |z_{\mathrm{P}}|\), as in steps 2 and 3 of the proof of lemma 1.131. These points are in \(G\). For \(G^+\) and \(G^-\) we add the number \(|y_{\mathrm{P}}|\).
  3. The sets \(G\), \(G^+\) and \(G^-\) are convex. Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be points of \(G\) and \(T = P + \lambda\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\) with \(0 \le \lambda \le 1\). The coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{T}}\) lie between the coordinates of the points \(P\) and \(Q\), so \(x_{\mathrm{T}} > 40\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{T}}| < c\), and for \(G^\pm\), \(y_{\mathrm{T}}\) has the same sign as \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{Q}}\). The points \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, 0)\) and \((x_{\mathrm{Q}}, y_{\mathrm{Q}}, 0)\) are at distance less than \(60\) from \(O\), so by lemma 1.129, item 3, the point \((x_{\mathrm{T}}, y_{\mathrm{T}}, 0)\) is also at distance less than \(60\) from \(O\). Convex sets are star-shaped, and any two of their points are joined by one segment, so they are also connected (definition 1.130).
  4. The sets \(G^+\) and \(G^-\) lie in the cut ring, because they lie in the ring and have no points with \(y = 0\).

2. The displacement on both sides of the cut.

  1. By theorem 4.106 there is a displacement field \(\vek v\) on the set \(G\), continuously differentiable on \(G\), with small strain tensor components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  2. The fields \(\vek u\) and \(\vek v\) are continuously differentiable on the connected open set \(G^+\) and have equal strains there. By corollary 1.135 there are a constant vector \(\vek a^+\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W^+\) such that \(\vek u(P) = \vek v(P) + \vek a^+ + \mat W^+\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) for every point \(P\) of \(G^+\). Likewise \(\vek u(P) = \vek v(P) + \vek a^- + \mat W^-\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) for \(P\) in \(G^-\).
  3. Let \(C\) be a point of the cut and \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) a sequence of points of the ring with \(y > 0\) converging to \(C\). Since \(C\) is in the open set \(G\), there is \(r > 0\) such that all points at distance less than \(r\) from \(C\) are in \(G\), and from some index on the terms \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) are that close to \(C\) (definition 1.65). These terms are in \(G^+\), and for them step 6 gives \(\vek u(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) = \vek v(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) + \vek a^+ + \mat W^+\,\vek r_{\mathrm{Q}_\mathrm{n}}\).
  4. The field \(\vek v\) is continuous at \(C\) (lemma 1.91), and the components of the vector \(\mat W^+\,\vek r_{\mathrm{Q}}\) are polynomials in the coordinates of the point \(Q\) (corollary 1.69). By lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points and lemma 1.60 on limit laws for sequences, applied to each component, \(\vek u(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) therefore converges to
    \[\vek u^+(C) = \vek v(C) + \vek a^+ + \mat W^+\,\vek r_{\mathrm{C}} .\]
    The limit does not depend on the first terms of the sequence, since the definition of the limit looks only at the terms from some index on. In the same way the values in sequences with \(y < 0\) converge to \(\vek u^-(C) = \vek v(C) + \vek a^- + \mat W^-\,\vek r_{\mathrm{C}}\). This is item 1.
  5. We subtract: \(\vek u^+(C) - \vek u^-(C) = (\vek a^+ - \vek a^-) + (\mat W^+ - \mat W^-)\,\vek r_{\mathrm{C}}\). Let \(\vek a = \vek a^+ - \vek a^-\) and \(\mat W = \mat W^+ - \mat W^-\). The matrix \(\mat W\) is antisymmetric, because \(\mat W^\T = (\mat W^+)^\T - (\mat W^-)^\T = -\mat W^+ + \mat W^- = -\mat W\). The numbers \(\vek a\) and \(\mat W\) do not depend on \(C\). This is item 2.

3. A field on the whole ring.

  1. Let \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(\mat W = \mat 0\), that is \(\vek a^+ = \vek a^-\) and \(\mat W^+ = \mat W^-\). Let \(\tilde{\vek u}(P) = \vek u(P)\) at points of the cut ring and \(\tilde{\vek u}(P) = \vek v(P) + \vek a^+ + \mat W^+\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) at points of \(G\). At points that are in both sets, that is in \(G^+\) and \(G^-\), the two formulas agree by step 6, so \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is well defined on the whole ring.
  2. Every point of the ring has around it a ball that lies in the cut ring or in \(G\), because both sets are open and together cover the ring. In this ball \(\tilde{\vek u}\) equals \(\vek u\) or \(\vek v + \vek a^+ + \mat W^+\,\vek r\). Partial derivatives are limits of difference quotients, which use only points near the point, so the partial derivatives of the field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) there equal the partial derivatives of one of these two continuously differentiable fields. The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is therefore continuously differentiable on the ring, and its strains are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), because the added \(\vek a^+ + \mat W^+\,\vek r\) does not change the strains (theorem 1.134, item 2).
  3. Conversely, let the ring have a continuously differentiable field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) with strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The cut ring is connected, so by corollary 1.135 \(\vek u(P) = \tilde{\vek u}(P) + \vek b + \mat V\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) at each of its points, with a constant vector \(\vek b\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat V\). The right side is continuous on the whole ring, so as in step 8 \(\vek u^+(C) = \vek u^-(C) = \tilde{\vek u}(C) + \vek b + \mat V\,\vek r_{\mathrm{C}}\), and \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{C}} = \vek 0\) at every point \(C\) of the cut.
  4. We insert the points of the cut \(C_1 = (50, 0, 0)\), \(C_2 = (51, 0, 0)\) and \(C_3 = (50, 0, c/2)\). The difference of the equations at \(C_2\) and \(C_1\) gives \(\mat W\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek 0\), and the difference at \(C_3\) and \(C_1\) gives \(\mat W\,(c/2)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek 0\). The columns \(x\) and \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat W\) are therefore zero (definition 1.96). By antisymmetry \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -W_{\mathrm{yx}}\) and \(W_{\mathrm{zy}} = -W_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero too, and the diagonal holds zeros, so \(\mat W = \mat 0\). The equation at \(C_1\) then gives \(\vek a = \vek 0\).

Source: BARBER §2.2.1 (PDF pp. 47-48) says that the sides of a cut in a multiply connected body can differ only by six numbers, the three translations and three rotations of a rigid displacement, so that each hole adds six conditions, and in footnote 5 sketches a proof with integrals whose path does not cross the cut. SADD (PDF pp. 53-54) writes the same conditions as Cesàro integrals around the hole. The proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says two things. First, the jump at the cut is not arbitrary. On each side the field agrees with the field \(\vek v\) that the theorem for star-shaped bodies gives in the segment \(G\) across the cut, and each side has its own small rigid displacement. The jump is the difference of these two rigid displacements, so it is the same rigid displacement at all points of the cut, determined by six numbers: the three components of the vector \(\vek a\) and the three elements \(W_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{yz}}\) of the matrix \(\mat W\). Second, the six numbers are exactly what the whole ring lacks. If they are zero, we glue the fields of the two sides together, and otherwise there is no field on the whole ring. The jump does not depend on which field \(\vek u\) on the cut ring we choose.
