By corollary 1.135 two such fields differ by a rigid displacement, which is continuous across the cut and moves both sides equally. The proof used only three properties of the ring: the cut ring is connected and simply connected, the cut lies in a convex open set, and this set without the cut falls into two convex parts. For another body with a hole and a cut with these properties the proof goes the same way. For bodies with several holes we make several cuts, and BARBER (PDF p. 48) says that each adds six conditions.

Let us try the lemma on the ring of section 1.18.5. We restate the setting. A thin steel ring with inner radius 40 mm and outer radius 60 mm lies in the plane \(z = 0\), with its centre at the origin \(O\). Every short fibre that lies along the ring, that is around the hole, shortens by one thousandth. Every short fibre that points towards the centre keeps its length. Right angles between these two kinds of fibres stay right. At a point \((x, y, z)\) of the ring the direction around the hole has the unit vector \(\vek e = (-y, x, 0)/\rho\) and the direction towards the centre \(\vek n = (x, y, 0)/\rho\), where \(\rho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\). The components

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -k\,\frac{y^2}{\rho^2} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,\frac{x^2}{\rho^2} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = k\,\frac{x\,y}{\rho^2} , \qquad k = 0{,}001 ,\]

with the other three zero, give exactly these strains. The vectors \(\vek n\), \(\vek e\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the directions of turned axes, and by (2.47) the components of the tensor in these axes are \(\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = 0\), \(\vek e^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek e = -k\) and \(\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek e = 0\), which we computed with SymPy. By section 1.17.4 the first two are the normal strains of fibres in the directions \(\vek n\) and \(\vek e\), and the third is the shear strain, which measures the change of the right angle between them. The functions are quotients of polynomials with the denominator \(\rho^2 > 1600\). By lemma 4.108, item 3, their partial derivatives are again quotients of polynomials with denominators that are powers of the number \(\rho^2\), so by item 2 of the same lemma they are continuous, and so are the second derivatives. SymPy checks that the functions satisfy all six compatibility equations at every point of the ring.

By theorem 4.119 the cut ring has a displacement field with these strains. We take \(P_0 = K_5 = (-50, 0, 0)\) and broken lines through the points \(K_1, \dots, K_8\) of the proof of lemma 1.131: to the upper points we go through \(K_4\), to the lower ones through \(K_6\). For the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the functions of the proof of the theorem are \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}} = -k\,y/\rho^2\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = k\,x/\rho^2\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), \(k\) times the functions of corollary 4.113. SymPy gives, in millimetres,

\[\vek u(K_3) = (-0{,}0785,\ 0,\ 0) , \qquad \vek u(K_7) = (-0{,}0785,\ 0,\ 0) ,\]

with the rotations \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(K_3) = -0{,}00157\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(K_7) = 0{,}00157\). The point \(K_3 = (0, 50, 0)\) moves along its circle towards \(K_5\), by \(0{,}001\) times the arc from \(K_5\) to \(K_3\), which is a quarter of the circumference \(2\pi \cdot 50\) mm \(= 314{,}16\) mm: \(0{,}001 \cdot 78{,}54\) mm \(= 0{,}0785\) mm. The point \(K_7\) moves equally far, also towards \(K_5\). The ring closes like a fan, symmetrically about \(K_5\), as in figure 1.154.

At the cut we get a jump. At points only \(10^{-6}\) mm from the cut, SymPy gives

\[\vek u(50,\ \pm 10^{-6},\ 0) = (0,\ \pm 0{,}1571,\ 0)\ \text{mm} , \qquad \omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(50,\ \pm 10^{-6},\ 0) = \mp 0{,}003142 ,\]

where the upper sign holds above the cut. At \(x = 41\) the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) is \(\pm 0{,}1288\) mm, at \(x = 59\) it is \(\pm 0{,}1854\) mm, and the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is smaller than \(10^{-8}\) mm in absolute value. As the points approach the cut, the values change only in the ninth decimal place. The jump of the displacement at all three points of the cut is therefore

\[\begin{aligned} &\vek u^+(C) - \vek u^-(C) = (0,\ 2\pi k\,x_{\mathrm{C}},\ 0) = \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{C}} , \\ &W_{\mathrm{yx}} = 2\pi k = 0{,}006283 , \\ &W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}006283 , \end{aligned}\]

and the other elements of the matrix \(\mat W\) and the vector \(\vek a\) are zero. At \(x_{\mathrm{C}} = 41\) mm this is \(0{,}2576\) mm, at \(50\) mm it is \(0{,}3142\) mm and at \(59\) mm \(0{,}3707\) mm. The jump of the rotation is the element \(W_{\mathrm{xy}}\) too: \(-0{,}003142 - 0{,}003142 = -0{,}006283\).

The numbers at the cut are computed at points near the cut. That \(\mat W\) really is not zero, let us also show without approximations. Let \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) be the rotation of the field \(\vek u\) on the cut ring, \(\omega^G_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the rotation of the field \(\vek v\) of the proof of the lemma on the set \(G\), and \(P = (45, 10, 0)\) a point of \(G^+\) and \(P' = (45, -10, 0)\) a point of \(G^-\).

  1. The fields \(\vek u\) and \(\vek v\) have continuous second partial derivatives (theorems 4.119 and 4.106) and the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By lemma 1.128, item 1, the partial derivatives of the functions \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\omega^G_{\mathrm{xy}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are therefore \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  2. On \(G^+\), \(\vek u = \vek v + \vek a^+ + \mat W^+\,\vek r\). The rotation of the field \(\vek a^+ + \mat W^+\,\vek r\) is \(\mat W^+\) (section 1.18.4), and the rotation of a sum is the sum of the rotations, because the partial derivative of a sum is the sum of the partial derivatives. Therefore \(W^+_{\mathrm{xy}} = \omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(P) - \omega^G_{\mathrm{xy}}(P)\), likewise \(W^-_{\mathrm{xy}} = \omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(P') - \omega^G_{\mathrm{xy}}(P')\), and
    \[W_{\mathrm{xy}} = \big(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(P) - \omega_{\mathrm{xy}}(P')\big) - \big(\omega^G_{\mathrm{xy}}(P) - \omega^G_{\mathrm{xy}}(P')\big) .\]
  3. Let \(\Omega(Q)\) be the integral of the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\) along a broken line in the cut ring from \(P'\) to \(Q\), which by theorem 4.114 is well defined and has the partial derivatives \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\). The difference \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} - \Omega\) has zero partial derivatives, so by lemma 1.133 it is constant on the connected cut ring. The first bracket in step 2 is therefore \(\Omega(P) - \Omega(P') = \Omega(P)\), the integral along the broken line \(P', K_8, K_7, \dots, K_2, P\), which goes around the hole along the lower, left and upper side. The segments between the points \(K_{\mathrm{i}}\) lie in the cut ring by step 2 of the third part of the proof of lemma 1.131. On the first and the last segment \(y\) does not change sign, and the square of the distance from the axis \(z\) is, by lemma 1.129, items 1 and 2, at most \(2500\) and at least \(2125 - 1125/4 > 1600\), so these two segments lie in the cut ring too.
  4. The function \(\omega^G_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the function of theorem 4.104 on the set \(G\), which is star-shaped with respect to \(P'\), differ by a constant by lemma 1.133. The second bracket is therefore the integral of the functions \(\psi\) along the segment from \(P'\) to \(P\). The set \(G\) is simply connected (lemma 4.107), so by step 2 of the proof of theorem 4.114 the integral of the segment from \(P\) to \(P'\) is the opposite of this integral. By steps 2 and 3, \(W_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is therefore the integral of the functions \(\psi\) along the closed broken line \(P', K_8, K_7, \dots, K_2, P, P'\) around the hole.
  5. As in step 5 of the proof of corollary 4.113, the numerator of the integrand on a segment with start \(A\) and vector \(\vek d\) is constant, \(k\,(x_{\mathrm{A}}\,d_{\mathrm{y}} - y_{\mathrm{A}}\,d_{\mathrm{x}})\). On the segment from \(P'\) to \(K_8\) it is \(k\,\big(45 \cdot (-30) - (-10) \cdot (-15)\big) = -1500\,k\), on the other segments \(-1500\,k\) or \(-2000\,k\), and on the last one, from \(P\) to \(P'\), \(-900\,k\) (with SymPy). The denominator \(x^2 + y^2\) is positive and at most \(2500\), so the integrand is at most \(-900\,k/2500 < 0\) everywhere. By lemma 3.39, item 3, every integral is negative, so \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} < 0\) and \(\mat W \ne \mat 0\). SymPy gives exactly \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -2\pi k\).

Where does \(2\pi k\) come from? On the circle of radius \(r\) the arc around the hole shortens by \(k \cdot 2\pi r\), and by this much the sides of the cut move apart on this circle. The gap is proportional to the radius, as for the rotation of the plate by the field \(\mat W\vek r\) in section 1.18.4, where the corner at distance \(r\) from \(O\) moves by \(W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,r\). The ratio of the gap to the radius is \(2\pi k\). At \(r = 40\) mm the gap is \(0{,}251\) mm and at \(r = 60\) mm it is \(0{,}377\) mm, as we computed in section 1.18.5. The upper side of the cut is turned relative to the lower one about the axis \(z\) through the centre of the ring. Since \(\mat W\) is not zero, by lemma 4.120, item 3, the whole ring has no displacement field with these strains, although the compatibility equations hold at every point of it. In section 1.18.5 we concluded this from the picture of the fan, and now it is proved. By step 4, \(W_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is the integral of the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\) around the hole, which in a simply connected set would be zero by theorem 4.112. For the ring this integral is the jump of the rotation.

With this we have proved theorem 1.137 of section 1.18.5 in full, for every body whose interior points form a connected and simply connected set. We added the displacement up along broken lines. Simple connectedness, through the grid on the square and small balls in which the theorem for star-shaped sets works, made sure that the sum does not depend on the choice of the line. In a body with a hole the compatibility equations are not enough: the cut body has a displacement field, but the field has a jump at the cut, which is a small rigid displacement, and a field of the whole body exists exactly when this jump is zero. In the next subsection we will use the theorem for the question whether the equation of virtual forces also demands compatibility.

4.7.10 Converse of the principle of virtual forces

In subsection 4.7.2 we proved the principle of virtual forces (theorem 4.97). Let us repeat the setting. Before loading the body occupies the set of points \(V\), which is a box or made of boxes. On the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) is prescribed, on the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the force per unit area. If \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the components of the small strain tensor of a displacement field \(\vek u\) that equals \(\bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), then for every statically admissible virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) the equation (4.65) holds,

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A .\]

A field is statically admissible if it is symmetric and continuously differentiable, satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force and has zero traction vector on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) (definition 4.96). For the statically indeterminate truss in subsection 4.7.5 the same equation with self-equilibrating virtual axial forces gave the condition that the changes of length of the bars fit together. Now let us ask the converse for a body. Let six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be given, of which we do not know whether they come from some displacement field, as for the strips of section 1.18.1. If the equation above holds for every statically admissible virtual stress field, are the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) compatible strains, that is, is there a displacement field from which we get them?

EP answers yes: the strains and displacements are compatible and consistent with the supports exactly when the equation holds for every statically admissible field (EP (4.4.5), p. 197). In the derivation EP assumes that a displacement field \(\vek u\) already exists, turns the equation into an integral of the difference \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} - \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\) multiplied by \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and concludes that the difference is zero because \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is arbitrary in the body (EP (4.4.9), (4.4.10), p. 198). The virtual field is not arbitrary, however, because it has to satisfy the equilibrium equations. How strong this restriction is, the following argument shows. Let \(\varphi\) be a function that is positive in the interior of a small box in the interior of the body and zero outside it, of the kind we built in subsection 4.5.5. If we were allowed to take the virtual field \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varphi\) with all other components zero, the right side of the equation would be zero, because the field does not reach the surface. By the fundamental lemma for boxes (lemma 4.83, item 2) the equation would then give \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) at every interior point, and we would get the same for every other component. The equation would demand that all strains are zero, while for true displacement fields, for instance in the hanging bar, the strains are not zero. Such a field is not in equilibrium. The first equilibrium equation reads \(\partial\varphi/\partial x = 0\) for it, and the bump is not constant along the axis \(x\). The equilibrium equations therefore restrict the admissible fields strongly, and so the equation demands less than \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\). We will show that it demands exactly the compatibility equations (1.68).

The goal of the subsection is a theorem that says this precisely, and a test on the strip with numbers. The model is the same as in theorem 4.97, with one difference: we do not compute the strains from a displacement field, but six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are given, where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) means the same as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}}\) the same as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}}\) the same as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). Let us list the assumptions and say for each where we use it.

  1. The strains are small, as in the whole section, so the principle of virtual forces holds in the form above. We need no material law, because none enters the equation.
  2. The functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body together with its surface. We need the second derivatives because the compatibility equations contain second derivatives of the strains and because we will move two derivatives from the virtual field to the strains. Theorem 1.137 has the same assumption.
  3. The body is a box or made of boxes, as in theorem 4.97, because we proved the principle only for such bodies. For the existence of a displacement field we will also need the set of interior points of the body to be connected and simply connected (definitions 1.130 and 1.136): any two of its points are joined by a broken line in it, and every closed curve in it can be shrunk continuously to a point without leaving it.

The route is the same as for the converse of the principle of virtual displacements in subsection 4.5.5. We take virtual fields that are nonzero only in a small box in the interior of the body. Such a field does not reach the surface, so the right side of the equation is zero, and the left side is an integral over the box. With integration by parts we move the derivatives from the virtual field to the strains and use the fundamental lemma. Two steps are new. First, we need fields in equilibrium that are zero outside the box. We will get them from a single function, through its second derivatives. Second, these fields contain second derivatives of the bump, so we need a bump that is smoother than the bump of subsection 4.5.5.

How do we get a field in equilibrium that is zero outside the box? It helps to start from the goal. Let \(\varphi\) be a function that is zero outside the box \(K\), and such that its first partial derivatives are zero on the faces of the box too. Integration by parts (corollary 3.41) moves a derivative from one function to the other, and in doing so it adds a minus sign and a term at the end points, which is zero here, because the function from which we moved the derivative is zero there. Integration by parts twice therefore moves two derivatives without changing the sign, for example

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2}\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V .\]

We will prove this below. The first compatibility equation (1.68) reads

\[\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} = 2\,\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} .\]

We want the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), after the derivatives are moved, to equal the left side of this equation minus the right side, multiplied by \(\varphi\). So we read the components of the virtual field straight off the equation. Next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) there must stand \(\partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\), next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) there must stand \(\partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\). The component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) appears twice in the double sum, as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), so we must have \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\). Let the other components be zero. Is this field in equilibrium? The first equilibrium equation gives

\[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y^2} - \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x\,\partial y} + 0 = 0 ,\]

because both third derivatives differentiate once with respect to \(x\) and twice with respect to \(y\), and by corollary 1.126 the order of differentiation does not matter. In the same way the left side of the second equilibrium equation is zero, and in the third all terms are zero. The field, which we chose only so that it would give a compatibility equation, is in equilibrium.

This is no coincidence. We chose the field so that its work on the strains of every displacement field with continuous derivatives up to third order is zero, since by theorem 1.127 such strains satisfy the compatibility equations. A stress field that does no work on any admissible virtual displacement, however, is in equilibrium without body force by the converse of the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.84). This argument is not a proof, because the converse requires the equation for all admissible virtual displacements, also for those without third derivatives. But it tells us why equilibrium and compatibility belong together. The equation of virtual work connects forces with displacements, and the condition that one side imposes on stress fields, the other side imposes on strains. For the proof the computation with derivatives above is enough.

We proceed in the same way with the fourth compatibility equation,

\[\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} = \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} .\]

Here \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) appears once in the double sum, and each of the three shear components twice. To avoid halves, we look for a field whose sum, after the derivatives are moved, gives twice the left side minus the right side. Next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) there must therefore stand \(2\,\partial^2\varphi/\partial y\,\partial z\), next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}}\) the derivative \(\partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\), next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}}\) the derivative \(-\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\), and next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) the derivative \(-\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial z\). This field is in equilibrium too.

Lemma 4.121 Virtual stress fields from one function (virtualna polja napetosti iz ene funkcije)

Let \(\varphi\) be a function of three variables that has continuous partial derivatives of first, second and third order in all of space.

  1. The field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) with the components
    \[\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2} , \qquad \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} , \qquad \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y} \tag{4.77}\]
    and the other components zero is symmetric at every point, its components are continuously differentiable in all of space, and it satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force at every point.
  2. The same holds for the field with the components
    \[\begin{aligned} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 2\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial z} , & \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} , \\ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = -\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y} , & \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial z} \end{aligned} \tag{4.78}\]
    and the other components zero.
  3. The same holds for the fields we get from the fields of items 1 and 2 when we rename the axes once or twice, \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\).
Proof

We must show that the two fields are symmetric, continuously differentiable and in equilibrium. We check equilibrium by differentiation, in which the third derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) cancel, because the order of differentiation does not matter.

1. The first field.

  1. By its definition \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\), and the other off-diagonal components are zero, so the field is symmetric.
  2. The components of the field are second partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) or zero. Their first partial derivatives are therefore third partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) or zero, which by hypothesis exist and are continuous in all of space. The components are therefore continuously differentiable (definition 1.90).
  3. Every point of space is an interior point of space, so by corollary 1.126 on the independence of the order of differentiation the third partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) do not depend on the order of differentiation at any point.
  4. The equilibrium equation with second index \(x\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y^2} - \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x\,\partial y} + 0 = 0 ,\]
    because the two third derivatives are equal by step 3.
  5. The equilibrium equation with second index \(y\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}}{\partial z} = -\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x^2} + 0 = 0 ,\]
    because both derivatives differentiate twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(y\).
  6. The equilibrium equation with second index \(z\) contains only the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), which are zero, so its left side is zero.

2. The second field.

  1. Symmetry and continuous differentiability follow as in steps 1 and 2 of the first part.
  2. The equilibrium equation with second index \(x\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} = 2\,\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y\,\partial z} - \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x\,\partial z} - \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial z\,\partial x\,\partial y} = 0 ,\]
    because all three third derivatives differentiate with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) and are equal by step 3 of the first part.
  3. The equilibrium equation with second index \(y\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}}{\partial z} = -\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial x\,\partial z} + 0 + \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial z\,\partial x^2} = 0 ,\]
    because both third derivatives differentiate twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(z\).
  4. The equilibrium equation with second index \(z\):
    \[\frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial z} = -\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial x^2} + 0 = 0 ,\]
    because both third derivatives differentiate twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(y\).

3. Renamed axes.

  1. When the axes are renamed, the equilibrium equations turn into one another, the equation with second index \(x\) into the equation with second index \(y\), this one into the equation with \(z\) and this one into the equation with \(x\). Symmetry and continuous differentiability do not change, and neither does the hypothesis on the function \(\varphi\). The steps of the first and second parts therefore hold with renamed axes.

Source: SADD (13.6.4), (13.6.10), (13.6.12) (PDF pp. 421-423), where the stress field is written with second derivatives of a symmetric matrix of functions. The field of item 1 is the case of (13.6.10) with a single nonzero function on the diagonal, the field of item 2 the case of (13.6.12) with a single function off the diagonal, with the opposite sign. SADD shows equilibrium for the general form (PDF p. 421). The proof by components is not from the source.

The lemma gives six families of virtual fields, one for each compatibility equation. Renaming the axes \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\) turns the first equation (1.68) into the second, the second into the third, the fourth into the fifth and the fifth into the sixth, as we saw in the proof of theorem 1.127. From the field (4.77) we get in this way for the second equation the field with the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial z^2\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial y\,\partial z\), and from the field (4.78) for the sixth equation the field with the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 2\,\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial z^2\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial z\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial y\,\partial z\).

The function \(\varphi\) is called a stress function (napetostna funkcija). The field (4.77) with a function that depends only on \(x\) and \(y\) was introduced for plane problems by Airy in 1862, and such a function is called the Airy stress function (Airyjeva napetostna funkcija) (BARBER (4.6), PDF p. 63, SADD (7.5.3), PDF p. 158). With it we will look for the stresses in plane bodies in chapter 11. SADD writes a more general formula, in which the stress field is obtained through second derivatives from a symmetric matrix of six functions (SADD (13.6.4), PDF p. 421). When only the functions on the diagonal are nonzero, they are called Maxwell stress functions, when only the functions off the diagonal, Morera stress functions (SADD (13.6.9)-(13.6.12), PDF pp. 422-423). SADD also states that it has been shown that every solution of an elasticity problem can be written in this form (SADD, PDF p. 421). We need less, only enough fields in equilibrium that are zero outside a small box.

Now we need the function \(\varphi\). The bump \(p_{\alpha\beta}(t) = (t - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - t)^2\) of subsection 4.5.5 is not smooth enough. Its first derivative is continuous, but its second derivative jumps at the points \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (figure 4.99, top). To the left of \(\alpha\) the second derivative is zero. To the right of \(\alpha\) it is the second derivative of the polynomial \((t - \alpha)^2\,(\beta - t)^2\), which near \(\alpha\) approaches the value \(2\,(\beta - \alpha)^2\): when we differentiate the first derivative \(2\,(t - \alpha)\,(\beta - t)\,(\alpha + \beta - 2t)\) once more and put \(t = \alpha\), only the term in which we differentiated the factor \(t - \alpha\) remains, which is \(2\,(\beta - \alpha)\,(\beta - \alpha)\). The field (4.77) with a bump made of the functions \(p_{\alpha\beta}\) would therefore jump on the faces of the box and would not be continuously differentiable, as definition 4.96, item 1, requires. Fourth powers help. Each additional factor \(t - \alpha\) gives one more derivative that is zero at \(\alpha\). The bump \((t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\) therefore has continuous derivatives up to third order (figure 4.99, bottom), and the field (4.77) made with it has continuous first partial derivatives, because these are third partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\).

Lemma 4.122 Fundamental lemma with smooth bumps (osnovna lema z gladkimi grbinami)

For numbers \(\alpha < \beta\) let \(q_{\alpha\beta}(t) = (t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\) for \(\alpha \le t \le \beta\) and \(q_{\alpha\beta}(t) = 0\) for other \(t\).

  1. The function \(q_{\alpha\beta}\) has a first, second and third derivative at every real number. All three are continuous and equal to zero at the points \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).
  2. For a box \(K = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) let \(\varphi(x, y, z) = q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\). The function \(\varphi\) has continuous partial derivatives of first, second and third order in all of space. The function \(\varphi\) and all these partial derivatives are zero at every point that does not lie in the interior of the box \(K\), that is, on its faces and outside it.
  3. Let \(g\) be a function of three variables, continuous on an open set \(D\). If for every box \(K\) that lies in \(D\), with the function \(\varphi\) of item 2,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 ,\]
    then \(g = 0\) at every point of \(D\).
Proof

We must show three items. In the first we follow the derivatives of the polynomial \((t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\) and show that they have zeros at the end points of the interval that are enough for three derivatives. We get the second from the first as for the bump in a box, the third as in lemma 4.83.

1. Derivatives of the bump.

  1. The function \(t - \alpha\) has the derivative \(1\), and the function \(\beta - t\) the derivative \(-1\) (lemma 1.81, items 1, 2 and 4). By the product rule and by induction on the natural number \(m\), \((t - \alpha)^m\) has the derivative \(m\,(t - \alpha)^{m-1}\): from \((t - \alpha)^{m+1} = (t - \alpha)\,(t - \alpha)^m\) we get the derivative \((t - \alpha)^m + (t - \alpha)\,m\,(t - \alpha)^{m-1} = (m + 1)\,(t - \alpha)^m\). Likewise \((\beta - t)^m\) has the derivative \(-m\,(\beta - t)^{m-1}\).
  2. Let \(r(t) = (t - \alpha)^m\,(\beta - t)^m\,s(t)\), where \(m \ge 1\) is a natural number and \(s\) a polynomial. By the product rule and by step 1,
    \[r'(t) = (t - \alpha)^{m-1}\,(\beta - t)^{m-1}\,\big(m\,(\beta - t)\,s(t) - m\,(t - \alpha)\,s(t) + (t - \alpha)\,(\beta - t)\,s'(t)\big) ,\]
    again a product of \((t - \alpha)^{m-1}\,(\beta - t)^{m-1}\) and a polynomial.
  3. Let \(r_0(t) = (t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\), and let \(r_1\), \(r_2\), \(r_3\) be its first, second and third derivatives. By step 2, used three times, \(r_{\mathrm{k}}(t) = (t - \alpha)^{4-k}\,(\beta - t)^{4-k}\,s_{\mathrm{k}}(t)\) with a polynomial \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\). Each \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) is therefore zero at \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), because the exponent \(4 - k\) is at least \(1\).
  4. For \(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\) let \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(t) = r_{\mathrm{k}}(t)\) for \(\alpha < t < \beta\) and \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(t) = 0\) for other \(t\). Then \(q_0 = q_{\alpha\beta}\), since \(r_0(\alpha) = r_0(\beta) = 0\) too. Let us show that for \(k = 0, 1, 2\) the function \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) is differentiable at every number \(t\) with the derivative \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}(t)\).
  5. Outside the interval \([\alpha, \beta]\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) is constantly zero on an open interval around \(t\), so its derivative is zero there, like \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). On the interval \((\alpha, \beta)\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) equals the polynomial \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\), so its derivative is \(r_{\mathrm{k}+1}(t) = q_{\mathrm{k}+1}(t)\).
  6. At the point \(\alpha\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha) = 0\). For \(h < 0\) the difference quotient \(\big(q_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha + h) - q_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha)\big)/h\) is zero. For \(0 < h < \beta - \alpha\) it equals by step 3
    \[\frac{r_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha + h)}{h} = h^{3-k}\,(\beta - \alpha - h)^{4-k}\,s_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha + h) ,\]
    which is a polynomial in \(h\) that is zero at \(h = 0\), because \(3 - k \ge 1\). A polynomial is continuous (corollary 1.64, item 2), so for every \(\eta > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\), which we take at most \(\beta - \alpha\), such that the absolute value of the quotient is less than \(\eta\) for \(0 < |h| < \delta\). By definitions 1.5 and 1.9, \(q_{\mathrm{k}}'(\alpha) = 0 = q_{\mathrm{k}+1}(\alpha)\). Likewise at the point \(\beta\), with the factor \((\beta - t)^{4-k}\) in place of \((t - \alpha)^{4-k}\).
  7. The functions \(q_1\), \(q_2\) and \(q_3\) are therefore the first, second and third derivatives of the function \(q_{\alpha\beta}\), and by step 3 they are zero at \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). They are continuous at every point. Outside \([\alpha, \beta]\) they are constantly zero on an open interval around the point, on \((\alpha, \beta)\) they equal polynomials, which are continuous. At the point \(\alpha\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha) = 0 = r_{\mathrm{k}}(\alpha)\) for \(k = 1, 2, 3\). For a given \(\eta > 0\) the continuity of the polynomial \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) at \(\alpha\) therefore gives \(\delta > 0\), which we take at most \(\beta - \alpha\), such that \(|q_{\mathrm{k}}(t)| = |r_{\mathrm{k}}(t)| < \eta\) for \(\alpha \le t < \alpha + \delta\), while to the left of \(\alpha\), \(q_{\mathrm{k}}(t) = 0\). Likewise at the point \(\beta\).

2. Bump in a box.

  1. In differentiating with respect to \(x\) the factors depending on \(y\) and \(z\) are constant (lemma 1.81, item 2), so \(\partial\varphi/\partial x = q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}'(x)\,q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\), and likewise for the other variables. Using this rule several times, every partial derivative of the function \(\varphi\) up to third order is a product of three factors, a derivative of the function \(q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}\) with respect to \(x\), a derivative of the function \(q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}\) with respect to \(y\) and a derivative of the function \(q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}\) with respect to \(z\), each of order at most \(3\). By item 1 these derivatives exist.
  2. Each factor is a continuous function of one coordinate and therefore a continuous function of the point, as in step 2 of item 1 of the proof of lemma 4.83. By corollary 1.69, item 1, all partial derivatives up to third order are therefore continuous in all of space.
  3. A point that does not lie in the interior of the box has at least one coordinate outside the open interval, for instance \(x \le \alpha_1\) or \(x \ge \beta_1\). There \(q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}\) and its derivatives up to third order are zero by item 1, so every product of step 1 is zero.

3. Fundamental lemma.

  1. We repeat steps 1 to 8 of item 2 of the proof of lemma 4.83, with the functions \(q_{\alpha\beta}\) in place of \(p_{\alpha\beta}\). The steps use only that the bump is nowhere negative and that the integral of the bump over its interval is positive. The first holds because both factors \((t - \alpha)^4\) and \((\beta - t)^4\) are powers with an even exponent.
  2. Only step 7 changes. Let \(\ell = \beta - \alpha\). On the middle half of the interval both factors \(t - \alpha\) and \(\beta - t\) are at least \(\ell/4\), so there \(q_{\alpha\beta}(t) \ge (\ell/4)^8\), and by additivity and the bound of the integral (lemma 3.39, items 2 and 3), \(\int_\alpha^\beta q_{\alpha\beta}\,\mathrm{d}t \ge \tfrac{\ell}{2}\,(\ell/4)^8 > 0\). The exact value is \(\ell^9/630\).

Source: EP Lemma 3.1 (pp. 140-141) for functions of one variable, with a different proof. The bumps with fourth powers and the proof are not from the sources.

The lemma repeated lemma 4.83 with a smoother bump. The proof of item 3 was the same, because it needed only that the bump is not negative and has a positive integral. Item 2 will ensure that the virtual field made from the bump is continuously differentiable and that it is zero on the faces of the box and outside it, together with the first derivatives of the bump that integration by parts will need.

What remains is moving the derivatives. For the bar we used integration by parts on an interval. In a box we use it along every segment parallel to the chosen axis, and then we integrate over the other two coordinates.

Lemma 4.123 Integration by parts twice with a smooth bump (dvakratna integracija po delih z gladko grbino)

Let \(K = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) be a box, \(\varphi\) the product of its three bumps from lemma 4.122, item 2, and \(g\) a function of three variables with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set \(D\) containing \(K\). Then for any two variables \(a\) and \(b\), each of them \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\), possibly equal,

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial a\,\partial b}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial a\,\partial b}\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{4.79}\]
Proof

We must show that each move of one derivative produces only a minus sign, because the terms on the faces of the box are zero. Two moves give two minus signs, so a plus.

  1. One move. Let \(f\) be a function continuous on \(D\) whose partial derivative with respect to \(a\) exists and is continuous on \(D\), and \(\psi\) a function continuously differentiable in all of space that is zero on both faces of the box perpendicular to the axis \(a\). Let us show that
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial a}\,\mathrm{d}V = -\int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial a}\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
    Let \(a = x\). Both functions under the integrals are continuous on \(K\) as products of continuous functions (corollary 1.69, item 1). By theorem 4.9 on the order of integration, item 2, the integral over \(K\) equals the iterated integral in which we integrate over \(x\) first.
  2. Let \(y\) and \(z\) be fixed, with \(\alpha_2 \le y \le \beta_2\) and \(\alpha_3 \le z \le \beta_3\). The segment from \((\alpha_1, y, z)\) to \((\beta_1, y, z)\) lies in \(K\), hence in \(D\). Since \(D\) is open, the points on the same line a little beyond the end points of the segment are in \(D\) too, so the functions \(x \mapsto f(x, y, z)\) and \(x \mapsto \psi(x, y, z)\) are differentiable on an open interval containing \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\), and their derivatives are the partial derivatives with respect to \(x\) and are continuous. By integration by parts (corollary 3.41)
    \[\int_{\alpha_1}^{\beta_1} f\,\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x = f(\beta_1, y, z)\,\psi(\beta_1, y, z) - f(\alpha_1, y, z)\,\psi(\alpha_1, y, z) - \int_{\alpha_1}^{\beta_1} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
    The points \((\alpha_1, y, z)\) and \((\beta_1, y, z)\) lie on the faces \(x = \alpha_1\) and \(x = \beta_1\), where \(\psi = 0\), so the term at the end points drops out.
  3. The inner integrals on the two sides are equal for every \(y\) and \(z\), so the iterated integrals over \(y\) and \(z\) are equal too. By theorem 4.9 these are the integrals over \(K\) of step 1. For \(a = y\) and \(a = z\) the steps are the same, with the roles of the coordinates swapped.
  4. The first move. Take \(f = g\) and \(\psi = \partial\varphi/\partial b\). By hypothesis the function \(g\) has continuous partial derivatives on \(D\). The function \(\psi\) is continuously differentiable in all of space, because by lemma 4.122, item 2, \(\varphi\) has continuous partial derivatives of second order, and by the same item it is zero on all faces of the box. By steps 1 to 3,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial a\,\partial b}\,\mathrm{d}V = -\int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial g}{\partial a}\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial b}\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  5. The second move. Take \(f = \partial g/\partial a\), move the derivative with respect to \(b\), and take \(\psi = \varphi\). The function \(f\) is continuous on \(D\), and its partial derivative with respect to \(b\), the second partial derivative \(\partial^2 g/\partial b\,\partial a\), is continuous on \(D\). The function \(\varphi\) is continuously differentiable in all of space and zero on the faces of the box. By steps 1 to 3,
    \[-\int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial g}{\partial a}\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial b}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial b\,\partial a}\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  6. The set \(D\) is open, and the second partial derivatives of the function \(g\) are continuous on it, so by theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives the derivative \(\partial^2 g/\partial b\,\partial a\) equals \(\partial^2 g/\partial a\,\partial b\) at every point of \(K\). For \(a = b\) this is not needed. Combining steps 4 and 5 we get (4.79).

Source: EP (4.4.8) (p. 197) moves one derivative with the Green-Gauss theorem, in a body of any shape. The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

The lemma says that two derivatives move from the bump to another function without a change of sign. Each move gives a minus sign, and two minus signs give a plus. The terms at the end points dropped out because the bump and its first partial derivatives are zero on the faces of the box. Now we have everything for the theorem.

Theorem 4.124 Converse of the principle of virtual forces (obrat načela virtualnih sil)

Let the body \(V\), the parts of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) be as in theorem 4.97. Let six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body together with its surface, and let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). If for every statically admissible virtual stress field \(\delta\ten\sigma\) (definition 4.96)

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]

where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal of the surface, then:

  1. the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) satisfy the compatibility equations (1.68) at every interior point of the body,
  2. if the set of interior points of the body is connected (definition 1.130) and simply connected (definition 1.136), there is a displacement field \(\vek u\), defined at the interior points of the body, with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order, whose small strain components equal \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every interior point.
Proof

We must show two items. For the first we take virtual fields from lemma 4.121 with a bump in a small box that does not reach the surface, and move the derivatives to the strains. The second follows from the first and theorem 4.119.

1. Compatibility equations.

  1. Let \(K = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) be a box that lies in the set of interior points of the body, and \(\varphi\) the product of its three bumps from lemma 4.122, item 2. By the same item \(\varphi\) has continuous partial derivatives up to third order in all of space. Let \(\delta\ten\sigma\) be the field (4.77) with this function. By lemma 4.121, item 1, it is symmetric, continuously differentiable in all of space, and satisfies the equilibrium equations without body force at every point.
  2. The components of the field are second partial derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) or zero, so by lemma 4.122, item 2, they are zero at every point that does not lie in the interior of the box \(K\). The points of the box \(K\) are interior points of the body, so no point of the surface lies in \(K\), and at every point of the surface all components of the field are zero. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) therefore \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\). The field satisfies all four conditions of definition 4.96 and is a statically admissible virtual stress field.
  3. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) too \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\), so the right side of the equation of the hypothesis is zero, and
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 .\]
  4. We add the planes \(x = \alpha_1\), \(x = \beta_1\), \(y = \alpha_2\), \(y = \beta_2\), \(z = \alpha_3\) and \(z = \beta_3\) to the grid of the body. By lemma 4.12 the integral over the body does not change, and the box \(K\) is a union of cells of the new grid. On the cells outside \(K\) the virtual field is zero, so the integrals over them are zero, and the integrals over the cells in \(K\) add up to the integral over \(K\) by lemma 4.10, item 3. Therefore \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\).
  5. In the double sum only the terms with the pairs \((x, x)\), \((y, y)\), \((x, y)\) and \((y, x)\) are nonzero. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), at every point
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} - 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y} .\]
  6. The functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body, hence also \(K\). The integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals (lemma 4.10, item 1). We use lemma 4.123 on each of the three terms, with \(g = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(a = b = y\), with \(g = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(a = b = x\), and with \(g = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(a = x\) and \(b = y\). By steps 4 and 5,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \Big( \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} - 2\,\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} \Big)\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 .\]
  7. Let \(c_1\) be the function in the brackets, the left side of the first equation (1.68) minus the right side. As a sum of multiples of continuous functions it is continuous on the set of interior points of the body (corollary 1.69, item 1), and this set is open (lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point). Step 6 holds for every box that lies in it, so by lemma 4.122, item 3, \(c_1 = 0\) at every interior point of the body. This is the first compatibility equation.
  8. We repeat steps 1 to 7 with the two fields we get from the field (4.77) when we rename the axes once or twice (lemma 4.121, item 3). The renaming turns the first compatibility equation into the second and the second into the third, as in the second part of the proof of theorem 1.127. The second and third equations therefore hold at every interior point.
  9. For the fourth equation we take the field (4.78) with the function \(\varphi\) of step 1. Steps 1 to 4 stay the same, by lemma 4.121, item 2. The nonzero terms of the double sum are those with the pairs \((x, x)\), \((y, z)\), \((z, y)\), \((x, z)\), \((z, x)\), \((x, y)\) and \((y, x)\), so at every point
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y\,\partial z} + 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} - 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y} - 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial z} .\]
  10. With lemma 4.123, used on each of the four terms, we get as in step 6
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} 2\,\Big( \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} - \frac{\partial^2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} \Big)\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 .\]
    The expression in the brackets is the left side of the fourth equation (1.68) minus the right side. As in step 7, with twice this expression in place of \(c_1\), the expression is zero at every interior point, and the fourth equation holds.
  11. We get the fifth and sixth equations as in step 8, with the two fields we get from the field (4.78) by renaming the axes.

2. Displacement field.

  1. The set of interior points of the body is open (lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point), and connected and simply connected by hypothesis. The functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on it, because they have them on an open set containing the body, and by item 1 they satisfy the compatibility equations on it. By theorem 4.119 on the sufficiency of the compatibility equations in a simply connected body there is therefore a displacement field on it with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order whose small strain components are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Source: EP (4.4.5), (4.4.9), (4.4.10) (pp. 197-198), where the converse follows from the arbitrariness of the virtual stresses, with a displacement field assumed. Stress functions: SADD (13.6.10), (13.6.12) (PDF pp. 422-423). The proof with stress functions and smooth bumps is not from the sources.

The proof showed how the equation of virtual forces demands compatibility. A virtual field made from a stress function is in equilibrium and is zero outside a small box, so the right side of the equation drops out for it. Integration by parts twice moved the derivatives from the field to the strains, and the work of the field on the strains became the integral of the left side of a compatibility equation minus the right side, multiplied by the bump. Since this integral is zero for every box, the difference is zero at every interior point by the fundamental lemma. The same three steps, a field that does not reach the surface, moving the derivatives and the fundamental lemma, gave the converse of the principle of virtual displacements in subsection 4.5.5. There one move of a derivative gave the equilibrium equations, here two moves gave the compatibility equations.

What does the theorem not say? EP gets from the equation also that the displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) equals the prescribed one, \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) (EP (4.4.10), p. 198). Our virtual fields are zero near the whole surface, so they say nothing about \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). The displacement field of item 2 is determined by the strains only up to a small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) (corollary 1.135, subsection 4.7.7), and the question is whether it can be chosen so that it fits the supports on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). The answer is given in subsection 4.7.11, with virtual fields that reach \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). Item 2 needs a connected and simply connected body, because we get it from theorem 4.119. For the ring of section 1.18.5 the compatibility equations hold at every point, but there is no displacement field (lemma 4.120). Our virtual fields are nonzero only in a small box and do not go around the hole, so for the ring they detect nothing. A field that goes around the hole is built at the end of subsection 4.7.11.

Let us test the theorem with numbers on the strip of section 1.18.1 (figure 4.101). We repeat the setting. A thin steel strip of length 200 mm and height 20 mm lies in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\). The axis \(x\) points along the strip, the origin \(O\) is at the middle of the left end, so the strip reaches from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 200\) mm and from \(y = -10\) mm to \(y = 10\) mm. For a computation in space let us give it a thickness of 2 mm, from \(z = -1\) mm to \(z = 1\) mm. No force acts on it and no support holds it, so \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty and the right side of the equation is zero for every virtual field. The prescribed strains are (1.64), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) with \(k = -10\) m⁻², the other components are zero. In section 1.18.3 we saw that the first compatibility equation does not hold for them, since the left side is \(2k = -20\) m⁻² and the right side zero. By the theorem there must therefore be a statically admissible virtual field for which the equation does not hold. Let us find it.

  1. Let the box \(K\) with edges 10 mm, 10 mm and 1 mm have its centre at the point with coordinates \(x = 100\) mm, \(y = 0\) and \(z = 0\). So it reaches from \(x = 95\) mm to \(x = 105\) mm, from \(y = -5\) mm to \(y = 5\) mm and from \(z = -0{,}5\) mm to \(z = 0{,}5\) mm and lies in the middle of the strip. It is 5 mm from the upper and lower edges of the strip and \(0{,}5\) mm from both faces of the strip, so all its points are interior points of the strip.
  2. As the stress function we take
    \[\varphi = \Phi_0\,\frac{q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)}{h_1^8}\,\frac{q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)}{h_2^8}\,\frac{q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)}{h_3^8} ,\]
    where \(h_1 = h_2 = 5\) mm and \(h_3 = 0{,}5\) mm are the halves of the edges of the box. Each of the three quotients has the value \(h^4 \cdot h^4/h^8 = 1\) at the centre of its interval. Since \(\varphi\) is a constant multiple of the product of three bumps from lemma 4.122, the field (4.77) with this function is statically admissible, as in steps 1 and 2 of the proof of the theorem. The number \(\Phi_0\) has the unit newton, so that the second derivatives of the function \(\varphi\) have the unit pascal.
  3. At the centre of the box the second derivative of the quotient with respect to \(y\) is \(-8/h_2^2\), which we compute with SymPy, so there \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -8\,\Phi_0/h_2^2\). Let us choose \(\Phi_0 = 3{,}125\) N, so that \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -8 \cdot 3{,}125\ \text{N}/(25 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2) = -1\) MPa. Figure 4.100 shows the signs of all three components of the field in the box.
  4. The only nonzero strain is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), so the left side of the equation, computed with SymPy directly, without moving derivatives, is
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} k\,y^2\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2}\,\mathrm{d}V = -4{,}194 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{J} .\]
    The right side is zero, so the equation does not hold for this statically admissible virtual field, as the theorem demands for strains that are not compatible.
  5. Let us check the number with lemma 4.123. Since \(\partial^2(k\,y^2)/\partial y^2 = 2k\), the left side equals \(2k \int_{\mathrm{K}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}V\). The integral of the function \(\varphi\) is the product of the number \(\Phi_0\) and three integrals along the edges, each of which is \(\tfrac{128}{315}\) of the length of the edge, which we compute with SymPy. Therefore \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = 3{,}125\ \text{N} \cdot \big(\tfrac{128}{315}\big)^3 \cdot 10\ \text{mm} \cdot 10\ \text{mm} \cdot 1\ \text{mm} = 2{,}097 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{N}\,\text{m}^3\) and \(2k \int_{\mathrm{K}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}V = -20\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot 2{,}097 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{N}\,\text{m}^3 = -4{,}194 \cdot 10^{-7}\) J, the same as in step 4.
  6. For the corrected strip of section 1.18.3 there is also \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\), and the left side gets the term \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} (-k\,x^2)\,\partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\,\mathrm{d}V = 4{,}194 \cdot 10^{-7}\) J, with SymPy. The sum is zero, as it must be, since we get these strains from the displacement field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). For \(k = -10\) m⁻² this strip is far outside small strains at its right end, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}4\) (section 1.18.3), which does not matter for this equality, because every term is linear in \(k\) and for a smaller \(k\) is only multiplied by the same number.
  7. For the strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\), \(R = 10\) m, which we bend into an arc, the left side is \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} (y/R)\,\partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\), with SymPy.

Why is the work zero for the strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\), but not for the strip with \(k\,y^2\)? Figure 4.101 shows the component \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) along the transverse segment through the centre of the box, at \(x = 100\) mm and \(z = 0\). In the middle there is compression of \(1\) MPa, between \(1{,}89\) mm and \(5\) mm from the middle there is tension, which is largest, \(0{,}653\) MPa, at \(3{,}27\) mm and fades to zero at the edge of the box. The area under the curve is zero, because the integral of the second derivative is the difference of the first derivatives at the end points, \(\int_{-\mathrm{h}_2}^{h_2} \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\,\mathrm{d}y = \partial\varphi/\partial y\,(h_2) - \partial\varphi/\partial y\,(-h_2) = 0\). The virtual forces on a transverse cut of the box therefore add up to zero. Their moment about the middle is zero too. By integration by parts

\[\int_{-\mathrm{h}_2}^{h_2} y\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2}\,\mathrm{d}y = \Big[ y\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y} \Big]_{-\mathrm{h}_2}^{h_2} - \int_{-\mathrm{h}_2}^{h_2} \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y = 0 - \big(\varphi(h_2) - \varphi(-h_2)\big) = 0 ,\]

where for \(\varphi\) and its derivative we wrote only the coordinate \(y\). A strain that is a linear function of \(y\) along the segment, like \(y/R\), therefore does no work on this field. The parabola \(k\,y^2\), however, is not linear. In the bands with tension, between \(1{,}89\) mm and \(5\) mm from the middle, the shortening is from \(3{,}6 \cdot 10^{-5}\) to \(2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), in the compressed band in the middle at most \(3{,}6 \cdot 10^{-5}\), so the contributions of the bands do not cancel. The contribution of the bands with tension, where the shortening is larger, prevails, and since there the product of a positive virtual stress and a negative strain is negative, the left side in step 4 is negative. The corrected strip makes up for this difference with the transverse fibres. The term with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\) on the field \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), which has the same picture turned by a right angle, gives exactly the opposite number.

Let us compare with the bracket with the post of subsection 4.7.5. There the numbers \(-\tfrac43\), \(\tfrac53\) and \(1\) were self-equilibrating virtual axial forces that balance the joint without any external force, and the equation (4.63) with them was the condition that the three changes of length come from one displacement of the joint. Three unknown axial forces and two equations of equilibrium give one such set of numbers, up to a multiple, and one compatibility condition. In a body the role of these numbers is played by the virtual fields made from stress functions. They are self-equilibrating too, since no virtual force acts on them, neither on the surface nor in the body. There are infinitely many such fields, six for every box in the body, and they give the six compatibility equations at every interior point.

4.7.11 The condition at the supports

Theorem 4.124 got the compatibility equations from the equation of virtual forces, and in a connected and simply connected body also a displacement field \(\vek u\) whose strains are the given functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Does this field fit the supports? EP also gets the condition \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) from the equation (EP (4.4.10), p. 198), but our virtual fields were zero near the whole surface and said nothing about \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). The field of item 2 is determined by the strains only up to a small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) (corollary 1.135). The goal of this subsection is to show that the equation of virtual forces demands that this displacement can be chosen so that the field equals the prescribed displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). We will prove this for a body held by a support in one piece, and for a bar welded at both ends. At the end we look at the ring of section 1.18.5, for which the equation demands more than the compatibility equations.

The idea is this. Suppose for a moment that the field \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body together with its surface. Steps 1 to 4 of the proof of theorem 4.97, in which we have not yet used the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), give for every statically admissible virtual stress field

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]

with the displacement \(\vek u\) on the right instead of the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\). The left side is the same as in the equation of virtual forces, which holds by assumption. Subtracting the two equations we get

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot(\vek u - \bar{\vek u})\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 .\]

Let us call the difference \(\vek w = \vek u - \bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) the mismatch (neujemanje). It says by how much the displacement that the strains give differs on the support from the displacement that the support prescribes. The virtual traction vector \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the virtual support force per unit area (subsection 4.7.2), so the equality says that the virtual support forces do no work on the mismatch. When the mismatch is a small rigid displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), the equality holds for every statically admissible field. A rigid displacement has no strains (theorem 1.134, item 2), so lemma 4.81, applied with it instead of the virtual displacement and with the virtual field instead of the stress, gives \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), and on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\). Forces in equilibrium do no work on a rigid displacement. We will show the converse: if the virtual support forces do no work on the mismatch for any statically admissible field, the mismatch is a small rigid displacement on every rectangle of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), and for a support in one piece the same one everywhere. Subtracting this rigid displacement from the field \(\vek u\) we get a field that fits the supports.

There are three obstacles on the way. First, the field \(\vek u\) of item 2 is defined only at the interior points of the body, while we need its values on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and the divergence theorem up to the surface. So we first show that the field extends continuously up to the surface together with its first derivatives. Second, we need virtual fields that give chosen virtual support forces on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). We will get them from the stress functions of lemma 4.121 with a bump in a small box that crosses a face of the support. Third, the rigid displacements on two neighbouring rectangles of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) have to be the same. For this we need a virtual field around their common side.

The model is the same as in theorem 4.124. The body is a body made of boxes, the parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) are made of whole outer faces of cells, the six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body together with its surface, and the equation of virtual forces holds for every statically admissible virtual stress field. We add three assumptions and say for each where we use it.

  1. The set of interior points of the body is connected and simply connected. Then the displacement field of item 2 of theorem 4.124 exists.
  2. Smooth supports. The prescribed displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) equals a field \(\bar{\vek u}\) whose components have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body. For a rigid wall \(\bar{\vek u} = \vek 0\), for a support that settles evenly \(\bar{\vek u}\) is a constant vector. We need the derivatives because we will move derivatives from the virtual field to the mismatch, along the face of the support: two derivatives for the component of the mismatch perpendicular to the face, and one for the other two components.
  3. A support in one piece. The part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is not empty, and any two of its rectangles are joined by a chain of its rectangles in which neighbouring rectangles have a common side and the cells of the body containing this side are not exactly two cells without a common face. We use this when we carry the rigid displacement from rectangle to rectangle. The last part of the condition excludes a side along which the body touches itself, like two cubes that meet only along an edge. Supports in several separate pieces are treated after the theorem.

First the mathematics for the first obstacle. We proved the divergence theorem 4.14 for functions that are continuously differentiable on an open set containing the whole body. The field of item 2, however, is known only at the interior points, because the formula of theorem 4.119 writes it with integrals along broken lines in the interior of the body. For a point outside the body there is no such line. What can we say if the function and its derivatives behave well towards the surface? On an interval the answer is already in the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 1. It only requires the function to be continuous on the closed interval and differentiable at its interior points, with a derivative that agrees with a function continuous on the closed interval. The first lemma carries this over to segments that lie on the faces of a box.

Lemma 4.125 Derivative up to the faces of a box (odvod do roba kvadra)

Let \(C = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) be a box, \(f\) a function continuous on \(C\) that has the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial y\) at every interior point of the box, and \(g\) a function continuous on \(C\) that equals \(\partial f/\partial y\) at every interior point of the box. Let \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) be a point of the box \(C\). Then:

  1. for any numbers \(y_1 \le y_2\) in the interval \([a_2, b_2]\)
    \[f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_2, z_{\mathrm{P}}) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_1, z_{\mathrm{P}}) = \int_{\mathrm{y}_1}^{y_2} g(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\,\mathrm{d}y ,\]
  2. if \(a_2 < y_{\mathrm{P}} < b_2\), the function \(y \mapsto f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) is differentiable at \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) and its derivative is \(g(P)\).

The same holds with \(x\) or \(z\) instead of \(y\).

Proof

We have to show that the integral of \(g\) along a segment parallel to the axis \(y\) is the difference of the values of \(f\) at the end points also when the segment lies on a face of the box. For segments in the interior this is the fundamental theorem of calculus, and a segment on a face we get as a limit of segments from the interior.

  1. Interior segment. Let \(x'\) and \(z'\) be numbers with \(a_1 < x' < b_1\) and \(a_3 < z' < b_3\), and let \(y_1 < y_2\). For \(y_1 = y_2\) both sides of item 1 are zero. The function \(G(y) = f(x', y, z')\) is continuous on \([y_1, y_2]\), because \(f\) is continuous on \(C\) and the distance between the points \((x', y, z')\) and \((x', y', z')\) is \(|y - y'|\). For \(y_1 < y < y_2\) the point \((x', y, z')\) is an interior point of the box, so by definition 1.25 \(G\) is differentiable there with derivative \(\partial f/\partial y\,(x', y, z') = g(x', y, z')\). The function \(y \mapsto g(x', y, z')\) is continuous on \([y_1, y_2]\) for the same reason as \(G\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 1,
    \[f(x', y_2, z') - f(x', y_1, z') = \int_{\mathrm{y}_1}^{y_2} g(x', y, z')\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  2. Segments from the interior. Let \(\bar x = (a_1 + b_1)/2\) and \(\bar z = (a_3 + b_3)/2\) and for \(n = 2, 3, \dots\)
    \[x_{\mathrm{n}} = \Big(1 - \frac1n\Big)\,x_{\mathrm{P}} + \frac1n\,\bar x , \qquad z_{\mathrm{n}} = \Big(1 - \frac1n\Big)\,z_{\mathrm{P}} + \frac1n\,\bar z .\]
    Since \(a_1 \le x_{\mathrm{P}} \le b_1\) and \(a_1 < \bar x < b_1\), \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) lies strictly between \(a_1\) and \(b_1\), and likewise \(z_{\mathrm{n}}\) lies strictly between \(a_3\) and \(b_3\). By step 1 the equality holds with \(x' = x_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(z' = z_{\mathrm{n}}\) for every \(n\).
  3. Left side. For \(y = y_1\) and for \(y = y_2\) the point \((x_{\mathrm{n}}, y, z_{\mathrm{n}})\) is at the distance \(e_{\mathrm{n}} = \tfrac1n\,\sqrt{(\bar x - x_{\mathrm{P}})^2 + (\bar z - z_{\mathrm{P}})^2}\) from the point \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), which goes to zero, so the sequence of these points converges to \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) (definition 1.65). The function \(f\) is continuous on \(C\), so by lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points and by lemma 1.60 on computing with limits of sequences the left side of step 1 converges to \(f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_2, z_{\mathrm{P}}) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_1, z_{\mathrm{P}})\).
  4. Right side. The function \(y \mapsto g(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) is continuous on \([y_1, y_2]\) for the same reason as in step 1, so it is integrable. Choose \(\eta > 0\). The function \(g\) is continuous on the closed and bounded set of points \(C\) (definition 1.74), so by theorem 4.6 there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|g(Q) - g(Q')| < \eta\) for any points \(Q\), \(Q'\) of the box with \(|QQ'| < \delta\). The points \((x_{\mathrm{n}}, y, z_{\mathrm{n}})\) and \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) are at the distance \(e_{\mathrm{n}}\). For every \(n\) with \(e_{\mathrm{n}} < \delta\) therefore \(-\eta < g(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y, z_{\mathrm{n}}) - g(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}}) < \eta\) for every \(y\), and by lemma 3.39, items 1 and 3, the integrals on the right side of step 1 and in item 1 of the lemma differ by at most \(\eta\,(y_2 - y_1)\). The right side of step 1 therefore converges to \(\int_{\mathrm{y}_1}^{y_2} g(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\,\mathrm{d}y\).
  5. The left and right sides of step 1 are equal for every \(n\), so by lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit their limits are equal too. This is item 1.
  6. Item 2. Let \(F(y) = \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{y} g(x_{\mathrm{P}}, t, z_{\mathrm{P}})\,\mathrm{d}t\) for \(y \in [a_2, b_2]\). By item 1 with \(y_1 = a_2\) and \(y_2 = y\) we have \(f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}}) = f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, a_2, z_{\mathrm{P}}) + F(y)\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus, item 2, \(F\) is differentiable at \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) with derivative \(g(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), and the term \(f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, a_2, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) is constant and does not change the derivative (lemma 1.81).
  7. For \(x\) and \(z\) the steps are the same, only with the roles of the coordinates exchanged.

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

The lemma has shown that the fundamental theorem of calculus holds also on segments lying on the faces of a box, when the derivative from the interior extends continuously up to the faces. We got from the interior to the face with a sequence of segments approaching it, and with uniform continuity, which made the integrals approach the integral on the face. With the lemma we get the divergence theorem for such functions.

Lemma 4.126 Divergence theorem up to the faces of a box (izrek o divergenci do roba kvadra)

Let \(C = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) be a box with surface \(S\) and outward normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\), \(f\) a function continuous on \(C\) that has the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x\) at every interior point of the box, and \(g\) a function continuous on \(C\) that equals \(\partial f/\partial x\) at every interior point of the box. Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{C}} g\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A .\]

The same holds with \(y\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and with \(z\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\) instead of \(x\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\).

Proof

We have to show the same as in the first part of the proof of theorem 4.14, only with the fundamental theorem of calculus on segments parallel to the axis \(x\) replaced by lemma 4.125.

  1. By lemma 4.125, item 1, with \(x\) instead of \(y\), for any numbers \(y\) and \(z\) with \(a_2 \le y \le b_2\) and \(a_3 \le z \le b_3\)
    \[\int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1} g(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}x = f(b_1, y, z) - f(a_1, y, z) .\]
  2. The function \(g\) is continuous on \(C\), so by theorem 4.9 on the order of integration, item 2, the integral over \(C\) equals the iterated integral in which we integrate first over \(x\), then over \(z\) and last over \(y\). Inserting step 1 and using the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.39, item 1) we get
    \[\int_{\mathrm{C}} g\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f(b_1, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y - \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f(a_1, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
    The integrals on the right exist because \(f\) is continuous on the faces of the box (definition 4.8).
  3. On the face \(x = b_1\) we have \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\), on the face \(x = a_1\) we have \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\), and on the other four faces \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). As in step 1 of the proof of theorem 4.14 the right side of step 2 is therefore \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  4. For \(y\) and \(z\) the steps are the same, with the inner integral over \(y\) or over \(z\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, theorem 1 (PDF p. 479) for the divergence theorem and LEBL2 thm. 10.6.4 (PDF p. 129) for Green's theorem in the plane assume continuous partial derivatives on an open set containing the body or the region. The version with derivatives that only extend continuously up to the faces, and its proof, are not from the sources.

Now let us show that a displacement field that has the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at the interior points of the body extends up to the surface. The idea is the same as for the summing along segments in subsection 4.7.7. Every cell of the body is a box, and every point of it, also a point on its face, is joined to its centre by a segment that does not leave the cell. We write the rotation and the displacement at the point as the value at the centre plus the integral of the changes along this segment. The integrals contain only the strains and their first derivatives, and these are defined and continuous also on the surface. The formula therefore gives values also at points of the surface. Because these segments stay in one cell, we get an extension for every cell separately.

Lemma 4.127 Displacement field up to the faces of the cells (polje pomikov do ploskev celic)

Let \(V\) be a body made of boxes (definition 4.11), \(D\) an open set containing \(V\), and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}}\), where the indices run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), functions with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on \(D\). Let \(\vek u\) be a displacement field defined at the interior points of the body, whose components have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order there and whose small strain tensor components equal \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every interior point. Then:

  1. For every cell \(C\) of the body there are functions \(U_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\), continuous on \(C\), such that \(U_{\mathrm{i}} = u_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) at every interior point of the cell, and \(\tfrac12\,(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}}) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every point of the cell. The functions \(U_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are uniquely determined by being continuous on \(C\) and agreeing with \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) or with \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) at the interior points. The field \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}} = (U_{\mathrm{x}}, U_{\mathrm{y}}, U_{\mathrm{z}})\) is called the extension (razširitev) of the field \(\vek u\) to the cell \(C\).
  2. Let \(C = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) be a cell of the body and \(P\) a point of it with \(a_2 < y_{\mathrm{P}} < b_2\).
