Then the function \(y \mapsto U_{\mathrm{i}}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) has the derivative \(H_{\mathrm{iy}}(P)\) at \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\), and the function \(y \mapsto H_{\mathrm{ij}}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) has the derivative
    \[\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial y}(P) + \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{iy}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jy}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}(P) .\]
    The same holds with \(x\) or \(z\) instead of \(y\).
  3. If the cells \(C\) and \(C'\) of the body have a common face, the functions \(U_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the cell \(C\) equal the functions \(U_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the cell \(C'\) at every point of this face.
Proof

We have to show three items. In the first we write the rotation and the displacement with integrals along segments from the centre of the cell, which make sense also on the faces of the cell. The second we get from lemma 4.125, the third with sequences of points.

1. Extension.

  1. Let \(P_0\) be the centre of the cell \(C\), and for a point \(P\) of the cell let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). The coordinate \(x\) of the point \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) is \((1 - t)\,x_{\mathrm{P}_0} + t\,x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and lies between \(x_{\mathrm{P}_0}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) for \(0 \le t \le 1\), as we saw for the box after definition 4.103, and likewise the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) therefore lies in the cell. If \(P\) is an interior point of the cell, all three coordinates lie strictly between the bounds of the cell, and the segment lies in the interior of the cell.
  2. Interior points of the cell are interior points of the body, so \(\vek u\) has continuous partial derivatives of first and second order at them. By lemma 1.128 on the derivatives of the rotation from derivatives of the strains, item 1, the components of the small rotation tensor \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\) (definition 1.116) have at the interior points of the cell the partial derivatives
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \psi_{\mathrm{ijk}} , \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{ijk}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
    The functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) are defined and continuous on the whole set \(D\), because they are differences of first partial derivatives of the functions \(\varepsilon\).
  3. Let \(P\) be an interior point of the cell. The function \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is continuously differentiable on the set of interior points of the cell, which is open. By lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment the function \(t \mapsto \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\) is therefore differentiable at every \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\) and has the continuous derivative \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \psi_{\mathrm{ijk}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 1,
    \[\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P) = \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P_0) + \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \psi_{\mathrm{ijk}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}t .\]
  4. The right side of step 3 makes sense at every point \(P\) of the cell, also on its faces, because by step 1 the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P\) lies in \(C\), and \(C\) lies in \(D\), where the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) are continuous. For a point \(P\) of the cell we denote it by \(\Omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P)\). By step 3, \(\Omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every interior point of the cell.
  5. Integrals along segments from \(P_0\) are continuous functions of the point. Let \(f\) be a function continuous on \(C\), \(k\) one of the indices, and \(\Phi(P) = \int_0^1 f(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}t\) for points \(P\) of the cell. The integrand is a continuous function of \(t\), because the points \(P_0 + t\,\vek d\) and \(P_0 + t'\,\vek d\) are at the distance \(|t - t'|\,|\vek d|\). By the extreme value theorem 1.78 there is a number \(M\) with \(|f| \le M\) on \(C\). Let \(\ell\) be the length of the longest edge of the cell, so that \(|d_{\mathrm{k}}| \le \ell\). Choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.6 there is \(\delta > 0\) with \(|f(Q) - f(Q')| < \eta/(4\ell)\) for any points \(Q\), \(Q'\) of the cell with \(|QQ'| < \delta\). Let \(P'\) be a point of the cell with \(|PP'| < \delta\) and \(|PP'| < \eta/(4M + 1)\), and \(\vek d' = \overrightarrow{P_0 P'}\). The points \(Q_{\mathrm{t}} = P_0 + t\,\vek d\) and \(Q'_{\mathrm{t}} = P_0 + t\,\vek d'\) are at the distance \(t\,|PP'| \le |PP'|\), and \(|d_{\mathrm{k}} - d'_{\mathrm{k}}| \le |PP'|\), because a component of the vector \(\overrightarrow{P'P} = \vek d - \vek d'\) is not longer than the vector. Therefore
    \[\begin{aligned} |f(Q_{\mathrm{t}})\,d_{\mathrm{k}} - f(Q'_{\mathrm{t}})\,d'_{\mathrm{k}}| &\le |f(Q_{\mathrm{t}}) - f(Q'_{\mathrm{t}})|\,|d_{\mathrm{k}}| + |f(Q'_{\mathrm{t}})|\,|d_{\mathrm{k}} - d'_{\mathrm{k}}| \\ &< \frac{\eta}{4\ell}\,\ell + M\,|PP'| < \frac{\eta}{4} + \frac{\eta}{4} . \end{aligned}\]
    By lemma 3.39, items 1 and 3, therefore \(|\Phi(P) - \Phi(P')| \le \eta/2 < \eta\), and by definition 1.67 \(\Phi\) is continuous at \(P\).
  6. By step 5 with \(f = \psi_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) for \(k = x, y, z\) and by the linearity of the integral, \(\Omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is continuous on \(C\). Let \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \Omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The function \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is continuous on \(C\), and at the interior points \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\), because the displacement gradient is the sum of the small strain tensor and the small rotation tensor (section 1.17.5).
  7. When we exchange \(i\) and \(j\), the function \(\psi_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) changes sign, and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ji}}(P_0) = -\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}(P_0)\). By the linearity of the integral therefore \(\Omega_{\mathrm{ji}} = -\Omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every point of the cell, and since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), we have \(\tfrac12\,(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}}) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  8. For a point \(P\) of the cell let
    \[U_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = u_{\mathrm{i}}(P_0) + \int_0^1 \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}(P_0 + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}t .\]
    The function \(U_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuous on \(C\) by step 5 with \(f = H_{\mathrm{ij}}\). At an interior point \(P\) the function \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuously differentiable with the partial derivatives \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so as in step 3 by lemma 1.132 and the fundamental theorem of calculus \(U_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\). The functions are uniquely determined. Let \(G\) be another function, continuous on \(C\), that equals \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) at the interior points, \(P\) a point of the cell and \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = P + \tfrac1n\,\overrightarrow{P P_0}\) for \(n = 2, 3, \dots\) Every coordinate of the point \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) lies strictly between the bounds of the cell, because \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) lies strictly between \(P\) and the centre \(P_0\), so \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) is an interior point and \(G(P_{\mathrm{n}}) = U_{\mathrm{i}}(P_{\mathrm{n}})\). The points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) converge to \(P\), so by lemma 1.68 and the uniqueness of the limit (lemma 1.41) \(G(P) = U_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\). The same holds for \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

2. Derivatives along the faces.

  1. The function \(U_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuous on \(C\), at the interior points it has the partial derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y = H_{\mathrm{iy}}\), and this is continuous on \(C\). By lemma 4.125, item 2, \(y \mapsto U_{\mathrm{i}}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) therefore has the derivative \(H_{\mathrm{iy}}(P)\) at \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\).
  2. The function \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is continuous on \(C\), and at the interior points it equals \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\). By lemma 1.128, item 2, it has there the partial derivative with respect to \(y\) equal to \(\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial y + \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{iy}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jy}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\). This expression is continuous on \(D\), hence on \(C\), so lemma 4.125, item 2, gives the claim for \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\). For \(x\) and \(z\) the steps are the same.

3. Common face.

  1. Let the common face lie in the plane \(x = c\), let the cell \(C\) lie on the side \(x \le c\) and the cell \(C'\) on the side \(x \ge c\), and let \(P\) be a point of the common face that lies on none of its sides. Let \(r > 0\) be smaller than the distances of the point \(P\) to the planes in which the faces of the cells \(C\) and \(C'\) lie, except the plane \(x = c\). A point \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < r\) has every coordinate within \(r\) of the coordinate of the point \(P\), because a component of a vector is not longer than the vector. For \(x_{\mathrm{Q}} \le c\) it therefore lies in \(C\), and for \(x_{\mathrm{Q}} \ge c\) in \(C'\). The point \(P\) is thus an interior point of the body.
  2. The field \(\vek u\) and its partial derivatives are continuous at \(P\) (lemma 1.91). The points \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = P + \tfrac1n\,\overrightarrow{P P_0}\) for \(n = 2, 3, \dots\) are interior points of the cell \(C\), because they lie strictly between \(P\) and the centre \(P_0\) of the cell, and they converge to \(P\). By step 8, \(U_{\mathrm{i}}(P_{\mathrm{n}}) = u_{\mathrm{i}}(P_{\mathrm{n}})\). By lemma 1.68 the left side tends to \(U_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\), because \(U_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuous on \(C\), and the right side to \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\). So \(U_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\), and likewise \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(P) = \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,(P)\). The same holds for the cell \(C'\), so the extensions of both cells are equal at \(P\).
  3. A point on a side of the common face is the limit of a sequence of points of the common face that do not lie on its sides, for instance of points lying strictly between it and the centre of the face. The extensions of both cells are continuous, so by lemma 1.68 and step 12 they are equal also there.

Source: The lemma and the proof are not from the sources. The rotation and the displacement written as integrals of the changes along a path are Cesàro integrals (BARBER, PDF p. 46, SADD (2.6.3)-(2.6.7), PDF pp. 52-53).

The lemma extended the field to every cell separately. Why not to the whole body at once? If two cells of the body touch only along an edge and have no common face, the points of this edge are not interior points of the body, and the field reaches them from two sides along different paths through the body. The lemma says nothing about such an edge. For cells with a common face the extensions are equal, because the points of the common face are interior points of the body, where the field is defined and continuous. For the strip of subsection 4.7.7 the field of the theorem is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and its extension is the same polynomial, which we can compute also on the faces of the strip. The lemma is needed for fields that we know only through integrals in the interior of the body, like the field of item 2 of theorem 4.124.

Now we can write the idea from the beginning of the subsection precisely. We write the mismatch on every rectangle of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) separately, with the extension to the cell the rectangle belongs to.

Lemma 4.128 Work of the virtual support forces on the mismatch (delo virtualnih sil podpor na neujemanju)

Let the body \(V\), the parts of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) and the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be as in theorem 4.124, and let the equation

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{u}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\bar{\vek u}\,\mathrm{d}A\]

hold for every statically admissible virtual stress field. Let \(\vek u\) be a displacement field defined at the interior points of the body, whose components have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order there and whose small strain tensor components equal \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every interior point. For a rectangle \(F\) of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) that is a face of the cell \(C\) let the mismatch be \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}} = \vek U_{\mathrm{C}} - \bar{\vek u}\) on \(F\), where \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}}\) is the extension of the field \(\vek u\) to the cell \(C\) (lemma 4.127). Then for every statically admissible virtual stress field

\[\sum_{\mathrm{F}} \int_{\mathrm{F}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek w_{\mathrm{F}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 , \tag{4.80}\]

where the sum runs over the rectangles of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\).

Proof

We have to show that the left side of the equation in the assumption equals the work of the virtual support forces on the extensions of the field \(\vek u\). On every cell this follows from the divergence theorem up to the faces of a box, as lemma 4.81 gave the principle of virtual forces.

  1. Let \(C\) be a cell of the body and \(U_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the functions of lemma 4.127, item 1. For \(i = x, y, z\) let \(v_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,U_{\mathrm{j}}\). The function \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuous on \(C\). At the interior points of the cell \(U_{\mathrm{j}} = u_{\mathrm{j}}\), and by the product rule (lemma 1.81) there
    \[\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big( \frac{\partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\,U_{\mathrm{j}} + \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,H_{\mathrm{ji}} \Big) .\]
    We denote the right side by \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\). The function \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuous on \(C\), because the components of the virtual field are continuously differentiable (definition 4.96, item 1).
  2. By lemma 4.126, with the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(\int_{\mathrm{C}} g_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{C}} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A\), where \(S_{\mathrm{C}}\) is the surface of the cell and \(\vek n\) its outward normal.
  3. Let us sum over \(i\). At every point of the cell \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \partial\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) by definition 4.96, item 3. In the double sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,H_{\mathrm{ji}}\) we exchange the names of the indices and use the symmetry \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ji}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so it also equals \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and half the sum of both, \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\tfrac12\,(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}})\). By lemma 4.127, item 1, this is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). So at every point of the cell \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  4. As in step 8 of the proof of lemma 4.81, \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\,U_{\mathrm{j}} = (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek U_{\mathrm{C}}\). By steps 2 and 3 and the linearity of the integral
    \[\int_{\mathrm{C}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{C}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek U_{\mathrm{C}}\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
  5. The integral over the body is the sum of the integrals over the cells (definition 4.11, item 1). A face that is not an outer face is common to two cells of the body. By lemma 4.127, item 3, the extensions of both cells are equal on it, while the outward normals of the two cells are opposite, so their contributions cancel, as in step 2 of the second part of the proof of theorem 4.14. What remains are the outer faces, each once, with the extension to the cell it belongs to.
  6. On the outer faces of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\) (definition 4.96, item 4). Therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{F}} \int_{\mathrm{F}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek U_{\mathrm{C}}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]
    where for every rectangle \(F\) of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) the cell \(C\) is the one \(F\) belongs to.
  7. The right side of the equation in the assumption is the sum of the integrals over the same rectangles (definition 4.11, item 3). Subtracting the equation in the assumption from the equality of step 6 and using the linearity of the integral over every rectangle we get (4.80).

Source: EP (4.4.5)-(4.4.10) (pp. 197-198), where the condition \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is written as part of the equation of virtual forces, with an assumed displacement field. The lemma and the proof are not from the sources.

The equality (4.80) is the precise form of the sentence at the beginning of the subsection: the virtual support forces do no work on the mismatch. If the mismatch is the same small rigid displacement on all rectangles of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the equality holds for every statically admissible field, as we saw at the beginning. Now we look for fields that show that there are no other possibilities.

Which virtual fields give chosen forces on a face of the support? Take a rectangle \(F\) of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and name the axes so that it lies in the plane \(x = c\) (figure 4.102). The outward normal of the face is \(s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), where \(s = 1\) if the cell of the face lies on the side \(x \le c\), and \(s = -1\) if it lies on the side \(x \ge c\). We write the stress function as a product \(\varphi = \chi(x)\,Q(y, z)\). The factor \(Q(y, z) = q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\) is a bump of lemma 4.122 on a rectangle \([\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) in the interior of the face \(F\), and the factor \(\chi\) is a bump on an interval around \(c\) that reaches to both sides of the face. The function \(\varphi\) is zero, together with its derivatives up to third order, outside the box \(K\) made of this interval and the rectangle, so the field (4.77) from it is zero outside \(K\) too. The box \(K\) meets the body only in the cell of the face \(F\) and the surface only on \(F\), so the field does not reach \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and is statically admissible. On \(F\) its virtual traction vector, the virtual support force per unit area, is

\[\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = s\,(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}) = s\,\Big(\chi(c)\,\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial y^2},\ -\chi'(c)\,\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y},\ 0\Big) .\]

The force perpendicular to the face is proportional to the value \(\chi(c)\), the force along the face to the derivative \(\chi'(c)\). We can choose both independently by moving the bump \(\chi\) with respect to the face. The symmetric bump \(q_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{h}}\) has the value \(h^8\) and the derivative zero at \(c\), while the bump \(q_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{h}/2}\), which reaches across the face only half as far, has the value \(h^8/16\) and the derivative \(-h^7/4\), as we compute with SymPy (figure 4.102, right).

What work do these forces do on the mismatch \(\vek w\)? We move the derivatives from the bump \(Q\) to the mismatch, as in lemma 4.123, only integrating over the face. Every move gives a minus, and we get

\[\int_{\mathrm{F}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek w\,\mathrm{d}A = s \int_{\mathrm{F}} Q\,\Big(\chi(c)\,\frac{\partial^2 w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y^2} + \chi'(c)\,\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}A .\]

By the equality (4.80) this is zero. With the symmetric bump and the fundamental lemma we therefore get \(\partial^2 w_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y^2 = 0\), with the other bump also \(\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = 0\). The first says that the component of the mismatch perpendicular to the face varies linearly along the axis \(y\). With the mismatch the face may move and tilt, but it does not curve. The second says that with the mismatch the face is not stretched along the axis \(y\). Two more fields of lemma 4.121 do the same, one for the axis \(z\) and one for shear in the plane of the face. Before we write this in a lemma, let us look at numbers.

Let us test the idea on the strip of subsection 4.7.7 (figure 4.103). Let us repeat the setting. A thin steel strip of length 200 mm, height 20 mm and thickness 2 mm lies from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 200\) mm, from \(y = -10\) mm to \(y = 10\) mm and from \(z = -1\) mm to \(z = 1\) mm. The prescribed strains are those of the corrected strip, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\) with the exaggerated \(k = -10\) m⁻², the others are zero. The strip is now welded to a wall at its left end. The left end, the face \(x = 0\), is \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), all the other surface is \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and unloaded. The field of theorem 4.106 is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and it is zero at the left end. If the wall is flat and rigid, \(\bar{\vek u} = \vek 0\), the mismatch is zero, and by the principle of virtual forces the equation holds for every statically admissible field. But what if the wall is curved, so that the end of the strip has to fit it with the displacement \(\bar u_{\mathrm{x}} = m\,y^2\), \(\bar u_{\mathrm{y}} = \bar u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), with \(m = 1\) m⁻¹? The mismatch is then \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = -m\,y^2\) and is not a rigid displacement.

  1. The box \(K\) with edges 10 mm, 10 mm and 1 mm has its centre at the centre of the left end of the strip. It reaches from \(x = -5\) mm to \(x = 5\) mm, from \(y = -5\) mm to \(y = 5\) mm and from \(z = -0{,}5\) mm to \(z = 0{,}5\) mm. Its right half, with \(x \ge 0\), lies in the strip.
  2. The stress function is as in the test of theorem 4.124, only with the centre of the box at the origin,
    \[\varphi = \Phi_0\,\frac{q_{-\mathrm{h}_1,\mathrm{h}_1}(x)}{h_1^8}\,\frac{q_{-\mathrm{h}_2,\mathrm{h}_2}(y)}{h_2^8}\,\frac{q_{-\mathrm{h}_3,\mathrm{h}_3}(z)}{h_3^8} ,\]
    with \(h_1 = h_2 = 5\) mm, \(h_3 = 0{,}5\) mm and \(\Phi_0 = 3{,}125\) N. The first quotient is a symmetric bump \(\chi\) with the value \(1\) at \(x = 0\). At the centre of the left end \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -1\) MPa, with SymPy.
  3. The outward normal of the left end is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), so the virtual force of the wall per unit area is \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = -(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\). At \(x = 0\) we have \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y = 0\), because the symmetric bump has derivative zero there, and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\), so the wall acts only perpendicular to the end, with the force \(-\partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\) per unit area. In the middle this is \(1\) MPa in the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the wall pushes the end of the strip. Between \(1{,}89\) mm and \(5\) mm from the middle the force is opposite, the wall pulls the end, most strongly with \(0{,}653\) MPa at \(3{,}27\) mm (figure 4.103). The total force and the total moment of these forces are zero, as in the test of theorem 4.124.
  4. The left side of the equation of virtual forces is
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \big(k\,y^2\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - k\,x^2\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\big)\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 ,\]
    with SymPy over the half of the box in the strip. Step 6 of the proof of lemma 4.128 says this too: the left side is the work of the forces of the wall on the extension of the field \(\vek u\), and this is zero at the left end.
  5. For the flat wall the right side is zero, and the equation holds. For a wall tilted about the axis \(z\), with \(\bar u_{\mathrm{x}} = \theta\,y\), the right side is \(\int_{\mathrm{F}} (-\partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2)\,\theta\,y\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), with SymPy, and the equation holds again. The tilted wall gives the mismatch \(-\theta\,y\), which is a rigid displacement, and the field of item 2 of theorem 4.124 may have such a displacement.
  6. For the curved wall the right side is
    \[\int_{\mathrm{F}} \Big(-\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2}\Big)\,m\,y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = -2m \int_{\mathrm{F}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}A = -1{,}032 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{J} ,\]
    where we moved the two derivatives by integrating by parts twice, because \(\partial^2(y^2)/\partial y^2 = 2\), and computed the integral with SymPy. The left side is zero and the right side is not, so the equation fails for this statically admissible virtual field.

A strip whose left end stays flat under the prescribed strains therefore cannot be welded to a curved wall without extra deformation, and the equation of virtual forces detects this. The right side is the work of the virtual forces of the wall on the displacement prescribed by the curved wall, and it has a simple meaning. The wall pulls the end of the strip in two bands closer to the edges of the box, where the end would have to move furthest to the right along the curved wall, and pushes it in the band in the middle. The pull on the bands that move to the right does negative work, and since the displacement there is larger, it prevails.

Now let us write the general statement.

Lemma 4.129 The mismatch on a face of the support is a rigid displacement (neujemanje na ploskvi podpore je togi premik)

Let the assumptions of lemma 4.128 hold, and let the prescribed displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) equal a field \(\bar{\vek u}\) whose components have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body. Then for every rectangle \(F\) of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) there are a constant vector \(\vek a_{\mathrm{F}}\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W_{\mathrm{F}}\) such that the mismatch is

\[\vek w_{\mathrm{F}}(P) = \vek a_{\mathrm{F}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{F}}\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} \qquad \text{for every point } P \text{ of the rectangle } F .\]
Proof

We have to show that on \(F\) the component of the mismatch perpendicular to the face is a linear function of the coordinates, and that the other two components are a rigid displacement in the plane of the face. We use virtual fields from bumps in boxes that cross the face, move the derivatives from the bump to the mismatch along the face and use the fundamental lemma.

1. Fields next to the face.

  1. We name the axes so that \(F\) lies in the plane \(x = c\), \(F = \{c\} \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\). Let \(C\) be the cell \(F\) belongs to, \(s = 1\) if \(C\) lies on the side \(x \le c\), and \(s = -1\) if it lies on the side \(x \ge c\). The outward normal of the face is \(s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). We write the mismatch simply \(\vek w\), without the index \(F\).
  2. Let \(h > 0\) be smaller than all edges of all cells of the grid, and let \(\alpha_2\), \(\beta_2\), \(\alpha_3\), \(\beta_3\) be numbers with \(a_2 < \alpha_2 < \beta_2 < b_2\) and \(a_3 < \alpha_3 < \beta_3 < b_3\). Let \(Q(y, z) = q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}(z)\) and let \(\chi\) be one of the functions \(q_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{h}}\) and \(q_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{h}/2}\) of lemma 4.122. The function \(\varphi(x, y, z) = \chi(x)\,Q(y, z)\) is the product of the three bumps of the box \(K = [c - h, c + h'] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\), where \(h' = h\) or \(h' = h/2\). By lemma 4.122, item 2, it has continuous partial derivatives up to third order in the whole space, which together with it are zero at every point that does not lie in the interior of the box \(K\).
  3. The box \(K\) and the body. The points of the box \(K\) with \(s\,(x - c) < 0\) have the coordinate \(x\) between \(c\) and \(c - s\,h\), and the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) strictly between \(a_2\) and \(b_2\) and between \(a_3\) and \(b_3\). Since \(h\) is smaller than the edges of the cell \(C\), these are interior points of the cell \(C\), hence interior points of the body. The points with \(s\,(x - c) > 0\) are for the same reason interior points of the cell of the grid on the other side of the face \(F\), which is not a cell of the body, because \(F\) is an outer face, or they lie outside the box the grid cuts. Such points are not in the body, as in step 1 of the proof of lemma 4.12. The points with \(x = c\) lie on \(F\). The only points of the surface of the body in \(K\) are therefore points of the face \(F\).
  4. Let \(\delta\ten\sigma\) be one of three fields: the field (4.77) with the function \(\varphi\), the field we get from it by renaming the axes twice (lemma 4.121, item 3), with the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial z^2\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\), \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial z\) and the others zero, or the field (4.78) with the function \(\varphi\). By lemma 4.121 it is symmetric, continuously differentiable in the whole space and in equilibrium without body force. Its components are second partial derivatives of \(\varphi\) or zero, so by step 2 they are zero at every point that does not lie in the interior of \(K\). By step 3 therefore \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\) on the whole surface except on \(F\), in particular on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and the field is statically admissible (definition 4.96).

2. Work on the face.

  1. By step 4, for each of the three fields the integrals in (4.80) over all rectangles except \(F\) are zero, and on \(F\) the integrand is zero outside the rectangle \(R = \{c\} \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\). Cutting \(F\) with the lines \(y = \alpha_2\), \(y = \beta_2\), \(z = \alpha_3\) and \(z = \beta_3\) we get by lemma 4.10, item 3, for a rectangle
    \[\int_{\mathrm{R}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek w\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 .\]
  2. The component \(j\) of the vector \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) is by Cauchy's formula (2.24) equal to \(s\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xj}}\). On \(R\) we have \(\chi(x) = \chi(c)\) and \(\chi'(x) = \chi'(c)\), so for the three fields of step 4 in turn
    \[\begin{aligned} \delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n &= s\,\big(\chi(c)\,Q_{\mathrm{yy}},\ -\chi'(c)\,Q_{\mathrm{y}},\ 0\big) , \\ \delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n &= s\,\big(\chi(c)\,Q_{\mathrm{zz}},\ 0,\ -\chi'(c)\,Q_{\mathrm{z}}\big) , \\ \delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n &= s\,\big(2\,\chi(c)\,Q_{\mathrm{yz}},\ -\chi'(c)\,Q_{\mathrm{z}},\ -\chi'(c)\,Q_{\mathrm{y}}\big) , \end{aligned}\]
    where an index on \(Q\) denotes a partial derivative, for instance \(Q_{\mathrm{yz}} = \partial^2 Q/\partial z\,\partial y = q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}'(y)\,q_{\alpha_3\beta_3}'(z)\). We checked all three lines with SymPy.
  3. Derivatives of the mismatch along the face. By lemma 4.127, item 2, and by the assumption on the field \(\bar{\vek u}\), the functions \(y \mapsto w_{\mathrm{i}}(c, y, z)\) and \(z \mapsto w_{\mathrm{i}}(c, y, z)\) have derivatives at the points of the face that do not lie on its sides, and these again have derivatives with respect to \(y\) and \(z\). All these derivatives are continuous functions of the point there, because they are differences of functions continuous on \(C\) and of derivatives of the field \(\bar{\vek u}\). We write them \(\partial w_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y\), \(\partial^2 w_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y^2\), \(\partial(\partial w_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial y)/\partial z\) and so on.
  4. Integration by parts along the face. For constant \(z\) the function \(y \mapsto Q(y, z)\) and its derivative are zero at \(\alpha_2\) and \(\beta_2\) (lemma 4.122, item 1). By integration by parts (corollary 3.41), used once or twice as in steps 4 and 5 of the proof of lemma 4.123, and by theorem 4.9 for a rectangle, therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{R}} Q_{\mathrm{yy}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{R}} Q\,\frac{\partial^2 w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y^2}\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad \int_{\mathrm{R}} Q_{\mathrm{y}}\,w_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}A = -\int_{\mathrm{R}} Q\,\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]
    the same with \(z\) instead of \(y\), and
    \[\int_{\mathrm{R}} Q_{\mathrm{yz}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{R}} Q\,\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{R}} Q\,\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]
    where in the first equality we moved the derivative with respect to \(y\) first, in the second the derivative with respect to \(z\) first.
  5. Inserting step 8 into step 5 with the forces of step 6 and dividing by \(s\) we get for the three fields
    \[\begin{aligned} &\int_{\mathrm{R}} Q\,\Big(\chi(c)\,\frac{\partial^2 w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y^2} + \chi'(c)\,\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 , \\ &\int_{\mathrm{R}} Q\,\Big(\chi(c)\,\frac{\partial^2 w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z^2} + \chi'(c)\,\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 , \\ &\int_{\mathrm{R}} Q\,\Big(2\,\chi(c)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big) + \chi'(c)\,\Big(\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\Big)\Big)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 , \end{aligned}\]
    and the third equality also with \(\partial(\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z)/\partial y\) instead of \(\partial(\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y)/\partial z\). We checked the signs with SymPy.
  6. The fundamental lemma. Let \(P\) be a point of the face \(F\) that lies on none of its sides, and \(R^*\) a rectangle on \(F\) with centre \(P\) that does not reach the sides of the face. The functions in the brackets of step 9 are continuous on \(R^*\) by step 7, and step 9 holds for every rectangle \(R\) in the interior of \(R^*\). Lemma 4.83, item 3, which is about a rectangle in a plane \(z = c\), we use with the roles of the coordinates exchanged, with \(y\) and \(z\) instead of \(x\) and \(y\). It holds also with the bumps \(q_{\alpha\beta}\) instead of \(p_{\alpha\beta}\), because its proof uses only that the bump is not negative and has a positive integral (item 3 of the proof of lemma 4.122). By it the functions in the brackets are zero on \(R^*\), in particular at \(P\).
  7. The symmetric bump \(\chi = q_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{h}}\) has \(\chi(c) = h^8 > 0\) and \(\chi'(c) = 0\), with SymPy. Step 10 with it gives at every point of the face that does not lie on a side
    \[\frac{\partial^2 w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y^2} = 0 , \qquad \frac{\partial^2 w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z^2} = 0 , \qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big) = 0 , \qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}\Big) = 0 .\]
  8. The bump \(\chi = q_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{h}/2}\) has \(\chi'(c) = -h^7/4 \neq 0\), with SymPy. The first terms in the brackets are zero by step 11, so step 10 with it gives
    \[\frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} = 0 , \qquad \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = 0 , \qquad \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial w_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y} = 0 .\]

3. The rigid displacement.

  1. Let \(F^\circ\) be the set of points of the face that do not lie on its sides. The function \(\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y\) has, for constant \(z\), the derivative zero with respect to \(y\) by step 11. By corollary 1.85 it is therefore constant on every closed interval in \((a_2, b_2)\), so it does not depend on \(y\). For constant \(y\) its derivative with respect to \(z\) is zero, so for the same reason it does not depend on \(z\). On \(F^\circ\) it is thus constant. We denote it by \(\lambda_{\mathrm{y}}\). Likewise \(\partial w_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z\) is constant on \(F^\circ\), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  2. The function \(w_{\mathrm{x}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{y}}\,y - \lambda_{\mathrm{z}}\,z\) has the derivative zero with respect to \(y\) and with respect to \(z\) on \(F^\circ\), so for the same reason it is constant, \(\lambda_0\). On \(F^\circ\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = \lambda_0 + \lambda_{\mathrm{y}}\,y + \lambda_{\mathrm{z}}\,z\).
  3. By step 12, \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) has, for constant \(z\), the derivative zero with respect to \(y\), so it depends only on \(z\): \(w_{\mathrm{y}}(c, y, z) = f(z)\), where \(f(z) = w_{\mathrm{y}}(c, y_0, z)\) for a chosen \(y_0\). Likewise \(w_{\mathrm{z}}(c, y, z) = g(y)\). The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are differentiable by step 7, and by step 12 \(f'(z) + g'(y) = 0\) for all points of \(F^\circ\). For the chosen \(y_0\) therefore \(f'(z) = -g'(y_0)\) for every \(z\). Let \(\theta = g'(y_0)\). The function \(f(z) + \theta\,z\) has derivative zero, so it is constant, \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}}\). The function \(g(y) - \theta\,y\) has the derivative \(g'(y) - \theta = -f'(z) - \theta = 0\), so it is constant, \(\kappa_{\mathrm{z}}\). On \(F^\circ\) therefore \(w_{\mathrm{y}} = \kappa_{\mathrm{y}} - \theta\,z\) and \(w_{\mathrm{z}} = \kappa_{\mathrm{z}} + \theta\,y\).
  4. Let \(\mat W_{\mathrm{F}}\) be the antisymmetric matrix with zeros on the diagonal and with \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{xz}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{zy}} = \theta\), \(W_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{zx}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{yz}} = -\theta\), and \(\vek a_{\mathrm{F}} = (\lambda_0,\ \kappa_{\mathrm{y}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{y}}\,c,\ \kappa_{\mathrm{z}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{z}}\,c)\). For a point \(P = (c, y, z)\) of \(F^\circ\)
    \[\begin{aligned} \vek a_{\mathrm{F}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{F}}\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \big(&\lambda_0 + \lambda_{\mathrm{y}}\,y + \lambda_{\mathrm{z}}\,z,\ \ \kappa_{\mathrm{y}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{y}}\,c - \lambda_{\mathrm{y}}\,c - \theta\,z, \\ &\kappa_{\mathrm{z}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{z}}\,c - \lambda_{\mathrm{z}}\,c + \theta\,y\big) , \end{aligned}\]
    which by steps 14 and 15 equals \(\vek w(P)\).
  5. A point \(P\) on a side of the face is the limit of the points \(P + \tfrac1n\,\overrightarrow{PM}\) of \(F^\circ\), where \(M\) is the centre of the face. The mismatch is continuous on \(F\), because \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(\bar{\vek u}\) are continuous, and so is the field \(\vek a_{\mathrm{F}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{F}}\,\vek r\). By lemma 1.68 they are therefore equal also at \(P\).

Source: EP (4.4.9), (4.4.10) (p. 198) gets the condition \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) from the virtual stresses on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) being arbitrary. The virtual fields with a bump next to a face and the proof are not from the sources.

The lemma has shown why the support forces demand a rigid mismatch. The forces perpendicular to the face, proportional to second derivatives of the bump, checked whether the component of the mismatch perpendicular to the face varies linearly along the face, that is, whether the face is only moved and tilted by the mismatch, not curved. The forces along the face checked whether the face is neither stretched nor sheared in its plane by the mismatch. These are exactly the properties of a rigid displacement of the face. For the strip against the curved wall the mismatch \(-m\,y^2\) was curved, and the first field detected it.

On every rectangle of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) the mismatch is therefore a rigid displacement, but possibly a different one on each. What if the rigid displacements on two neighbouring rectangles \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) differ? On their common side \(E\) both rigid displacements equal the mismatch, which is a single one there when the extensions of the cells of both rectangles agree on \(E\). The difference of the two rigid displacements is therefore zero on the segment \(E\). A rigid displacement that is zero at two points is a small rotation about the line through these points, like a door turning about its hinges. So the difference is a rotation about the side \(E\). It is detected by the virtual field from a bump in a box around a point of the side \(E\), which crosses both rectangles (figure 4.104). The forces of this field on \(F_1\) and on \(F_2\) are in equilibrium together, but the forces on \(F_2\) alone have a moment about the side \(E\), and a rotation about \(E\) does work on this moment. How can \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) be placed? Along the side \(E\) the grid has four cells. Among them the body has one cell, both of whose faces through \(E\) are outer faces, two cells with a common face, for which \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) lie in the same plane, or three cells surrounding a re-entrant edge. Assumption 3 excludes only two cells without a common face.

Now we have everything for the theorem.

Theorem 4.130 Converse of the principle of virtual forces at the supports (obrat načela virtualnih sil na podporah)

Let the body \(V\), the parts of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be as in theorem 4.124, and let the equation of virtual forces hold for every statically admissible virtual stress field. Assume further:

  1. the set of interior points of the body is connected (definition 1.130) and simply connected (definition 1.136),
  2. the prescribed displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) equals a field \(\bar{\vek u}\) whose components have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the body,
  3. \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is not empty, and any two of its rectangles are joined by a chain of its rectangles in which neighbouring rectangles have a common side and the cells of the body containing this side are not exactly two cells without a common face.

Then there is a displacement field \(\tilde{\vek u}\), defined at the interior points of the body, with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order, whose small strain tensor components equal \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every interior point and whose extension to the cell of every rectangle of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) (lemma 4.127) equals \(\bar{\vek u}\) on this rectangle.

Proof

We have to show that the mismatches on all rectangles of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) are one single rigid displacement. On every rectangle separately this is lemma 4.129, neighbouring rectangles are joined by the field around their common side, and all rectangles by the chain of assumption 3.

1. The field and the mismatch.

  1. By theorem 4.124, item 2, which we may use because of assumption 1, there is a displacement field \(\vek u\) at the interior points of the body with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order and with the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By lemma 4.127 it has an extension \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}}\) to every cell \(C\) of the body.
  2. By lemma 4.129, which we may use because of assumption 2, for every rectangle \(F\) of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) the mismatch \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}} = \vek U_{\mathrm{C}} - \bar{\vek u}\), where \(C\) is the cell of the rectangle \(F\), equals on \(F\) the rigid displacement \(\vek R_{\mathrm{F}} = \vek a_{\mathrm{F}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{F}}\,\vek r\).

2. Neighbouring rectangles.

  1. Let \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) be neighbouring rectangles of the chain of assumption 3, with the common side \(E\), and let \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) be their cells. First we extend the grid by one layer of cells on every side of the box it cuts, as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 4.12. The new cells lie outside the body, so the cells of the body, its outer faces and the rectangles of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) do not change, while no side of a cell of the body lies on the surface of the box of the grid any more. The grid therefore has four cells containing \(E\). Not all four can be cells of the body, because then every face through \(E\) would be common to two cells of the body, while \(F_1\) is an outer face. By assumption 3 the cells of the body among them are therefore one cell, two cells with a common face, or three cells, which can be ordered so that the middle one has a common face with the first and with the last.
  2. The extensions of the cells \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are equal on \(E\). For one cell \(C_1 = C_2\). For two cells each has one outer face through \(E\), so \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are these two cells, \(E\) lies on their common face, and by lemma 4.127, item 3, the extensions are equal on it. For three cells the outer faces through \(E\) are the faces of the first and the last cell bordering the missing cell, so \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are the first and the last, and by the same item of the lemma their extensions on \(E\) equal the extension of the middle cell. Since the prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) is a single one, the mismatches \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}_1}\) and \(\vek w_{\mathrm{F}_2}\) are equal on \(E\), and by step 2 \(\vek R_{\mathrm{F}_1} = \vek R_{\mathrm{F}_2}\) on \(E\).
  3. We name the axes so that \(E\) is parallel to the axis \(z\), \(E = \{(c, d, z) : e_1 \le z \le e_2\}\), and so that \(F_2\) lies in the plane \(y = d\). Let \(\vek D = \vek R_{\mathrm{F}_2} - \vek R_{\mathrm{F}_1} = \vek a_{\mathrm{D}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\,\vek r\), where \(\vek a_{\mathrm{D}} = \vek a_{\mathrm{F}_2} - \vek a_{\mathrm{F}_1}\) and \(\mat W_{\mathrm{D}} = \mat W_{\mathrm{F}_2} - \mat W_{\mathrm{F}_1}\) is antisymmetric. By step 4, \(\vek D\) is zero at the end points \(A = (c, d, e_1)\) and \(B = (c, d, e_2)\) of the side. From \(\vek D(B) - \vek D(A) = \mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\,(\vek r_{\mathrm{B}} - \vek r_{\mathrm{A}}) = (e_2 - e_1)\,\mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek 0\) it follows that \(W_{\mathrm{xz}} = W_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\), and by antisymmetry also \(W_{\mathrm{zx}} = W_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\). From \(\vek D(A) = \vek 0\) it follows that \(\vek a_{\mathrm{D}} = -\mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\,\vek r_{\mathrm{A}}\). With \(\theta = W_{\mathrm{yx}} = -W_{\mathrm{xy}}\) therefore
    \[\vek D(P) = \mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\,(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} - \vek r_{\mathrm{A}}) = \big(-\theta\,(y - d),\ \theta\,(x - c),\ 0\big) ,\]
    a rotation about the line through \(E\).
  4. The field around the side. Let \(h > 0\) be smaller than all edges of all cells of the grid, \(e_1 < z_1 < z_2 < e_2\) and
    \[\varphi(x, y, z) = q_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{h}}(x)\,q_{\mathrm{d}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{d}+\mathrm{h}}(y)\,q_{\mathrm{z}_1 \mathrm{z}_2}(z) ,\]
    the product of the bumps of the box \(K = [c - h, c + h] \times [d - h, d + h] \times [z_1, z_2]\) (lemma 4.122). Let \(\delta\ten\sigma\) be the field (4.77) with this function. By lemma 4.121 it is symmetric, continuously differentiable and in equilibrium, and as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 4.129 it is zero at every point that does not lie in the interior of \(K\).
  5. The box \(K\) lies in the union of the four cells of the grid along \(E\), because \(h\) is smaller than their edges and \(e_1 < z_1 < z_2 < e_2\). The points of the surface of the body in \(K\) therefore lie on the outer faces of these cells through \(E\), the other faces of these cells \(K\) does not reach. In all three cases of step 3 the outer faces through \(E\) are exactly \(F_1\) and \(F_2\). The field is therefore zero on the whole surface except on \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), which belong to \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), and it is statically admissible.
  6. By (4.80) and step 2, \(\int_{\mathrm{F}_1} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek R_{\mathrm{F}_1}\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{F}_2} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek R_{\mathrm{F}_2}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\). The rigid displacement \(\vek R_{\mathrm{F}_1}\) has no strains (theorem 1.134, item 2), so lemma 4.81, applied with the virtual field instead of the stress and with \(\vek R_{\mathrm{F}_1}\) instead of the virtual displacement, gives \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek R_{\mathrm{F}_1}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), where by step 7 only the faces \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) contribute. Subtracting the equalities, what remains is
    \[\int_{\mathrm{F}_2} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek D\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 .\]
  7. The outward normal of the face \(F_2\) is \(s_2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(s_2 = \pm 1\), so on \(F_2\) by Cauchy's formula (2.24) \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = s_2\,(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}) = s_2\,(-\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y,\ \partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2,\ 0)\). On \(F_2\) we have \(y = d\) and by step 5 \(\vek D = (0, \theta\,(x - c), 0)\), so the integrand is
    \[s_2\,\theta\,(x - c)\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} = s_2\,\theta\,(x - c)\,q_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{h}}''(x)\,q_{\mathrm{d}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{d}+\mathrm{h}}(d)\,q_{\mathrm{z}_1 \mathrm{z}_2}(z) .\]
  8. The rectangle \(F_2\) lies on one side of the side \(E\), so the part of \(F_2\) in \(K\) is the set of points with \(x\) between \(c\) and \(c + h\) or between \(c - h\) and \(c\) and with \(z_1 \le z \le z_2\). The integrand of step 9 is zero at the other points of \(F_2\), because the field is zero there (step 6), so the integral over \(F_2\) equals the integral over this rectangle (lemma 4.10, item 3, for a rectangle, as in step 5 of the proof of lemma 4.129). The function \(\chi = q_{\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{h}}\) and its derivative are zero at \(c \pm h\), so by integration by parts (corollary 3.41)
    \[\begin{aligned} \int_{\mathrm{c}}^{c+h} (x - c)\,\chi''(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &= \big[(x - c)\,\chi'(x)\big]_{\mathrm{c}}^{c+h} - \int_{\mathrm{c}}^{c+h} \chi'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &= 0 - \big(\chi(c + h) - \chi(c)\big) = \chi(c) , \end{aligned}\]
    and on the interval from \(c - h\) to \(c\) in the same way \(-\chi(c)\).
  9. By steps 8 to 10 and by theorem 4.9 for a rectangle therefore
    \[\pm\,s_2\,\theta\,\chi(c)\,q_{\mathrm{d}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{d}+\mathrm{h}}(d) \int_{\mathrm{z}_1}^{z_2} q_{\mathrm{z}_1 \mathrm{z}_2}(z)\,\mathrm{d}z = 0 .\]
    All three factors after \(\theta\) are positive: \(\chi(c) = h^8\), \(q_{\mathrm{d}-\mathrm{h},\mathrm{d}+\mathrm{h}}(d) = h^8\), and the integral of the bump is positive (item 3 of the proof of lemma 4.122). Therefore \(\theta = 0\), \(\vek D = \vek 0\) and \(\vek R_{\mathrm{F}_1} = \vek R_{\mathrm{F}_2}\). We also checked all three arrangements of figure 4.104 with SymPy.

3. One rigid displacement.

  1. By assumption 3 any two rectangles of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) are joined by a chain in which neighbouring rectangles are always neighbours as in step 3. By steps 3 to 11 neighbouring rectangles have the same rigid displacement, so all rectangles of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) have the same rigid displacement \(\vek R = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\).
  2. Let \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u - \vek R\) at the interior points of the body. The field \(\vek R\) has constant first partial derivatives and a zero small strain tensor (theorem 1.134, item 2), so \(\tilde{\vek u}\) has continuous partial derivatives of first and second order and the same small strain tensor components as \(\vek u\), namely \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). For every cell \(C\) the field \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}} - \vek R\) is continuous on \(C\) and equals \(\tilde{\vek u}\) at the interior points, with derivatives \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} - W_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so it is the extension of the field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) to \(C\) in the sense of lemma 4.127.
  3. On a rectangle \(F\) of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) with the cell \(C\), by step 2 and step 12, \(\vek U_{\mathrm{C}} - \vek R = \bar{\vek u} + \vek w_{\mathrm{F}} - \vek R_{\mathrm{F}} = \bar{\vek u}\).

Source: EP (4.4.5), (4.4.9), (4.4.10) (pp. 197-198), where the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) follows from the virtual stresses on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) being arbitrary, with an assumed displacement field. EP does not discuss how the supports are arranged. The theorem and the proof are not from the sources.

The proof assembled the condition at the supports from local pieces. The virtual fields from bumps in boxes crossing a face of the support showed that the mismatch is a rigid displacement on every rectangle. The fields around common sides showed that it is the same one on neighbouring rectangles, because otherwise it would differ by a rotation about the common side, on which the forces of the field would do work. The chain carried this displacement over the whole support. Subtracting it we got a field that fits the support. For the strip welded to a flat wall this is simply the field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), which is zero at the left end. For the tilted wall with \(\bar u_{\mathrm{x}} = \theta\,y\) the theorem gives a field that differs from it by a small rotation about the axis \(z\), with \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = \theta\). For the curved wall the equation does not hold, and the theorem says nothing about it.

What about supports in several separate pieces? Take the bar welded at both ends between two walls, as in figure 4.85. The bar is the box \(V = [0, L] \times [-b_2, b_2] \times [-b_3, b_3]\), the axis \(x\) points along the bar, the origin \(O\) is at the centre of the left end. The faces \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) are \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the other four faces, the mantle of the bar, are \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). By lemma 4.129 the mismatch at each end is a rigid displacement, \(\vek R_0\) at the left and \(\vek R_{\mathrm{L}}\) at the right, but possibly a different one at each. The ends have no common side, so a field around a side does not help. We need virtual fields that carry forces through the whole bar from one wall to the other. The difference \(\vek D = \vek R_{\mathrm{L}} - \vek R_0\) is a rigid displacement determined by six numbers, the three components of the vector \(\vek a_{\mathrm{D}}\) and the three elements of the antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\) above the diagonal, so we need six such fields. Physically these are virtual states in which the walls pull the bar apart, bend it about the axis \(z\) and about the axis \(y\), twist it, and shear it in the direction of the axis \(y\) and of the axis \(z\) (figure 4.105).

At the right end with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) the virtual force of the wall per unit area is \(\vek t = (\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\). We write its work on the rigid displacement \(\vek D\) with the total force \(\vek F\) and the total moment \(\vek M\) about \(O\) (definition 2.32). For a point \((L, y, z)\) of the right end \((\mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\,\vek r)\cdot\vek t = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}\,t_{\mathrm{i}}\), and since \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -W_{\mathrm{yx}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{xz}} = -W_{\mathrm{zx}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{yz}} = -W_{\mathrm{zy}}\) and the diagonal elements are zero,

\[(\mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\,\vek r)\cdot\vek t = W_{\mathrm{zy}}\,(y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}}) + W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,(z\,t_{\mathrm{x}} - L\,t_{\mathrm{z}}) + W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,(L\,t_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,t_{\mathrm{x}}) .\]

The brackets are the components \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) of the vector product \(\vek r \times \vek t\) (definition 2.30), the moment about \(O\) of the force on a patch. The work is therefore

\[\int (\vek a_{\mathrm{D}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\,\vek r)\cdot\vek t\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek a_{\mathrm{D}}\cdot\vek F + W_{\mathrm{zy}}\,M_{\mathrm{x}} + W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,M_{\mathrm{y}} + W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,M_{\mathrm{z}} , \tag{4.81}\]

with \(\vek F = \int \vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\) and \(\vek M = \int \vek r \times \vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\) over the right end. A field whose forces at the right end have only one of the six numbers \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(F_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{z}}\) different from zero therefore detects exactly one number of the rigid displacement \(\vek D\).

Corollary 4.131 Converse at the supports for a bar welded at both ends (obrat na podporah pri palici, privarjeni na obeh koncih)

Let the body be the box \(V = [0, L] \times [-b_2, b_2] \times [-b_3, b_3]\), let \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) consist of the faces \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) of the other four faces. Let the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be as in theorem 4.124, let the equation of virtual forces hold for every statically admissible virtual stress field, and let the prescribed displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) equal a field \(\bar{\vek u}\) whose components have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order on an open set containing the box. Then there is a displacement field \(\tilde{\vek u}\), defined at the interior points of the box, with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order, whose small strain tensor components equal \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every interior point and whose extension to the box (lemma 4.127) equals \(\bar{\vek u}\) at both ends.

Proof

We have to show that the rigid displacements of the mismatch at the two ends are equal. For each of the six numbers of a rigid displacement we build a statically admissible field that detects it.

1. The field and the mismatch.

  1. The set of interior points of the box is convex, hence star-shaped (definition 4.103), and by theorem 4.124, item 1, the compatibility equations hold in it. By theorem 4.106 there is a displacement field \(\vek u\) at the interior points with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order and with the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The box is a single cell, so by lemma 4.127 \(\vek u\) has one extension \(\vek U\) to the whole box.
  2. By lemma 4.129 the mismatch \(\vek U - \bar{\vek u}\) is the rigid displacement \(\vek R_0\) at the left end and the rigid displacement \(\vek R_{\mathrm{L}}\) at the right end. Let \(\vek D = \vek R_{\mathrm{L}} - \vek R_0 = \vek a_{\mathrm{D}} + \mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\,\vek r\).
  3. Let \(\delta\ten\sigma\) be a statically admissible virtual field and \(\vek t\) its virtual traction vector at the right end. By (4.80) the work on the mismatch, \(\int_{\mathrm{x}=0} (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n)\cdot\vek R_0\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{L}} \vek t\cdot\vek R_{\mathrm{L}}\,\mathrm{d}A\), is zero. As in step 8 of the proof of theorem 4.130, the work on the rigid displacement \(\vek R_0\) over the whole surface is zero too, where only the ends contribute, because \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\) on the mantle. The difference of the two equalities is \(\int_{\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{L}} \vek t\cdot\vek D\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), so by (4.81)
    \[\vek a_{\mathrm{D}}\cdot\vek F + W_{\mathrm{zy}}\,M_{\mathrm{x}} + W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,M_{\mathrm{y}} + W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,M_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 ,\]
    where \(W_{\mathrm{zy}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(W_{\mathrm{yx}}\) are elements of the matrix \(\mat W_{\mathrm{D}}\).

2. Six fields.

  1. Let \(\sigma_0 > 0\) be a number, \(T = q_{\mathrm{s}_1 \mathrm{s}_2}\) a bump of lemma 4.122 with \(0 < s_1 < s_2 < b_2^2\) and \(s_2 < b_3^2\), and \(a(y, z) = q_{-\beta_2,\beta_2}(y)\,q_{-\beta_3,\beta_3}(z)\) with \(0 < \beta_2 < b_2\) and \(0 < \beta_3 < b_3\). The six fields have the following components different from zero, together with their symmetric pairs,
    \[\begin{aligned} &\text{1:}\ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_0 , \qquad \text{2:}\ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_0\,y , \qquad \text{3:}\ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_0\,z , \\ &\text{4:}\ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -z\,T(y^2 + z^2) ,\ \ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = y\,T(y^2 + z^2) , \\ &\text{5:}\ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = x\,\frac{\partial a}{\partial y} ,\ \ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -a , \qquad \text{6:}\ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = x\,\frac{\partial a}{\partial z} ,\ \ \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -a . \end{aligned}\]
  2. The fields are statically admissible. The components of fields 1 to 3 are polynomials. The function \(T\) has continuous derivatives up to third order (lemma 4.122, item 1). The function \(f\) that assigns to a point of space with coordinates \((p_1, p_2, p_3)\) the number \(f(p_1, p_2, p_3) = T(p_1)\) has the partial derivatives \(T'(p_1)\), \(0\) and \(0\). These are continuous functions of the point, because \(T'\) is a continuous function of a single coordinate, as in step 2 of item 2 of the proof of lemma 4.122, so \(f\) is continuously differentiable in the whole space. The map \(\Phi(x, y, z) = (y^2 + z^2, 0, 0)\) has polynomials as components, so it is continuously differentiable in the whole space. By the chain rule (lemma 4.43) the function \(T(y^2 + z^2) = f(\Phi(x, y, z))\) is therefore continuously differentiable in the whole space, with the derivative \(2y\,T'(y^2 + z^2)\) with respect to \(y\) and \(2z\,T'(y^2 + z^2)\) with respect to \(z\). The function \(a\) is the product of a function of \(y\) alone and a function of \(z\) alone, which have continuous derivatives up to third order (the same lemma, item 1), so as in the proof of item 2 of the same lemma it has continuous partial derivatives up to third order. The components of all fields are therefore products and sums of continuously differentiable functions and are continuously differentiable in the whole space (lemma 1.81, corollary 1.69, item 1). The equilibrium equations with second index \(y\) and \(z\) contain only derivatives with respect to \(x\) of the components \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), which do not depend on \(x\), so they hold. The equation with second index \(x\) reads \(\partial(-z\,T)/\partial y + \partial(y\,T)/\partial z = -z\,T' \cdot 2y + y\,T' \cdot 2z = 0\) for field 4 and \(\partial a/\partial y - \partial a/\partial y = 0\) for field 5, and for the others it is zero at once. We also checked all of this with SymPy. On the faces of the mantle \(y = \pm b_2\) with normal \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \pm(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, 0, 0)\). This is zero, because there \(y^2 + z^2 \ge b_2^2 > s_2\) and so \(T = 0\), and because \(|y| = b_2 > \beta_2\) and so \(a = 0\). Likewise on the faces \(z = \pm b_3\).
  3. Forces at the right end. We write those of \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(F_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{z}}\) that are not zero. The integrals that vanish do so by the fundamental theorem of calculus, because the integrand is the derivative of a function that has the same value at both limits: \(\int_{-\mathrm{b}_2}^{b_2} y\,\mathrm{d}y = 0\), \(z\,T(y^2 + z^2)\) is by the chain rule the derivative with respect to \(z\) of the function \(\tfrac12\,\mathcal T(y^2 + z^2)\), where \(\mathcal T(s) = 0\) for \(s \le s_1\) and \(\mathcal T(s) = \int_{\mathrm{s}_1}^s T\) for \(s > s_1\). The function \(\mathcal T\) has the derivative \(T(s)\) at every number, for \(s > s_1\) by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 2, while for \(s < s_1\) it is constant and \(T(s) = 0\). At \(s_1\) both one-sided derivatives are zero, the right one by the same item of the theorem, because \(T(s_1) = 0\). So we use the chain rule as in step 5. Likewise \(y\,T(y^2 + z^2)\) is the derivative of \(\tfrac12\,\mathcal T(y^2 + z^2)\) with respect to \(y\). The functions \(\partial a/\partial y\) and \(\partial(y\,a)/\partial y = a + y\,\partial a/\partial y\) are derivatives with respect to \(y\) of functions that are zero at \(y = \pm b_2\), and \(z\,q_{-\beta_3,\beta_3}(z) = z\,(\beta_3^2 - z^2)^4\) is the derivative of the function \(-\tfrac1{10}\,(\beta_3^2 - z^2)^5\). So we get
    \[\begin{aligned} &\text{1:}\ F_{\mathrm{x}} = 4\,b_2 b_3\,\sigma_0 , \quad \text{2:}\ M_{\mathrm{z}} = -\sigma_0 \int y^2\,\mathrm{d}A , \quad \text{3:}\ M_{\mathrm{y}} = \sigma_0 \int z^2\,\mathrm{d}A , \\ &\text{4:}\ M_{\mathrm{x}} = \int (y^2 + z^2)\,T(y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A , \quad \text{5:}\ F_{\mathrm{y}} = -\int a\,\mathrm{d}A , \quad \text{6:}\ F_{\mathrm{z}} = -\int a\,\mathrm{d}A , \end{aligned}\]
    and for each field the other numbers are zero. For field 6 the computations are the same as for field 5, with \(y\) and \(z\) exchanged.
  4. All the numbers listed are different from zero. The integrals in them have continuous nonnegative integrands, which are positive at the point \((y, z) = (b_2/2, 0)\) for field 2, at the point \((0, b_3/2)\) for field 3, at the point \((\sqrt{(s_1 + s_2)/2}, 0)\) for field 4 and at the point \((0, 0)\) for fields 5 and 6. By definition 1.67 of continuity, applied to the integrand as a function of the point \((L, y, z)\) of the right end, the integrand is larger than half its value at such a point on a small square around it, and by the additivity and monotonicity of the integral (lemma 4.10, items 3 and 4, for a rectangle) the integral is positive.
  5. Step 3 with fields 1 to 6 gives in turn \(a_{\mathrm{D},\mathrm{x}} = 0\), \(W_{\mathrm{yx}} = 0\), \(W_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\), \(W_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\), \(a_{\mathrm{D},\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and \(a_{\mathrm{D},\mathrm{z}} = 0\). By antisymmetry \(\mat W_{\mathrm{D}} = \mat 0\), so \(\vek D = \vek 0\) and \(\vek R_{\mathrm{L}} = \vek R_0\).

3. The field.

  1. As in steps 13 and 14 of the proof of theorem 4.130, \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u - \vek R_0\) is the field we seek.

Source: The fields with linear \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) correspond to bending by a moment, field 4 to shear in a thin tube under twisting (SADD (9.6.8), PDF p. 269, BARBER (16.56)-(16.58), PDF pp. 261-262), and fields 5 and 6 to a cantilever with a force at its end, for which \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is proportional to \(x\,y\) (BARBER (5.36)-(5.38), PDF p. 75). The fields with bumps and the proof are not from the sources.

Let us test the corollary with numbers (figure 4.105). A steel bar of length \(L = 200\) mm has a square cross section \(20\ \text{mm} \times 20\ \text{mm}\), so \(b_2 = b_3 = 10\) mm. We take fields 2 and 3 with \(\sigma_0\,y/b_2\) and \(\sigma_0\,z/b_3\) instead of \(\sigma_0\,y\) and \(\sigma_0\,z\), so that the stress at the edge of the cross section is \(\sigma_0 = 1\) MPa. For field 4 we take \(s_1 = (4\ \text{mm})^2\) and \(s_2 = (8\ \text{mm})^2\) and multiply the bump \(T\) by a number such that \(T = \sigma_0/(6\ \text{mm})\) halfway between \(s_1\) and \(s_2\), at \(s = 40\ \text{mm}^2\). The shear stress \((\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}) = T\,(-z, y)\) is perpendicular to the vector \((y, z)\), so tangent to circles around the axis of the bar, and has the magnitude \(\rho\,T(\rho^2)\), where \(\rho\) is the distance from the axis. At \(\rho = \sqrt{40}\) mm \(= 6{,}32\) mm this is \(1{,}05\) MPa. For fields 5 and 6 we take \(\beta_2 = \beta_3 = 8\) mm and multiply the bump \(a\) by a number such that \(a = \sigma_0\) on the axis of the bar. SymPy gives at the right end

\[\begin{aligned} &F_{\mathrm{x}} = 400\ \text{N} , \quad M_{\mathrm{z}} = -1{,}333\ \text{N}\,\text{m} , \quad M_{\mathrm{y}} = 1{,}333\ \text{N}\,\text{m} , \\ &M_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}4085\ \text{N}\,\text{m} , \quad F_{\mathrm{y}} = F_{\mathrm{z}} = -42{,}27\ \text{N} . \end{aligned}\]

At the left end the force and the moment are opposite for every field, which we checked with SymPy, since the field is in equilibrium. For fields 5 and 6 this is not obvious at first sight. The forces at the ends, for field 5 \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = 42{,}27\) N at the left and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -42{,}27\) N at the right, form a pair of equal and opposite forces with lever arm \(L\), which would turn the bar, but it is balanced by the stress \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = L\,\partial a/\partial y\) at the right end, whose moment about \(O\) is \(L \int a\,\mathrm{d}A = 0{,}2\ \text{m} \cdot 42{,}27\ \text{N} = 8{,}454\) N m, and so \(M_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The work of field 1 on the rigid displacement \(\vek D\) is \(400\ \text{N} \cdot a_{\mathrm{D},\mathrm{x}}\), and the equation of virtual forces demands that it is zero. So the right wall must not move along the bar relative to the left wall by a displacement other than the one the strains of the bar give. The other fields demand the same for the remaining five numbers.

What about a general body with several separate supports, for instance a horizontal bar on three supports or a plate glued in several places? The idea is the same: we need statically admissible fields that carry a force and a moment in each of the three directions through the body between any two supports. For the bar we wrote them with formulas, because the bar is a box along which the forces can flow along the axis. For a body of arbitrary shape we get them only by solving problems with boundary conditions, in which we look for stresses in equilibrium with prescribed forces on part of the surface. Such problems are the subject of chapter 11, and we will come back to this question there. Until then we do not claim the general case.

Finally let us return to the ring of section 1.18.5. Let us repeat the setting. A thin steel ring with inner radius 40 mm and outer radius 60 mm lies in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), with its centre at the origin \(O\), and is 2 mm thick, from \(z = -c\) to \(z = c\) with \(c = 1\) mm. No support holds it and no force acts on it, so \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty, the whole surface is \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and the right side of the equation of virtual forces is zero for every field. The prescribed strains are those of subsection 4.7.9: every short fibre around the hole shortens by \(k = 0{,}001\), every fibre towards the centre keeps its length, and the right angles between the two kinds of fibres stay right. With the distance from the axis \(z\), \(\rho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), the components are

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -k\,\frac{y^2}{\rho^2} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,\frac{x^2}{\rho^2} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = k\,\frac{x\,y}{\rho^2} ,\]

and the other three are zero. In subsection 4.7.9 we saw that they satisfy the compatibility equations at every point of the ring, that the cut ring has a displacement field with these strains, and that the jump of this field across the cut \(y = 0\), \(x > 0\) is the small rigid displacement \(\mat W\,\vek r\) with \(W_{\mathrm{yx}} = 2\pi k = 0{,}006283\) and \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}006283\), where we subtract the displacement below the cut from the displacement above it. Since the jump is not zero, by lemma 4.120, item 3, the whole ring has no displacement field. Does the equation of virtual forces detect this?

Fields from bumps in small boxes do not help. For them, by the proof of theorem 4.124, the left side of the equation is the integral of the left side of a compatibility equation minus the right side, multiplied by the bump, and for the ring this is zero. We need a field that goes around the hole (figure 4.106).

  1. Let the stress function depend only on \(s = x^2 + y^2\), the square of the distance from the axis: \(\varphi = F(x^2 + y^2)\). Let \(s_1 = (45\ \text{mm})^2\), \(s_2 = (55\ \text{mm})^2\), \(\Phi_0 = 10\) N and
    \[F(s) = \Phi_0\,\frac{\int_0^{s} q_{\mathrm{s}_1 \mathrm{s}_2}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t}{\int_{\mathrm{s}_1}^{s_2} q_{\mathrm{s}_1 \mathrm{s}_2}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t} \qquad \text{for } s \ge 0 .\]
    The bump \(q_{\mathrm{s}_1 \mathrm{s}_2}\) is zero outside the interval \([s_1, s_2]\), so \(F = 0\) for \(s \le s_1\) and \(F = \Phi_0\) for \(s \ge s_2\), and in between \(F\) rises. The function is constant near the inner face of the ring, and constant with another value near the outer face.
  2. For \(s > 0\) the derivative of \(F\) is a multiple of the bump \(q_{\mathrm{s}_1 \mathrm{s}_2}\) (fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 2), which has continuous derivatives up to third order (lemma 4.122, item 1), so there \(F\) has continuous derivatives up to fourth order. For \(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\) let \(F^{(k)}\) be the derivative of \(F\) of order \(k\) and \(f_{\mathrm{k}}\) the function that assigns to a point \((p_1, p_2, p_3)\) of the open half-space with \(p_1 > 0\) the number \(F^{(k)}(p_1)\). The half-space is open, because every point at a distance less than \(p_1\) from a point with \(p_1 > 0\) has a positive first coordinate. The partial derivatives of \(f_{\mathrm{k}}\) are \(F^{(k+1)}(p_1)\), \(0\) and \(0\), continuous functions of the point as in step 5 of the proof of corollary 4.131, so \(f_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuously differentiable. The map \(\Phi(x, y, z) = (x^2 + y^2, 0, 0)\) has polynomials as components and maps the open set of points with \(x^2 + y^2 > 0\) into this half-space. By the chain rule (lemma 4.43) the function \(F^{(k)}(x^2 + y^2) = f_{\mathrm{k}}(\Phi(x, y, z))\) is therefore continuously differentiable on this set, with the derivative \(2x\,F^{(k+1)}(x^2 + y^2)\) with respect to \(x\), \(2y\,F^{(k+1)}(x^2 + y^2)\) with respect to \(y\) and zero with respect to \(z\). By the product rule (lemma 1.81) every partial derivative of \(\varphi\) up to third order is therefore on this set a sum of products of polynomials in \(x\) and \(y\) with the functions \(F^{(k)}(x^2 + y^2)\), \(k \le 3\), and it is continuous there (corollary 1.69, item 1). On the open set of points with \(x^2 + y^2 < s_1\), which contains the axis \(z\), we have \(\varphi = 0\). The partial derivatives of \(\varphi\) up to third order are therefore continuous in the whole space. The field (4.77) with this function is therefore by lemma 4.121 symmetric, continuously differentiable and in equilibrium without body force.
  3. By the chain rule, with SymPy, the components of the field are
    \[\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2F' + 4y^2 F'' , \qquad \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 2F' + 4x^2 F'' , \qquad \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -4\,x\,y\,F'' ,\]
    where \(F'\) and \(F''\) are evaluated at \(s = x^2 + y^2\). For \(s \le s_1\) and \(s \ge s_2\), \(F'\) and \(F''\) are zero, so the field is zero at all points of the ring that are less than 45 mm or more than 55 mm from the axis, that is, near the inner and the outer face. On the flat faces \(z = \pm c\) with normal \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) we have \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \pm(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}) = \vek 0\), because these components of the field (4.77) are zero. The field is statically admissible.
  4. At every point of the ring, with SymPy,
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = -k\,\big(2F'(s) + 4s\,F''(s)\big) .\]
    The integrand is zero for \(s \le s_1\) and \(s \ge s_2\), and in between it is a polynomial in \(s\), which we get by inserting the polynomials \(F'\) and \(F''\) into the formula. The integral over the ring is therefore the integral of this polynomial over the cylinder with radius 55 mm and height \(2c\), minus the integral of the same polynomial over the cylinder with radius 45 mm. Why may we compute it like this? Let \(Z_{\mathrm{r}}\) be the cylinder of the points with \(x^2 + y^2 \le r^2\) and \(|z| \le c\). The planes \(x = \pm\tfrac35\,r\) cut it into three bodies between two graphs, as the round bar was cut in section 4.2.6, so \(Z_{\mathrm{r}}\) is a set with volume and the integral over it is the sum of three iterated integrals (theorem 4.33 and corollary 4.68, item 1). The ring and the annular shells between the radii 40 mm and 45 mm, 45 mm and 55 mm, and 55 mm and 60 mm are closed and bounded sets whose boundaries lie in the boundaries of the cylinders \(Z_{40}\), \(Z_{45}\), \(Z_{55}\) and \(Z_{60}\). These boundaries have zero volume, so by lemma 4.26, items 1 and 2, these sets are sets with volume too. By additivity (lemma 4.32, item 4) the integral over the ring is the sum of the integrals over the three shells. On the first and the third the integrand is zero, on the middle one it equals the polynomial, and the integral of the polynomial over the middle shell is by the same item the difference of the integrals over \(Z_{55}\) and \(Z_{45}\). The iterated integrals over the pieces of the two cylinders, computed with SymPy, give
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 4\pi\,k\,c\,\Phi_0 = 4\pi \cdot 0{,}001 \cdot 1\ \text{mm} \cdot 10\ \text{N} = 1{,}257 \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{J} .\]
    Summing over a grid with NumPy gives the same number.
  5. The right side is zero, the left side is not. The equation of virtual forces fails for this statically admissible field.

So for the ring the equation of virtual forces demands more than the compatibility equations. What does the number tell us? Let us look at the field on the cut \(y = 0\), \(x > 0\). The part of the ring below the cut has the outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) there, and the virtual traction vector \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}})\) is the force with which the part above the cut acts on the part below it. On the cut \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -4\,x\,y\,F'' = 0\), so this is \((0, \delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, 0)\) with \(\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 2F' + 4x^2 F''\), the stress along the ring. Between 45 mm and \(50{,}31\) mm from the axis it is tension, at most \(0{,}905\) MPa at \(48{,}43\) mm, between \(50{,}31\) mm and 55 mm compression, at most \(0{,}993\) MPa at \(52{,}18\) mm, with SymPy (figure 4.106). The total force on the cut is zero, because \(2F' + 4x^2 F''\) is the derivative with respect to \(x\) of the function \(2x\,F'(x^2)\), which is zero at 45 mm and at 55 mm. The moment about the axis \(z\), however, is not zero. Since \(x\,\big(2x\,F'(x^2)\big)' = \big(2x^2 F'(x^2)\big)' - 2x\,F'(x^2)\) and \(2x\,F'(x^2)\) is the derivative of the function \(F(x^2)\), by the fundamental theorem of calculus

\[M_{\mathrm{z}} = 2c \int_{45\ \text{mm}}^{55\ \text{mm}} x\,\delta\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\mathrm{d}x = 2c\,\Big[2x^2 F'(x^2) - F(x^2)\Big]_{45\ \text{mm}}^{55\ \text{mm}} = -2c\,\Phi_0 = -0{,}02\ \text{N}\,\text{m} .\]

The field is therefore as if the ring were bent in its plane by a moment of \(0{,}02\) N m, which the cross section at the cut passes from one side of the cut to the other, without anything holding it from outside.

Let us compare the moment with the jump of the displacement across the cut, \(\mat W\,\vek r\) with \(W_{\mathrm{yx}} = 2\pi k = 0{,}006283\). The product is

\[\begin{aligned} -W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,M_{\mathrm{z}} &= -2\pi k \cdot (-2c\,\Phi_0) = 4\pi\,k\,c\,\Phi_0 \\ &= -0{,}006283 \cdot (-0{,}02\ \text{N}\,\text{m}) = 1{,}257 \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{J} , \end{aligned}\]

exactly the left side of step 4, not only in numbers but as an expression. In this example the left side of the equation of virtual forces is therefore the product of the rotation \(W_{\mathrm{yx}}\) between the two sides of the cut about the axis \(z\) and the moment \(M_{\mathrm{z}}\) that the field carries across the cut, with the opposite sign. The agreement has a reason, which we only describe here. On the cut ring the strains come from a displacement field. The computation of the proof of lemma 4.128, done on the cut ring, would turn the left side into the work of the virtual forces on both sides of the cut: on the lower side with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the force \(\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) acts on the displacement below the cut, on the upper side with outward normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the force \(-\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) acts on the displacement above the cut. Together this would give \(-\int (\delta\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\cdot\mat W\,\vek r\,\mathrm{d}A = -W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,M_{\mathrm{z}}\), because on the cut \(\mat W\,\vek r = (0, W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,x, 0)\). We do not prove this computation here. It would need the divergence theorem on the cut ring, which is not a body made of boxes, and the displacement field together with its first derivatives up to both sides of the cut, while lemma 4.120 gives only the limits of the displacement. So we also do not claim that for all strains of the ring the equation with such a field measures exactly the rotation \(W_{\mathrm{yx}}\), and we do not build fields that would carry a force or a moment about other axes around the hole. What is proved is what we wanted to know: the strains of the ring satisfy the compatibility equations at every point, the whole ring has no displacement field, and the equation of virtual forces fails for the field of figure 4.106.

The section has shown the following. Virtual forces are forces that we imagine in equilibrium, and their work on the true displacements is, for a truss, the sum of the products of the virtual axial forces and the true changes of length, and for a body the integral of the products of the virtual stresses and the true strains. We proved this by taking the scalar product of the equilibrium of the virtual forces with the true displacement, and for a body with the lemma on internal virtual work through the surface, used with the roles swapped. Since only equilibrium and geometry enter, it holds for every material. With a unit virtual force we got both parts of the displacement of the joint, \(2{,}721\) mm to the left and \(10{,}71\) mm down. For linear elastic materials we got from the principle that the true stress field has the smallest total complementary energy among all fields in equilibrium, and from this that a displacement is the derivative of the complementary energy with respect to a force. For the bracket with the post the smallest energy gave forces that equilibrium could not, and its condition was the condition that the changes of length of the bars fit together. Finally we showed that the converse holds too. If the equation of virtual forces holds for every statically admissible virtual stress field, the strains satisfy the compatibility equations, and in a connected and simply connected body we get from them a displacement field that fits a support in one piece, or the walls between which a bar is welded. For compatibility, self-equilibrating virtual fields made from stress functions that are nonzero only in a small box were enough, for the supports fields from boxes that cross a face of the support or the common side of two faces, and for the bar also six fields that carry forces from wall to wall. For the ring a field that goes around the hole showed that the equation demands more than the compatibility equations. In all computations of this section we multiplied the forces of one state by the displacements of another. In section 4.8 we take as the two states two true loadings of the same body and show that the work of the first loading on the displacements of the second equals the work of the second on the displacements of the first.
